s23b-s-081501-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Drugs harm the cardiovascular system in a handful of recurring ways: they damage myocytes, constrict coronary arteries, disturb ion channels (arrhythmias and QT prolongation), retain salt and water, or push blood pressure too far up or down. Recognizing the pattern and the mechanism is the Step 1 task.

Cancer therapy

DrugMain cardiovascular toxicityMechanism and features
Anthracyclines (doxorubicin, daunorubicin)Dilated cardiomyopathy, heart failureCumulative dose–dependent myocyte injury from topoisomerase IIβ–mediated DNA damage and iron-dependent free radical generation; can appear years after treatment and is largely irreversible. Risk is higher with older age, chest radiation, pre-existing heart disease and combined trastuzumab. Dexrazoxane, an iron chelator that also interferes with topoisomerase IIβ binding, reduces the risk.
Trastuzumab (anti-HER2 antibody)Fall in ejection fraction, heart failureBlocks HER2 (ERBB2) survival signalling in cardiomyocytes, causing dysfunction (stunning) rather than cell death; not cumulative dose–dependent and usually reversible when the drug is held.
Fluoropyrimidines (5-fluorouracil, capecitabine)Chest pain, ischemia, arrhythmiaCoronary vasospasm, often during or shortly after infusion, with normal coronary anatomy.
Immune checkpoint inhibitorsMyocarditis (can be fulminant), often with myositis or myasthenia-like weaknessT-cell–mediated inflammation; troponin rise, conduction block; treated with high-dose glucocorticoids.
VEGF pathway inhibitors (bevacizumab, multikinase inhibitors)Hypertension, thrombosisReduced nitric oxide production and capillary rarefaction.
High-dose cyclophosphamideAcute hemorrhagic myocarditisEndothelial injury; acute and dose-related.
Chest radiationPremature coronary disease, valve thickening, constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathyFibrosis of all cardiac layers, appearing years to decades later.
Anthracycline vs trastuzumab: anthracycline damage is cumulative, structural (myocyte loss on biopsy) and mostly permanent; trastuzumab dysfunction is not dose-related and recovers after the drug is stopped.

Sympathomimetic drugs of abuse

  • Cocaine blocks presynaptic reuptake of norepinephrine, dopamine and serotonin. Excess norepinephrine at α1 receptors constricts coronary arteries while β1 stimulation raises heart rate and contractility, so oxygen demand rises as supply falls. Cocaine also promotes platelet aggregation and thrombosis, accelerates atherosclerosis, and blocks fast Na+ channels (wide QRS, ventricular arrhythmias). Results: myocardial infarction (even in young people with normal coronaries), aortic dissection, stroke, arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy.
  • Amphetamines and methamphetamine release catecholamines from nerve terminals; chronic use causes a dilated cardiomyopathy and pulmonary hypertension.
  • Phencyclidine (PCP) is an NMDA receptor antagonist that also has sympathomimetic effects: hypertension and tachycardia with violent agitation, vertical or rotatory nystagmus and analgesia.
Why β-blockers are avoided in acute cocaine toxicity: blocking β2-mediated vasodilation leaves α1-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, which can worsen coronary spasm and hypertension.

Antihypertensives: class-specific adverse effects

ClassAdverse effectMechanism
ACE inhibitorsDry cough; angioedemaACE (kininase II) also degrades bradykinin and substance P; their accumulation causes cough and, more rarely, angioedema (more common in Black patients). Not IgE-mediated.
ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aldosterone antagonistsHyperkalemia; rise in creatinineLess aldosterone → less K+ secretion by principal cells of the collecting duct; loss of efferent arteriolar constriction lowers GFR, sharply so with bilateral renal artery stenosis. All are teratogenic in the second and third trimesters (renin–angiotensin system inhibitors).
Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, nifedipine)Ankle edema, flushing, headache, reflex tachycardia, gingival hyperplasiaEdema comes from precapillary arteriolar dilation that raises capillary hydrostatic pressure, not from salt retention; diuretics barely help, while adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB (which dilates the venous side) reduces it.
Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem)Bradycardia, AV block, constipation (verapamil), worsening of heart failure with reduced ejection fractionCa2+ channel block in nodal tissue and myocardium; additive with β-blockers.
α1 blockers (prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin)First-dose orthostatic hypotension and syncopeLoss of α1-mediated venous and arteriolar constriction on standing; start low and at bedtime.
MinoxidilHypertrichosis, marked salt and water retention, reflex tachycardia, pericardial effusionOpens ATP-sensitive K+ channels in arteriolar smooth muscle → hyperpolarization → relaxation; given with a β-blocker and a loop diuretic.
HydralazineReflex tachycardia, fluid retention, drug-induced lupus (slow acetylators)Direct arteriolar dilator (raised cGMP).
ClonidineRebound hypertension if stopped abruptlyCentral α2 agonist; sudden loss of sympathetic suppression.

Digoxin toxicity

Digoxin inhibits the Na+/K+-ATPase. Higher intracellular Na+ reduces Ca2+ extrusion by the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, increasing contractility; excess intracellular Ca2+ causes delayed afterdepolarizations. Digoxin also increases vagal tone. Toxicity gives nausea, vomiting, anorexia, confusion and visual changes (blurred, yellow-green tinted vision), and almost any arrhythmia combining increased automaticity with impaired conduction: frequent PVCs, bidirectional VT, atrial tachycardia with AV block, and AV block. Acute overdose causes hyperkalemia (pump inhibition throughout the body). Toxicity is precipitated by hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia, renal failure and drugs that raise digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein or renal clearance (amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine, clarithromycin).

Drug-induced QT prolongation

Most culprit drugs block the hERG channel (IKr): class IA and III antiarrhythmics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, azole antifungals, methadone, ondansetron, haloperidol and other antipsychotics, citalopram and tricyclic antidepressants. Tricyclics also block fast Na+ channels, widening the QRS, which is treated with sodium bicarbonate.

Other drug–heart interactions worth knowing: nitrates with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil) cause profound hypotension; thiazolidinediones and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs cause fluid retention and can precipitate heart failure; triptans and ergots cause vasospasm; fluoroquinolones carry a warning for aortic aneurysm and dissection; clozapine can cause myocarditis.

s23b-s-090101-ck-01.bodyHtml:
The aims in a patient with a sore throat are to find the minority with group A streptococcal (GAS) infection, to avoid antibiotics for the viral majority, and not to miss the red flags: a threatened airway, a deep neck abscess, or acute HIV infection presenting as pharyngitis.

Step 1: look for red flags

  • Stridor, drooling, inability to swallow saliva, a muffled ("hot potato") voice, trismus or a toxic appearance.
  • Neck swelling, pain on neck movement or unilateral palatal bulging.
  • Any of these redirect you to airway assessment and imaging (contrast CT of the neck) rather than a throat swab.

Step 2: decide whether testing is worth doing

Clinical scores built on fever, tonsillar exudate or swelling, tender anterior cervical nodes, absence of cough and age (higher in children 3–14, lower over 45) estimate the probability of GAS. They are used to decide whom to test, not to treat without testing.

  • Do not test when the illness is clearly viral: cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness, conjunctivitis or oral ulcers.
  • Children under 3 are usually not tested, because GAS pharyngitis and rheumatic fever are uncommon at that age.
  • Test with a rapid antigen detection test (RADT) or a molecular test when features suggest GAS.
ResultChild or adolescentAdult
RADT positiveTreatTreat
RADT negativeBack up with throat culture (RADT sensitivity is imperfect and rheumatic fever risk is highest in this age group)Culture back-up usually not needed

Step 3: treat GAS

  • First line: oral penicillin V or amoxicillin for 10 days, or a single dose of intramuscular benzathine penicillin G when adherence is doubtful.
  • Penicillin allergy without anaphylaxis: a first-generation cephalosporin (cephalexin).
  • Immediate-type allergy (anaphylaxis, angioedema): clindamycin, azithromycin or clarithromycin.
  • Treating within about 9 days of symptom onset prevents acute rheumatic fever. Testing household contacts without symptoms and "test of cure" swabs are not routinely recommended.
  • Analgesics (acetaminophen, NSAIDs) for pain; avoid aspirin in children.

Infectious mononucleosis: management

  • Suspect in an adolescent or young adult with marked fatigue, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical nodes and splenomegaly. A CBC shows lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes; aminotransferases are often mildly raised.
  • Confirm with a heterophile antibody test; if negative early in the illness, repeat it or send EBV-specific serology. Consider an HIV test (antigen/antibody plus RNA if acute infection is possible) when the heterophile test is negative.
  • Care is supportive. Avoid contact sports and heavy lifting for at least 3–4 weeks from onset, longer while the spleen is enlarged, because of splenic rupture.
  • Glucocorticoids are reserved for complications such as impending airway obstruction from tonsillar enlargement, severe autoimmune hemolytic anemia or severe thrombocytopenia. Antivirals are not used.
  • Amoxicillin given in error often causes a rash; record it but do not label the patient penicillin-allergic.

Peritonsillar abscess

  • Severe unilateral throat pain, fever, trismus, muffled voice, drooling, and a bulging soft palate with the uvula deviated away from the affected side.
  • Peritonsillar cellulitis (no pus collection) may settle with antibiotics alone; an abscess needs drainage (needle aspiration or incision and drainage) plus antibiotics covering streptococci and oral anaerobes (for example ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin). Contrast CT helps when the diagnosis is unclear or deeper extension is suspected.
  • Tonsillectomy is considered for recurrent abscesses.

Retropharyngeal abscess

  • A febrile young child who refuses to move the neck (especially extension), drools, and may have stridor or a muffled voice.
  • Lateral neck film: widened prevertebral soft tissue. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck defines an abscess.
  • Admit for IV antibiotics (for example ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin); surgical drainage for a large abscess, airway compromise or failure to improve.
  • Complications: airway obstruction, rupture with aspiration, internal jugular thrombophlebitis and descending mediastinitis.

Lemierre syndrome is septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein after pharyngitis, usually from Fusobacterium necrophorum: a young adult with sore throat, then neck swelling and septic pulmonary emboli. It needs IV antibiotics with anaerobic cover.

Diphtheria

In an unvaccinated or under-vaccinated patient (often after travel) with a gray adherent pharyngeal membrane and bull neck, treat on suspicion: isolate, obtain diphtheria antitoxin through public health, start erythromycin or penicillin, monitor the ECG for myocarditis, notify public health and give contacts prophylaxis and vaccination.

Croup

Diagnosis is clinical; radiographs are not needed for typical cases. Treatment is graded by severity:

SeverityFindingsManagement
MildBarking cough, no stridor at restSingle dose of oral dexamethasone; home with advice on return signs
ModerateStridor at rest, mild retractionsDexamethasone plus nebulized epinephrine (racemic or L-epinephrine); observe for several hours after epinephrine because its effect wears off
SevereMarked retractions, agitation or lethargy, hypoxemiaRepeated nebulized epinephrine, dexamethasone, oxygen, admission (often ICU); intubation with a smaller tube if failing
  • Keep the child calm and with the caregiver; agitation worsens obstruction.
  • Suspect another diagnosis if the child is toxic, does not respond to epinephrine, is outside the usual age, or has recurrent episodes (subglottic stenosis, hemangioma, foreign body, bacterial tracheitis).

Epiglottitis

  • A toxic, drooling child sitting in the tripod position is an airway emergency. Do not lie the child down, examine the throat with a tongue depressor, start an IV or send them alone to radiology, because agitation can provoke complete obstruction.
  • Secure the airway first, in a controlled setting (usually the operating room) with anesthesia and an ENT surgeon ready for a surgical airway.
  • Then obtain blood cultures and an epiglottic culture and start IV antibiotics: a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone), adding vancomycin when MRSA is a concern.
  • When Hib is confirmed, rifampin prophylaxis is given to household contacts if the household includes a child who is not fully immunized.
  • Adults present with severe odynophagia and muffled voice out of proportion to the pharyngeal findings; flexible laryngoscopy confirms, and many can be observed closely in an ICU with airway equipment ready.

Acute rhinosinusitis

Most episodes are viral and resolve within 7–10 days. Suspect bacterial sinusitis when there is:

  • persistent symptoms for 10 days or more without improvement;
  • severe onset: high fever (39°C or higher) with purulent discharge or facial pain for 3–4 consecutive days at the start; or
  • "double worsening": improvement followed by new fever or worse symptoms.
  • Viral rhinosinusitis: symptomatic care (saline irrigation, analgesics, intranasal glucocorticoid); antibiotics do not help.
  • Bacterial sinusitis: amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate (doxycycline or a respiratory fluoroquinolone with beta-lactam allergy in adults); watchful waiting is an option for mild cases in adults with reliable follow-up.
  • Imaging is not used for uncomplicated sinusitis. Order contrast CT (and MRI if needed) for orbital signs (periorbital swelling, proptosis, painful or limited eye movement, reduced vision), severe headache, altered mental status or cranial nerve palsies.

Invasive fungal sinusitis

In a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis, neutropenia, transplant immunosuppression or high-dose glucocorticoids, facial pain or numbness, nasal congestion and a black eschar on the turbinate or palate signal mucormycosis until proven otherwise. Management is urgent and combined: surgical debridement of necrotic tissue, IV liposomal amphotericin B started without waiting for culture, and reversal of the predisposition (correct ketoacidosis, reduce immunosuppression). Endoscopic biopsy shows broad non-septate hyphae.

Pertussis

  • Suspect in anyone with a cough lasting 2 weeks or more with paroxysms, whoop or post-tussive vomiting, and in infants with apnea or cyanotic spells.
  • Test with nasopharyngeal PCR (best in the first 3–4 weeks of cough) with or without culture.
  • Treat with a macrolide; azithromycin is preferred, and is the drug of choice in infants under 1 month (erythromycin is linked to infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis). TMP-SMX is an alternative in patients over 2 months who cannot take macrolides.
  • Give post-exposure prophylaxis (the same regimen) to household contacts and to people at high risk or in contact with them (infants, pregnant women in the third trimester).
  • Infants under about 4 months, or any infant with apnea, cyanosis or feeding difficulty, are admitted.
  • Prevention: Tdap during every pregnancy, ideally at 27–36 weeks, so that maternal antibodies protect the newborn; DTaP series for infants; Tdap for adolescents and adults.

Common cold

Supportive care only. Antibiotics do not shorten colds or prevent bacterial complications. Avoid over-the-counter cough and cold medicines in young children; honey can ease cough in children over 1 year (never under 1 year because of infant botulism).

Allergic rhinitis

  • Allergen avoidance where practical.
  • Intranasal glucocorticoid is the most effective first-line drug for persistent or moderate–severe symptoms, especially congestion; a second-generation oral or intranasal antihistamine is an alternative for mild or intermittent symptoms.
  • Leukotriene receptor antagonists are less effective (and montelukast carries a warning about neuropsychiatric effects).
  • Limit topical decongestants to a few days. Refer for allergy testing and allergen immunotherapy when symptoms persist despite medical therapy.

s23b-s-090102-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Management of pneumonia turns on three questions: where was it acquired, how sick is the patient (where to treat), and does the patient have risk factors for resistant organisms?

Diagnosis

Pneumonia is a clinical syndrome (fever, cough, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, crackles or bronchial breathing) confirmed by a new infiltrate on chest x-ray. Older adults may present only with confusion, falls or tachypnea. Measure oxygen saturation. In outpatients, microbiological testing is usually not needed. In hospitalized patients with severe pneumonia, or with risk factors for MRSA or Pseudomonas, obtain blood cultures and a sputum Gram stain and culture before antibiotics; test for influenza and SARS-CoV-2 when they circulate; consider pneumococcal and Legionella urine antigens in severe disease or when an outbreak or water exposure is suspected. Procalcitonin is not a reason to withhold antibiotics in proven pneumonia.

Where to treat

Severity tools support judgement. CURB-65 gives one point each for Confusion, Urea (BUN) above 19–20 mg/dL, Respiratory rate 30/min or more, Blood pressure under 90 systolic or 60 diastolic, and age 65 or older: 0–1 points usually allows outpatient care, 2 points favors admission, 3 or more points suggests severe pneumonia. Hypoxemia, inability to take oral drugs, and social factors also justify admission. Septic shock needing vasopressors or respiratory failure needing ventilation defines severe pneumonia and an ICU bed.

Empiric antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia (adults)

SettingTypical choices
Outpatient, healthy, no recent antibioticsAmoxicillin, or doxycycline; a macrolide alone only where pneumococcal macrolide resistance is low
Outpatient with comorbidities (heart, lung, liver or kidney disease, diabetes, alcohol use disorder, cancer, asplenia)Amoxicillin-clavulanate or a cephalosporin, plus a macrolide or doxycycline; or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) alone
Inpatient, not severeA beta-lactam (ceftriaxone, ampicillin-sulbactam) plus a macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone
Inpatient, severe (ICU)A beta-lactam plus a macrolide, or a beta-lactam plus a respiratory fluoroquinolone (not a fluoroquinolone alone)
Prior MRSA or Pseudomonas in the airway, or recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics plus local riskAdd MRSA cover (vancomycin or linezolid) and/or antipseudomonal cover (piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, meropenem), obtain cultures, and de-escalate when results allow

Treat for at least 5 days and until the patient is clinically stable (afebrile, normal heart and respiratory rate, adequate oxygenation, eating). Switch from IV to oral therapy once stable. Systemic glucocorticoids are suggested by current guidance for severe CAP requiring ICU care, not for non-severe pneumonia, and are avoided in influenza pneumonia. A follow-up chest x-ray is not routine; consider it at 6–8 weeks in smokers or older adults to exclude an underlying cancer if symptoms persist.

Fluoroquinolones carry tendon rupture, QT prolongation, aortic aneurysm, dysglycemia and C difficile risk, and they are active against M tuberculosis; an empiric fluoroquinolone can mask TB and delay diagnosis.

Hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia

Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) starts 48 hours or more after admission; ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) starts 48 hours or more after intubation. Organisms include S aureus (including MRSA), Pseudomonas and other resistant gram-negative rods. Obtain respiratory cultures (endotracheal aspirate in VAP), then start an antipseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime or meropenem), adding vancomycin or linezolid when MRSA risk is present (IV antibiotics within 90 days, high local MRSA rates, septic shock) and a second antipseudomonal drug of a different class for the highest-risk patients. Seven days is enough for most patients who respond. Prevention of VAP: head of bed raised 30–45°, daily sedation interruption and spontaneous breathing trials, oral care.

Aspiration pneumonia and lung abscess

Chemical aspiration pneumonitis is managed with suctioning and support; antibiotics are not needed unless pneumonia develops. For aspiration pneumonia, use the regimen for the setting (community or hospital); dedicated anaerobic coverage is added only for lung abscess or empyema. A lung abscess is treated with a beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor (ampicillin-sulbactam) or clindamycin, often for several weeks until the cavity resolves; most drain through the airway. Percutaneous or surgical drainage is reserved for failure. In a cavity that does not resolve, look for an obstructing cancer by bronchoscopy.

Prevention

Pneumococcal conjugate vaccination is recommended for all adults 50 and older and for younger adults with risk conditions; influenza vaccine every year for everyone 6 months and older; smoking cessation; and aspiration precautions (upright feeding, swallow assessment after stroke).

A pneumonia that does not improve after 72 hours of appropriate antibiotics: re-image for empyema or abscess, review cultures for resistance, and think of non-infectious mimics (organising pneumonia, cancer, vasculitis, pulmonary edema) and of TB or fungi.

s23b-s-090102-ck-02.bodyHtml:
Tuberculosis: diagnosis

Suspect active pulmonary TB in a patient with cough for more than 2–3 weeks, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats or weight loss, especially with risk factors (birth in a high-prevalence country, homelessness, incarceration, HIV, diabetes, immunosuppression). Get a chest x-ray. If TB is possible, place the patient in airborne isolation (single negative-pressure room, N95 respirators for staff) and collect three sputum samples (at least one early morning) for acid-fast smear and mycobacterial culture, with a NAAT on at least one, which also screens for rifampin resistance. Induced sputum or bronchoscopy is used when the patient cannot produce sputum. Test for HIV in everyone with TB. Isolation can stop when TB is excluded, or, for confirmed TB, once the patient is on effective therapy, improving and the smears have converted.

Tuberculosis: treatment of active disease

Drug-susceptible pulmonary TB is treated with an intensive phase of 2 months of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, followed by a continuation phase of 4 months of isoniazid and rifampin (6 months in all); longer courses are used for some sites and for cavitary disease with positive cultures at 2 months. Ethambutol can be stopped once susceptibility to the first-line drugs is shown. Give pyridoxine with isoniazid. Directly observed therapy supports adherence. Report every case to the public health department, which traces contacts.

Monitoring and adverse effects

  • Hepatotoxicity (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide): check baseline liver tests, and monitor them in people at risk (alcohol use, liver disease, HIV, pregnancy). If aminotransferases rise above 3 times the upper limit with symptoms, or above 5 times without symptoms, stop the hepatotoxic drugs; if needed, continue with non-hepatotoxic drugs; reintroduce the first-line drugs one at a time after the liver tests settle.
  • Visual acuity and color vision at baseline and monthly on ethambutol.
  • Drug interactions with rifampin (contraceptives, warfarin, antiretrovirals, azoles).
  • In HIV, start antiretroviral therapy within weeks of starting TB therapy and watch for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.

Latent TB infection

Screen with an IGRA or TST people who are at risk of infection or of progression (contacts of active cases, people from high-prevalence countries, healthcare workers, people with HIV, people starting TNF inhibitors, residents of congregate settings). A positive test needs a chest x-ray and symptom review to exclude active disease. If active disease is excluded, treat latent infection. Shorter rifamycin-based regimens are preferred for their completion rates: 3 months of weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine, 4 months of daily rifampin, or 3 months of daily isoniazid plus rifampin; 6–9 months of isoniazid is an alternative. Never give a single drug to someone with active TB: it selects resistance.

A positive IGRA does not mean active TB, and a negative IGRA does not exclude active TB. Diagnose active disease with x-ray and sputum testing.

Fungal pneumonia

Consider endemic mycoses when pneumonia does not respond to antibiotics in someone who lives in or travelled to an endemic area. Use antigen testing (urine/serum Histoplasma antigen), serology (Coccidioides), and culture or histology of sputum or tissue. Treat mild to moderate disease with itraconazole and severe or disseminated disease with liposomal amphotericin B, then step down to itraconazole. Immunocompetent patients with mild acute histoplasmosis or coccidioidomycosis often need only observation.

For invasive aspergillosis (neutropenic fever with nodules and a halo sign on CT, positive serum galactomannan), voriconazole is first line. ABPA is treated with systemic glucocorticoids, with itraconazole to reduce relapses. A symptomatic aspergilloma with significant hemoptysis may need resection or bronchial artery embolization.

Pneumocystis pneumonia

In a patient with HIV and a CD4 count below 200/mm3 with subacute dyspnea and diffuse ground-glass opacities, confirm by staining induced sputum or BAL fluid; serum beta-D-glucan is supportive. Treat with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 21 days. Add prednisone, started with the antibiotic, when the room-air PaO2 is below 70 mm Hg or the A–a gradient is 35 mm Hg or more; it lowers mortality. Alternatives for sulfa intolerance include IV pentamidine, primaquine with clindamycin, or atovaquone for mild disease (check G6PD before primaquine or dapsone). Prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is given when the CD4 count is below 200/mm3 and stopped after sustained recovery on antiretroviral therapy.

Influenza

Treat with an antiviral (oseltamivir) every patient who is hospitalized, severely ill or at high risk of complications (age 65 or older, pregnancy, chronic disease, immunosuppression, nursing-home residents, children under 2), whatever the time since symptom onset. Otherwise healthy outpatients benefit most when treatment starts within 48 hours. Vaccinate everyone 6 months and older every year; a live attenuated vaccine is avoided in pregnancy and immunosuppression.

RSV bronchiolitis in infants

Diagnosis is clinical: an infant with a few days of rhinorrhea, then cough, tachypnea, wheeze and crackles. Routine viral testing and chest x-rays are not needed. Care is supportive: nasal suctioning, hydration, and oxygen if saturation stays below about 90%; high-flow nasal cannula for rising work of breathing. Bronchodilators, glucocorticoids and antibiotics are not recommended. Admit infants with apnea, hypoxemia, poor feeding with dehydration or marked distress; young age, prematurity and congenital heart or lung disease raise risk. Prevention: a long-acting monoclonal antibody (nirsevimab) for young infants entering their first RSV season, unless the mother received the RSV vaccine during pregnancy.

Legionella

Suspect Legionella in severe pneumonia with high fever, diarrhea, confusion, hyponatremia or raised aminotransferases, or with exposure to contaminated water. Send a urine antigen (detects serogroup 1) and respiratory culture or PCR. Treat with a respiratory fluoroquinolone or azithromycin; report clusters to public health.

s23b-s-090101-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Most sore throats are viral (rhinovirus, adenovirus, coronaviruses, influenza, Epstein–Barr virus). The bacterial cause that matters most is group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes), responsible for about 20–30% of pharyngitis in school-age children and a much smaller share in adults. It matters because of its suppurative complications and its immune sequelae, not because the throat infection itself is dangerous.

Group A streptococcal pharyngitis

Organism

  • Gram-positive cocci in chains, catalase-negative, beta-hemolytic (complete lysis on blood agar).
  • Identified in the lab by bacitracin sensitivity and a positive PYR test; group B streptococci are bacitracin-resistant.
  • M protein is the main antiphagocytic surface protein and the antigen behind type-specific immunity; one-line exam link: antibodies against M protein cross-react with cardiac proteins in rheumatic fever.

Presentation

Abrupt sore throat, fever, tonsillar swelling or exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes and palatal petechiae, typically without cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness or conjunctivitis. Children may have headache, abdominal pain and vomiting. A sandpaper-like rash that spares the area around the mouth, with a strawberry tongue, indicates scarlet fever (pyrogenic exotoxin).

Complications

TypeComplicationTiming and key point
SuppurativePeritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess, cervical lymphadenitis, otitis media, sinusitisDuring or soon after the infection
NonsuppurativeAcute rheumatic feverAbout 2–4 weeks after pharyngitis; molecular mimicry (type II hypersensitivity); prevented by timely antibiotics
NonsuppurativePost-streptococcal glomerulonephritisAbout 1–3 weeks after pharyngitis (longer after skin infection); immune-complex disease (type III); not prevented by antibiotics

Rheumatic fever follows pharyngitis only, whereas glomerulonephritis follows pharyngitis or skin infection (impetigo). Antibiotics reduce the risk of rheumatic fever but do not reliably prevent glomerulonephritis.

Treatment, by mechanism

Penicillin V or amoxicillin (beta-lactams that bind penicillin-binding proteins and block peptidoglycan cross-linking) for 10 days, or one intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G. Group A Streptococcus has never developed clinically meaningful penicillin resistance. With penicillin allergy, a first-generation cephalosporin is used if the reaction was not immediate-type; macrolides or clindamycin (50S ribosomal inhibitors) are used after anaphylaxis, though macrolide resistance occurs.

Infectious mononucleosis

  • Epstein–Barr virus (a herpesvirus) spreads in saliva, infects oropharyngeal epithelium and then B cells, entering through CD21 (complement receptor 2).
  • The "atypical lymphocytes" on the smear are not infected cells: they are activated CD8+ cytotoxic T cells responding to infected B cells.
  • Infected B cells make polyclonal antibodies, including heterophile antibodies that agglutinate sheep or horse red cells (the monospot test). The test may be negative in the first week and is often negative in young children; EBV-specific antibodies (viral capsid antigen IgM) help then.
  • Classic triad: fever, exudative pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy, typically posterior cervical as well as anterior; plus fatigue, splenomegaly, mild transaminase rise and sometimes palatal petechiae.
  • Amoxicillin or ampicillin given for a presumed streptococcal sore throat commonly causes a pruritic maculopapular rash; this is not a true penicillin allergy.
  • The enlarged spleen can rupture, so contact sports are avoided during recovery (usually for at least 3–4 weeks).
  • EBV persists latently in B cells and is linked to Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease.

A mononucleosis-like illness with a negative heterophile test suggests cytomegalovirus, acute HIV infection or toxoplasmosis; acute HIV must not be missed in an adolescent or adult with risk factors.

Diphtheria (recognition)

Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a club-shaped gram-positive rod; disease is now rare where children are vaccinated. Pharyngeal infection forms a gray, adherent pseudomembrane that bleeds when scraped, with marked neck swelling ("bull neck"). The exotoxin inhibits protein synthesis (EF-2 inactivation), and its systemic effects are myocarditis with conduction block and cranial or peripheral neuropathy. Treatment is diphtheria antitoxin plus an antibiotic; prevention is the toxoid vaccine (DTaP in childhood, Td or Tdap boosters).

Deep neck space infections: anatomy that matters

Peritonsillar abscessRetropharyngeal abscess
WhoAdolescents and young adultsMostly children under 5 (retropharyngeal nodes regress later); adults after trauma or instrumentation
LocationBetween the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor muscleBetween the pharyngeal constrictors and the alar fascia, in front of the prevertebral fascia
SignsTrismus, muffled voice, uvula pushed to the opposite side, bulging soft palateFever, neck stiffness or pain on extension, drooling, sometimes stridor
OrganismsPolymicrobial: group A Streptococcus, oral anaerobes, Staphylococcus aureus

Behind the retropharyngeal space lies the danger space (between the alar and prevertebral fascia), which runs from the skull base to the posterior mediastinum. Infection that tracks down it causes mediastinitis, which is why deep neck abscesses are treated urgently.

s23b-s-090101-s1-02.bodyHtml:
The upper airway narrows most in young children, so a small amount of swelling causes a large rise in resistance: by Poiseuille's law, resistance rises with the fourth power of a falling radius. That is why croup and epiglottitis are emergencies in toddlers and why stridor is the sign to respect.

Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis)

  • Usual cause: parainfluenza virus (a paramyxovirus with hemagglutinin-neuraminidase); others include RSV, influenza, human metapneumovirus and SARS-CoV-2.
  • Age: about 6 months to 3 years, often in autumn and winter, after a day or two of coryza.
  • Inflammation narrows the subglottic trachea, the narrowest part of the young child's airway, giving a barking (seal-like) cough, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor, worse at night and with agitation.
  • Diagnosis is clinical. If a film is taken, the anteroposterior neck view shows a tapered subglottic air column, the steeple sign.

Epiglottitis (supraglottitis)

  • Classic cause: Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib). Its polyribosylribitol phosphate (PRP) capsule is the antigen in the Hib vaccine, conjugated to a protein carrier so that infants mount a T-cell-dependent response. Since routine vaccination, cases are fewer and also come from Streptococcus pneumoniae, S pyogenes and S aureus; adults are now a large share of cases.
  • Rapid onset of high fever, severe sore throat, drooling, difficulty swallowing, a muffled voice and a toxic child sitting forward in the tripod position; little or no cough.
  • The lateral neck film (only if the child is stable and accompanied by someone who can manage the airway) shows a swollen epiglottis, the thumb sign.
FeatureCroupEpiglottitisBacterial tracheitis
OnsetGradual, after coryzaHoursCroup-like start, then sudden worsening
AppearanceUsually non-toxicToxic, drooling, tripodToxic, high fever
CoughBarkingAbsent or minimalPresent, with thick secretions
Typical organismParainfluenza virusHib (unvaccinated), streptococci, S aureusS aureus
Imaging signSteeple sign (AP view)Thumb sign (lateral view)Ragged tracheal wall, membranes

Pertussis

Bordetella pertussis is a small gram-negative coccobacillus that attaches to ciliated respiratory epithelium. Its toxins paralyze cilia and, through pertussis toxin, raise cAMP in host cells; a one-line exam link is the striking lymphocytosis it causes.

StageDurationFeatures
Catarrhal1–2 weeksCoryza and mild cough; the most contagious stage and the least recognizable
Paroxysmal2–6 weeks or longerBursts of cough followed by an inspiratory whoop, post-tussive vomiting, well between attacks
ConvalescentWeeks to monthsCough gradually fades

Young infants often do not whoop; they present with apnea, cyanosis or gagging, and they carry most of the deaths. Immunity from the acellular vaccine wanes, so adolescents and adults get prolonged cough and pass the infection to infants. Macrolides (azithromycin) treat the infection and reduce spread, but they shorten the cough only if started early.

Rhinosinusitis

  • Viral rhinosinusitis (the common cold, mostly rhinovirus) is far more common than bacterial. Colored nasal discharge reflects neutrophils, not bacteria.
  • Acute bacterial sinusitis complicates a minority of colds; the usual organisms are S pneumoniae, nontypeable H influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis, the same trio as otitis media.
  • Invasive fungal sinusitis is a different disease of the immunocompromised:
    • Mucormycosis (Rhizopus, Mucor): diabetic ketoacidosis, neutropenia, glucocorticoids and iron overload treated with deferoxamine. Broad, ribbon-like, non-septate hyphae branching at wide (near right) angles invade vessels and cause infarction and black necrotic tissue on the turbinates or palate, with spread to the orbit, cavernous sinus and brain.
    • Aspergillus: narrow, septate hyphae with acute-angle branching, mainly in profound neutropenia.

Acidosis and high free iron favor Rhizopus, which explains its link to diabetic ketoacidosis and deferoxamine therapy.

Allergic rhinitis

A type I hypersensitivity reaction: allergen cross-links IgE bound to FcεRI on mucosal mast cells, which release histamine and leukotrienes within minutes (sneezing, itch, watery discharge), followed by a late phase driven by eosinophils and Th2 cytokines (congestion). Exam clues are pale, boggy turbinates, a transverse nasal crease, infraorbital darkening ("allergic shiners") and associated asthma or eczema. Intranasal glucocorticoids are the most effective single therapy; second-generation H1 antihistamines are less sedating because they cross the blood–brain barrier poorly.

Topical decongestants (alpha-agonists such as oxymetazoline) used for more than a few days cause rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa).

s23b-s-090102-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Lower respiratory tract infection means infection below the larynx: the trachea and bronchi (acute bronchitis, bronchiolitis), the lung parenchyma (pneumonia) and the necrotic sequelae of pneumonia (lung abscess). Pneumonia is the clinically important one: an inflammatory filling of alveoli or interstitium, usually by organisms that reach the lung by microaspiration of oropharyngeal flora or inhalation of droplets, less often by blood.

Host defences and how they fail

Normal defences are the cough and gag reflexes, the mucociliary escalator, secretory IgA, alveolar macrophages and surfactant proteins that opsonize organisms. Anything that blunts these raises risk: reduced consciousness (alcohol, seizures, sedatives, stroke) impairs airway protection; smoking and viral infection paralyze or strip cilia; chronic lung disease and cystic fibrosis trap mucus; loss of splenic function and hypogammaglobulinemia leave encapsulated bacteria unopsonized; neutropenia allows invasive moulds; and loss of CD4 T cells allows Pneumocystis, mycobacteria and endemic fungi to progress.

Patterns of pneumonia

PatternWhat fills which spaceTypical organisms
LobarExudate filling all alveoli of a lobe or segment; air bronchogramsStreptococcus pneumoniae (most common), Klebsiella, Legionella
BronchopneumoniaPatchy foci centered on bronchioles, often multilobarStaphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, gram-negative rods, anaerobes
Interstitial ("atypical")Inflammation of alveolar walls with little intra-alveolar exudate; diffuse reticular shadowingMycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, respiratory viruses, Pneumocystis
CavitaryNecrosis with an air-filled space, often with a fluid levelAnaerobes (abscess), S aureus, Klebsiella, M tuberculosis, endemic fungi

Stages of untreated lobar pneumonia

  1. Congestion (first day): vascular engorgement, alveolar fluid with many bacteria and few neutrophils.
  2. Red hepatization (days 2–3): alveoli packed with neutrophils, red cells and fibrin; the lobe is red, airless and liver-like.
  3. Gray hepatization (days 4–6): red cells break down; the fibrinopurulent exudate persists and the lobe turns gray-brown.
  4. Resolution: enzymatic digestion of the exudate, cleared by macrophages and coughing; normal architecture usually returns. Organization into fibrous tissue occurs if the exudate is not cleared.

Organism clues at the bedside

OrganismLaboratory recognitionClinical setting and clues
S pneumoniaeGram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci, alpha-hemolytic, optochin-sensitive; urine antigenMost common cause at every age beyond the neonate; abrupt fever, rigors, rusty sputum, pleuritic pain
H influenzaeSmall gram-negative coccobacilli; needs factors X and VCOPD and smokers
Klebsiella pneumoniaeEncapsulated, lactose-fermenting, mucoid gram-negative rodAlcohol use disorder, diabetes; thick "currant jelly" sputum; upper-lobe necrosis
S aureusGram-positive cocci in clusters, coagulase-positiveAfter influenza; injection drug use (septic emboli); cavitating, rapidly progressive
Pseudomonas aeruginosaOxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting gram-negative rodCystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, ventilated patients, recent broad-spectrum antibiotics
Legionella pneumophilaStains poorly with Gram stain (silver stain); grows on buffered charcoal yeast extract with cysteine and iron; urine antigen detects serogroup 1Contaminated water (cooling towers, hot tubs); high fever, diarrhea, confusion, hyponatremia, raised liver enzymes
M pneumoniaeNo cell wall: invisible on Gram stain, resistant to beta-lactams; cold agglutinins (IgM) may cause hemolysisYoung adults in close quarters (students, recruits); dry cough, headache, "walking pneumonia"; x-ray looks worse than the patient
Anaerobes (oral flora)Mixed flora, foul-smelling sputumAspiration with poor dentition or reduced consciousness; abscess
The atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Legionella) do not respond to beta-lactams: Mycoplasma has no peptidoglycan, and Legionella and Chlamydophila live inside cells. Macrolides, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones cover them.

Aspiration and lung abscess

Aspiration of gastric contents causes a chemical pneumonitis within hours (acid injury, often in a witnessed event during sedation). Aspiration of colonized oropharyngeal secretions causes aspiration pneumonia, which over 1–2 weeks may necrose into a lung abscess: a thick-walled cavity with an air–fluid level, from mixed anaerobes (Peptostreptococcus, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, Bacteroides) with or without streptococci. Gravity decides the site. Lying on the back, material runs into the posterior segment of the upper lobes and the superior segment of the lower lobes; upright, it falls to the basal segments of the lower lobes. The right side is favored because the right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical.

Same anatomy, different clinic: an inhaled peanut in a toddler and an aspirated bolus in a sedated adult both tend to enter the right main bronchus.

Acute bronchitis and bronchiolitis

Acute bronchitis in adults is almost always viral: cough for up to 3 weeks with normal vital signs and a clear chest examination. Antibiotics do not help. Bronchiolitis is a viral lower-airway infection of infants and children under 2, most often respiratory syncytial virus (RSV): necrosis of bronchiolar epithelium, mucus plugs and air trapping produce wheeze, crackles and tachypnea after a few days of coryza.

Hyponatremia, diarrhea and confusion with a lobar pneumonia that fails a beta-lactam: think Legionella and send a urine antigen.

s23b-s-090102-s1-02.bodyHtml:
Tuberculosis

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an aerobic, non-motile rod with a waxy, mycolic acid–rich wall that resists decolorization (acid-fast on Ziehl-Neelsen stain) and slows growth (culture takes weeks). It spreads by airborne droplet nuclei from people with active pulmonary disease.

Primary infection

Inhaled bacilli are taken up by alveolar macrophages, usually in the subpleural lower or middle lung, and multiply inside them because the organism blocks phagolysosome maturation. Bacilli travel to hilar lymph nodes. After 3–8 weeks, macrophages present antigen with IL-12, CD4 Th1 cells release interferon-gamma, and activated macrophages form caseating granulomas (epithelioid macrophages, Langhans giant cells, a rim of lymphocytes, central cheese-like necrosis). The subpleural focus is the Ghon focus; with the involved hilar node it is the Ghon complex, which may later calcify (Ranke complex). In most people the infection is contained but bacilli survive: latent TB infection, without symptoms or infectiousness. TNF-alpha holds granulomas together, so TNF inhibitors can unmask latent TB.

Progressive primary and reactivation disease

Young children and people with HIV may progress straight from primary infection to progressive pneumonia, lymph node disease, miliary spread or meningitis. In adults most active disease is reactivation, seeded in the well-oxygenated apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes: cough for weeks, hemoptysis, night sweats, fever and weight loss, with fibrocavitary upper-lobe disease on x-ray. Risk factors include HIV, diabetes, silicosis, end-stage kidney disease, malnutrition, TNF inhibitors and glucocorticoids, and recent infection.

Tests for infection

The tuberculin skin test (TST) and interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) detect a T-cell memory response; neither separates latent from active disease. IGRA is not affected by prior BCG vaccination, which makes it the better choice in BCG-vaccinated people. Active disease is diagnosed from sputum: acid-fast smear, nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT, which can also detect rifampin resistance) and mycobacterial culture with susceptibility testing.

Antituberculous drugs

DrugMechanismKey adverse effects
IsoniazidProdrug activated by mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase (KatG); inhibits mycolic acid synthesisHepatitis; peripheral neuropathy from pyridoxine (vitamin B6) depletion, so B6 is given with it; drug-induced lupus; inhibits CYP450
RifampinInhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymeraseOrange-red urine, tears and sweat; hepatitis; strong CYP450 induction (lowers levels of warfarin, oral contraceptives, many antiretrovirals)
PyrazinamideConverted to pyrazinoic acid; works in acidic phagolysosomesHepatitis; hyperuricemia and gout
EthambutolInhibits arabinosyltransferase (arabinogalactan synthesis)Optic neuritis: reduced acuity and red-green color vision
Slow acetylators (a genetic NAT2 variant) build higher isoniazid levels and have more neuropathy and drug-induced lupus.

Endemic mycoses

These dimorphic fungi grow as moulds in soil (infectious spores) and as yeasts or spherules at body temperature. Most infections are mild or silent; disseminated disease occurs mainly with impaired cell-mediated immunity.

FungusWhere and howTissue formClinical clues
Histoplasma capsulatumOhio and Mississippi river valleys; bird and bat droppings, cavesSmall (2–4 µm) yeasts inside macrophagesHilar adenopathy, calcified granulomas; disseminated disease in AIDS with pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, oral ulcers; urine/serum antigen
Blastomyces dermatitidisOhio/Mississippi valleys, Great Lakes; wooded soil near waterLarge yeasts with a thick double-contoured wall and broad-based buddingPneumonia plus verrucous skin lesions, bone and prostate involvement
Coccidioides speciesSouthwestern US (Arizona, central California), northern Mexico; dust after digging or earthquakesLarge spherules filled with endospores"Valley fever": pneumonia with erythema nodosum and arthralgia; dissemination to skin, bone and meninges

Mild disease often needs no treatment or an oral azole (itraconazole); severe or disseminated disease is treated with amphotericin B first.

Opportunistic lung infections

Pneumocystis jirovecii is a fungus that lacks ergosterol in its membrane. It causes pneumonia in people with CD4 counts below 200/mm3, on long-term glucocorticoids or after transplant: subacute dyspnea, dry cough, hypoxemia that worsens with exertion, raised LDH and bilateral ground-glass opacities. Silver stain of induced sputum or BAL shows cysts shaped like crushed ping-pong balls. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole blocks two sequential steps of folate synthesis (dihydropteroate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase).

Aspergillus fumigatus has septate hyphae that branch at acute angles. It causes a spectrum: allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis in asthma or cystic fibrosis (IgE-mediated and immune-complex hypersensitivity, eosinophilia, very high IgE, central bronchiectasis); aspergilloma, a fungus ball growing in an old cavity (often after TB) that may cause hemoptysis; and invasive aspergillosis in prolonged neutropenia, with vascular invasion and infarction.

Influenza is an orthomyxovirus with a segmented genome; hemagglutinin binds sialic acid and neuraminidase releases new virions. Reassortment of segments causes pandemic shifts; point mutations cause yearly drifts. Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir) stop viral release. Secondary bacterial pneumonia after influenza is classically from S pneumoniae or S aureus.

Cell-mediated immunity defends against intracellular organisms and fungi: TB, endemic mycoses and Pneumocystis cluster in HIV, TNF-inhibitor and steroid exposure. Neutrophils defend against moulds and bacteria: invasive aspergillosis clusters in neutropenia.

s23b-s-090201-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Solitary pulmonary nodule

A pulmonary nodule is a rounded opacity up to 3 cm across, surrounded by lung; a larger lesion is a mass and is treated as cancer until proved otherwise. Most incidental nodules are benign (granulomas, intrapulmonary lymph nodes, hamartomas, scars), but a nodule is also how early, curable lung cancer presents. The task is to estimate the probability of malignancy and match the workup to it.

Step 1: look for old images

The cheapest and most powerful test is a prior chest radiograph or CT. A solid nodule that has not grown for 2 years or more is very likely benign. A nodule that is new or growing raises the probability sharply. Subsolid (ground-glass or part-solid) nodules are the exception: slow-growing adenocarcinomas can look stable for years, so these are followed for longer, about 5 years.

Step 2: features that settle it without more tests

  • Benign calcification (diffuse, central, laminated or popcorn) or macroscopic fat (hamartoma): no further workup.
  • Very small solid nodules (under 6 mm) in a patient at low risk: no routine follow-up is needed; the chance of cancer is well under 1%.

Step 3: estimate risk and choose a path

Risk rises with age, smoking history, emphysema, family history, prior cancer, nodule size, spiculated margin, upper-lobe location and growth. Validated calculators combine these, but the logic is what is tested:

ProbabilityTypical pictureUsual approach
LowSmall, smooth, young never-smokerCT surveillance (or none if tiny)
IntermediateSolid nodule over 8 mm, some risk factors, no benign featuresPET-CT, and/or nonsurgical biopsy
HighSpiculated, growing, upper lobe, heavy smokerStaging, then surgical resection (diagnostic and therapeutic) if fit; biopsy first if surgery is risky or the diagnosis would change management
  • Surveillance means repeat low-dose CT at set intervals; the interval shortens as size and risk rise.
  • PET-CT helps for solid nodules over about 8 mm. False negatives: small nodules, ground-glass lesions, carcinoid tumors and mucinous adenocarcinomas. False positives: infection, active granulomas, sarcoidosis, rheumatoid nodules. PET-CT also stages the mediastinum.
  • Tissue: CT-guided transthoracic needle biopsy for peripheral nodules (main risk: pneumothorax); bronchoscopy with navigation or endobronchial ultrasound for central lesions and nodes. A nondiagnostic biopsy does not exclude cancer.
  • Surgery (wedge resection or lobectomy with lymph node evaluation) for high-probability nodules in fit patients.

Exam trap. Do not order PET-CT or biopsy for a nodule with benign calcification or fat, or for a nodule that has been stable for years: the answer is reassurance. Do not use sputum cytology or tumor markers to evaluate a nodule.

Screening is different from an incidental nodule. Annual low-dose CT is recommended for adults aged 50 to 80 with a 20 pack-year history who smoke now or quit within the past 15 years; nodules found on screening are managed with structured categories built on the same logic.

Benign masses of the upper airway

Hoarseness

Hoarseness that lasts beyond about 4 weeks, or sooner in a smoker or with red flags (stridor, hemoptysis, dysphagia, neck mass, weight loss), needs laryngoscopy before any empiric treatment such as a proton pump inhibitor. Imaging comes after visualisation, not instead of it.

LesionClueManagement
Vocal fold nodulesBilateral, voice overuse, child or teacherVoice therapy first; surgery rarely
Vocal fold polypUnilateral, after strain, smokerVoice rest and therapy; microlaryngeal excision if persistent
Respiratory papillomatosisChild, progressive hoarseness then stridorRepeated surgical debulking; adjuvant therapy in severe disease; protect the airway
Laryngeal carcinomaOlder smoker, persistent hoarsenessBiopsy at laryngoscopy; see malignant neoplasms

Nasal masses

  • Bilateral inflammatory polyps: intranasal corticosteroid spray and saline irrigation first; a short course of oral glucocorticoids for severe obstruction; endoscopic sinus surgery when medical therapy fails; biologics that block type 2 inflammation (for example anti-IL-4 receptor antibody) for severe recurrent disease. Long-term oral steroids are avoided.
  • Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease: avoid aspirin and nonselective NSAIDs; leukotriene modifiers help; aspirin desensitisation followed by daily aspirin, usually after sinus surgery, reduces polyp regrowth.
  • Polyps in a child: sweat chloride test for cystic fibrosis.
  • A unilateral mass in an adult (obstruction, bloody discharge): CT of the sinuses and biopsy, looking for inverted papilloma or carcinoma.
  • Adolescent boy with recurrent unilateral epistaxis and a posterior nasal mass: contrast CT and MRI, no office biopsy; embolization then endoscopic resection.

Pearl. Epistaxis in a teenage boy that is recurrent, unilateral and heavy, with nasal obstruction, is an angiofibroma until imaging says otherwise; routine anterior nosebleeds in children come from Kiesselbach plexus and are not associated with a mass.

s23b-s-090202-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Prevention and screening

Stopping smoking at any age lowers risk and improves outcomes even after diagnosis; offer counselling with pharmacotherapy (varenicline, nicotine replacement, bupropion) at every visit. Screening with annual low-dose CT (LDCT) lowers lung cancer mortality in high-risk adults. Under the US Preventive Services Task Force recommendation, screen adults 50–80 years old with a ≥ 20 pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years; stop once a person has not smoked for 15 years or has a health problem that limits life expectancy or the ability or willingness to have curative surgery. Begin with shared decision-making (false positives, incidental findings, radiation, overdiagnosis). Chest radiography and sputum cytology are not screening tests.

Pack-years = packs per day × years smoked. One pack a day for 22 years is 22 pack-years; half a pack a day for 30 years is only 15.

Presentation

Cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, weight loss, chest pain, a pneumonia that does not clear, hoarseness, or a paraneoplastic or metastatic presentation (bone pain, seizure, jaundice). Any adult smoker with hemoptysis or a nonresolving infiltrate needs a CT of the chest.

Evaluation: diagnose and stage together

  1. CT chest with contrast (including the upper abdomen for liver and adrenals).
  2. PET-CT for apparently curable disease, to find nodal and distant spread; brain MRI for stage II and above, any neurologic symptoms, and in small cell carcinoma.
  3. Tissue from the site that gives the highest stage, so one procedure both diagnoses and stages: endobronchial ultrasound-guided needle aspiration (EBUS) of enlarged or PET-positive mediastinal nodes; bronchoscopy for central tumours; CT-guided needle biopsy for peripheral ones; thoracentesis for an effusion (a malignant effusion is M1 disease).
  4. For nonsquamous NSCLC (and many squamous), molecular testing for targetable alterations (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, KRAS G12C, MET, RET, NTRK and others) and PD-L1 expression before first-line systemic therapy.
  5. Pulmonary function (FEV1, DLCO) before resection to predict postoperative lung function.

Treatment by type and stage

SituationUsual approach
NSCLC, early stage (I–II), fitAnatomic resection (lobectomy, or segmentectomy for small peripheral tumours) with lymph node sampling; adjuvant or perioperative systemic therapy for higher-risk disease
NSCLC, early stage, not fit for surgeryStereotactic body radiotherapy
NSCLC, locally advanced unresectable (stage III)Concurrent chemoradiation followed by consolidation immunotherapy (or targeted therapy when a driver is present)
NSCLC, metastaticTargeted therapy if a driver alteration is found (e.g., an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor); otherwise immune checkpoint inhibitor alone or with chemotherapy; palliative care alongside
SCLC, limited stagePlatinum-etoposide chemotherapy with concurrent thoracic radiation; surgery only for the rare small node-negative nodule
SCLC, extensive stagePlatinum-etoposide plus an immune checkpoint inhibitor
Early palliative care alongside cancer treatment in metastatic lung cancer improves quality of life and mood; it is not an alternative to treatment.

Oncologic emergencies and complications

  • SVC syndrome: CT with contrast confirms the obstruction. Without airway compromise or cerebral edema, get a tissue diagnosis first, because treatment depends on histology (chemotherapy for SCLC and lymphoma, radiation or stenting for others). Stridor, laryngeal edema or confusion call for urgent endovascular stenting. Elevate the head of the bed.
  • Hypercalcemia of malignancy: IV isotonic saline, calcitonin for a fast effect, and a bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid) or denosumab for lasting control.
  • SIADH: fluid restriction; hypertonic saline for severe symptoms (seizure, coma) with a limited rate of correction; treating the cancer is what ends it.
  • Malignant pleural effusion: therapeutic thoracentesis, then an indwelling pleural catheter or pleurodesis if it recurs.
  • Spinal cord compression from bone metastases: high-dose glucocorticoids and urgent MRI of the whole spine, then radiation or surgery.
Do not irradiate or stent an SVC obstruction blindly in a stable patient; a biopsy that shows small cell carcinoma or lymphoma changes treatment to chemotherapy.

s23b-s-090202-ck-02.bodyHtml:
Hoarseness

Most hoarseness follows a viral laryngitis and settles within 2–3 weeks. Visualise the larynx (flexible laryngoscopy, usually by an otolaryngologist) when hoarseness persists beyond about 4 weeks or sooner when there is a concerning feature: tobacco or heavy alcohol use, recent neck or chest surgery or intubation, a neck mass, hemoptysis, dysphagia, odynophagia, stridor or weight loss. Do not start empiric acid suppression, antibiotics or corticosteroids before the larynx has been seen in such a patient, and do not order CT before laryngoscopy.

The adult neck mass

In an adult over about 40, a firm neck mass that has persisted for more than 2–3 weeks without signs of infection is cancer until proved otherwise, most often a nodal metastasis from a head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. Evaluation:

  1. Full head and neck examination including flexible laryngoscopy (nasopharynx, oropharynx, larynx).
  2. Contrast-enhanced CT (or MRI) of the neck.
  3. Fine-needle aspiration of the node (with HPV/p16 testing in the oropharyngeal pattern, EBV testing when nasopharyngeal carcinoma is possible).
  4. Examination under anaesthesia with biopsies if the primary is not obvious; PET-CT for staging.
Do not start with an open excisional biopsy of a suspected metastatic squamous node: it can seed the neck and complicate definitive treatment. Fine-needle aspiration comes first. Antibiotics are appropriate only when the history suggests infection, with prompt reassessment.

Treatment principles

Early-stage tumours are treated with a single modality, surgery or radiation, chosen to preserve function (voice, swallowing). Locally advanced disease needs combined therapy: surgery followed by radiation (with chemotherapy for high-risk features) or chemoradiation with a platinum drug. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is treated with radiation and chemotherapy rather than surgery. HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer has a better prognosis. After treatment, follow-up looks for recurrence, second primaries (lung CT screening criteria still apply), hypothyroidism after neck radiation, dry mouth, dental decay and osteoradionecrosis (dental assessment before radiation). Continued smoking worsens outcomes.

PresentationThink ofNext step
Smoker, hoarse for 6 weeksGlottic carcinomaLaryngoscopy
40-year-old nonsmoker, painless cystic level II nodeHPV-related oropharyngeal SCCFNA with p16; examine tonsils and tongue base
Adult with new unilateral middle-ear effusion and a neck nodeNasopharyngeal carcinomaNasopharyngoscopy and biopsy
Hoarseness after thyroid surgery or with a lung massRecurrent laryngeal nerve palsyLaryngoscopy, then image the nerve's course
A neck mass in a child or young adult is usually reactive or congenital; the same mass in a 55-year-old smoker is usually metastatic squamous carcinoma.

s23b-s-090203-ck-01.bodyHtml:
New lung nodules in a patient with cancer

  • Multiple nodules in someone with a known, disseminating cancer: confirm with tissue from the most accessible site if the diagnosis or the tumor's markers would change treatment (for example, re-testing receptors in breast cancer), then systemic therapy.
  • A single new nodule: sample it. A smoker with a past melanoma or head and neck cancer may have a new primary lung cancer, which is treated differently.
  • Pulmonary metastasectomy can be curative in selected patients: the primary is controlled, there is no disease outside the lung, every nodule can be removed, and enough lung will remain. Classic examples are osteosarcoma and soft-tissue sarcomas, colorectal cancer and renal cell carcinoma.
  • Germ cell tumors and gestational choriocarcinoma are highly chemosensitive: even widespread lung metastases are often cured with chemotherapy, and serum markers (hCG, AFP) track response.

Malignant pleural effusion

Diagnosis

  1. Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis for any new, unexplained effusion large enough to tap: protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cell count, Gram stain and culture, and cytology. Draining a large volume at the same time relieves dyspnea.
  2. Apply Light criteria. Malignancy gives an exudate, often bloody and lymphocytic.
  3. If cytology is negative and suspicion remains, repeat it once; if still negative, thoracoscopic pleural biopsy (or image-guided biopsy of pleural thickening) has the highest yield and is the test of choice for suspected mesothelioma.
FluidPoints to
TransudateHeart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome
Lymphocytic exudateMalignancy, tuberculosis, post-cardiac injury, lymphoma
Neutrophilic exudate, low pH, low glucoseComplicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema
Bloody exudateMalignancy, pulmonary infarction, trauma
Milky, high triglyceridesChylothorax (lymphoma, thoracic duct injury)

A malignant effusion from lung cancer means stage IV (M1a) disease, and from any cancer it marks advanced disease; treatment becomes systemic and symptom-directed.

Treatment of recurrent symptomatic effusions

  • Asymptomatic effusions need no drainage.
  • The first large-volume thoracentesis also tests whether breathing improves and whether the lung re-expands.
  • If fluid returns and the lung re-expands: an indwelling tunneled pleural catheter (drained at home) or talc pleurodesis (through a chest tube or at thoracoscopy). Patient preference, prognosis and local expertise guide the choice.
  • If the lung is trapped (a visceral pleural rind stops re-expansion), pleurodesis fails because the pleural layers cannot meet: use an indwelling pleural catheter.
  • Repeated thoracenteses alone suit only patients with a very short life expectancy or slow reaccumulation.

Exam trap. Removing a very large volume at once (classically more than about 1.5 L) or draining against chest discomfort risks re-expansion pulmonary edema: cough, hypoxemia and new opacities in the re-expanded lung within hours. Stop when symptoms appear.

Mesothelioma

Suspect it with a unilateral effusion and nodular or rind-like pleural thickening in someone with occupational asbestos exposure (shipyards, insulation, construction, brake work, boilers). CT shows the pleural disease; fluid cytology is often nondiagnostic, so thoracoscopic biopsy is the usual diagnostic step. Treatment is given by specialised teams: systemic therapy (chemotherapy or immune checkpoint inhibitor combinations) for most, surgery in selected patients, and an indwelling catheter or pleurodesis for the effusion. The prognosis is poor; epithelioid histology does best. Exposure history matters for workers' compensation.

Superior vena cava syndrome

  • Diagnosis: contrast CT of the chest shows the obstruction, collaterals and the mass.
  • Stable patient (most cases): obtain a tissue diagnosis first (bronchoscopy, endobronchial ultrasound, mediastinoscopy, CT-guided biopsy, or a peripheral node), because treatment depends on histology: chemotherapy for small cell carcinoma, lymphoma and germ cell tumors; radiation for many non-small cell cancers. Avoid glucocorticoids before a possible lymphoma is biopsied. Elevate the head of the bed.
  • Life-threatening features (stridor or laryngeal edema, confusion or obtundation from cerebral edema, hemodynamic compromise): urgent endovascular stenting relieves obstruction within hours; radiation is an alternative; protect the airway.
  • Catheter-related thrombosis: anticoagulation, removal of the device if possible.

Goals of care

Most patients with a malignant effusion, lymphangitic spread or SVC obstruction have advanced disease. Alongside cancer treatment, address breathlessness directly (drainage, opioids for refractory dyspnea, oxygen only if hypoxemic), discuss prognosis and preferences early, and involve palliative care. Choose procedures that minimise time in hospital: an indwelling pleural catheter is managed at home, whereas pleurodesis usually needs an admission.

Pearl. SVC syndrome is rarely an emergency by itself; airway or brain involvement is what makes it one.

s23b-s-090201-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Benign respiratory tumors matter on the exam for three reasons: they cause symptoms by their location (hoarseness, nasal obstruction, epistaxis, stridor), a few carry a defined infectious or genetic cause, and some must be told apart from cancer. Most are recognised by where they sit and what they are made of.

Larynx

Vocal fold nodules and polyps

Both come from phonotrauma: repeated forceful vibration of the vocal folds injures the superficial lamina propria (Reinke space), which responds with edema, then fibrosis. They are reactive, not neoplastic, and have no malignant potential.

  • Nodules are bilateral and symmetric, at the junction of the anterior and middle thirds of the folds, the point of maximal contact during vibration. Typical patients are people who use their voice heavily: teachers, singers, coaches, children who shout.
  • Polyps are usually unilateral, larger and often hemorrhagic or gelatinous; a single episode of vocal strain can start one. Smoking and reflux add to the injury.
  • Polypoid corditis (Reinke edema) is diffuse, bilateral swelling of the whole membranous fold in long-term smokers; the voice drops in pitch.

Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis

Exophytic, wart-like squamous papillomas of the larynx caused by HPV types 6 and 11, the low-risk types that also cause anogenital warts. The juvenile form follows vertical transmission during birth and presents in early childhood with progressive hoarseness and then stridor; an adult form also exists. Histology shows fibrovascular cores covered by squamous epithelium with koilocytes. The lesions recur after removal because latent virus remains in nearby normal-looking mucosa; malignant change is rare. HPV vaccination is expected to reduce new cases.

Bridge. Low-risk HPV (6, 11) makes benign papillomas; high-risk HPV (16, 18) makes oropharyngeal and cervical carcinoma through E6 (p53 degradation) and E7 (Rb inactivation). A child with wart-like laryngeal masses points to the low-risk types.

Nose and nasopharynx

Inflammatory nasal polyps

Nasal polyps are edematous outgrowths of sinonasal mucosa rich in eosinophils, not true neoplasms. In adults they usually reflect chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, a type 2 (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) inflammatory disease; they are bilateral, pale, grape-like and insensitive to touch, and cause obstruction and loss of smell.

  • Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease: asthma + nasal polyps + respiratory reactions to aspirin and other COX-1 inhibitors. Blocking COX-1 removes the brake from prostaglandin E2, and arachidonic acid is shunted down the 5-lipoxygenase pathway, so cysteinyl leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4) surge. The reaction is not IgE-mediated. Selective COX-2 inhibitors are usually tolerated.
  • A child with nasal polyps has cystic fibrosis until proved otherwise (sweat chloride test). Primary ciliary dyskinesia also causes chronic sinusitis, but polyps are less typical.
  • A unilateral polyp in an adult is not routine: think of inverted papilloma (below) or a malignancy.

Sinonasal (inverted) papilloma

Arises from the lateral nasal wall, is unilateral, and grows inward: the squamous or transitional epithelium invaginates into the underlying stroma rather than outward. It is locally aggressive, recurs if incompletely removed, and is associated with squamous cell carcinoma in a minority of cases, which is why it is excised completely.

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

A benign but locally destructive, highly vascular tumor that arises near the sphenopalatine foramen in the posterior nasal cavity and occurs almost only in adolescent boys; hormonal influence is suspected. It presents with unilateral nasal obstruction and recurrent, often profuse, unilateral epistaxis. Histology: stellate fibroblasts in collagen with many thin-walled, slit-like vessels that lack a normal muscle coat, which explains why it bleeds so readily.

Exam trap. Never biopsy a suspected angiofibroma in the office: the bleeding can be torrential. Imaging makes the diagnosis; treatment is surgical, often after preoperative embolization.

Lung

Pulmonary hamartoma

The most common benign lung tumor. It is a disorganised mix of tissues native to the lung: mature hyaline cartilage, fat, smooth muscle and loose connective tissue, with clefts lined by respiratory epithelium. Despite the name, it is a true benign neoplasm with clonal genetic changes. It is usually a peripheral, well-circumscribed, slowly growing nodule found incidentally in middle-aged adults. On CT, fat within the nodule or popcorn calcification (clumped calcified cartilage) is essentially diagnostic.

Granulomas

Healed granulomas from histoplasmosis (Ohio and Mississippi river valleys), coccidioidomycosis (desert Southwest) or tuberculosis are the most common cause of a benign solitary nodule. They often calcify densely, centrally or in concentric layers, and may come with calcified hilar or mediastinal nodes.

What makes a nodule look benign or malignant

FeatureFavors benignFavors malignant
CalcificationDiffuse, central, laminated, popcornNone, or stippled/eccentric
MarginSmooth, well definedSpiculated, lobulated, irregular
FatPresent (hamartoma)Absent
GrowthSolid nodule stable for 2 years or moreGrowth on serial imaging
SizeSmallLarger (risk rises steeply above 8 mm)
PatientYoung, never smokedOlder, smoker, emphysema, prior cancer
Location—Upper lobe

Pearl. Bronchial carcinoid tumors are often listed with benign tumors because they grow slowly, but they are low-grade malignant neuroendocrine neoplasms that can metastasise; they are covered with malignant lung tumors.

s23b-s-090202-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Primary lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in both sexes. Most cases are caused by tobacco smoke; other exposures add risk (radon, asbestos, occupational carcinogens such as arsenic and chromium, prior chest radiation), and they multiply rather than simply add (asbestos plus smoking). Clinically the tumours split into small cell lung cancer (SCLC), about 15%, and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), about 85%, because the two behave and are treated differently. Metastases to the lung from other primaries are more common than primary lung cancer and are covered with the metastatic neoplasms.

Where the tumour sits predicts what it does

Tumours arising from large central bronchi (squamous cell, small cell, carcinoid) tend to cause cough, hemoptysis, wheeze localised to one side, and post-obstructive pneumonia or collapse. Peripheral tumours (adenocarcinoma, large cell) are often silent until they invade the pleura or chest wall, and are the ones found as nodules on imaging.

TypeUsual site and patientHistologyAssociations
AdenocarcinomaPeripheral; most common type overall and in people who never smoked, women and younger patientsGland formation, mucin; TTF-1 and napsin A positive. A lepidic pattern grows along intact alveolar walls (in situ or minimally invasive forms)Driver alterations (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, KRAS and others) that may be targetable; hypertrophic osteoarthropathy and clubbing
Squamous cell carcinomaCentral (hilar), strongly smoking-related, more common in menKeratin pearls, intercellular bridges; p40/p63 positiveCavitation; hypercalcemia from PTH-related peptide (PTHrP)
Small cell carcinomaCentral, almost only in smokers, fast-growing, metastasises earlySmall round blue cells with scant cytoplasm, nuclear molding, crush artifact; neuroendocrine markers (chromogranin, synaptophysin, CD56)SIADH, ectopic ACTH, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration and encephalomyelitis (anti-Hu)
Large cell carcinomaPeripheral; diagnosis of exclusionUndifferentiated large cells without glandular or squamous featuresPoor prognosis; occasionally hCG secretion with gynecomastia
Carcinoid tumourCentral endobronchial polyp; younger patients, not smoking-relatedWell-differentiated neuroendocrine nests; chromogranin positiveRecurrent pneumonia or hemoptysis from obstruction; carcinoid syndrome is uncommon and usually needs metastases
Two neuroendocrine tumours sit at opposite ends of one spectrum: the typical carcinoid is slow and often cured by resection, while small cell carcinoma is aggressive and usually already spread at diagnosis.

Molecular basis

Smoking-related cancers carry many mutations, especially in TP53 and (in squamous and small cell tumours) loss of RB1 function, which is nearly universal in SCLC. Adenocarcinomas in people who never smoked more often carry a single driver: activating EGFR mutations (a receptor tyrosine kinase), or ALK or ROS1 gene fusions that produce constitutively active kinases. These are inhibited by small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitors. KRAS mutations, common in smokers' adenocarcinoma, lock Ras in its GTP-bound active state. Immune checkpoint inhibitors block PD-1 on T cells or its ligand PD-L1 on tumour cells, releasing a brake on antitumour T-cell activity; their adverse effects are autoimmune (pneumonitis, colitis, thyroiditis, hepatitis, hypophysitis).

Paraneoplastic syndromes

  • Hypercalcemia: PTHrP from squamous cell carcinoma (low PTH, high calcium, low or normal phosphate).
  • SIADH: ADH from small cell carcinoma; euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine.
  • Ectopic ACTH: small cell carcinoma or carcinoid; hypokalemia, hypertension, hyperpigmentation and weakness often outpace the classic cushingoid look; high-dose dexamethasone does not suppress cortisol.
  • Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome: antibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels reduce acetylcholine release; proximal weakness that improves with repeated effort, reduced reflexes and autonomic symptoms (dry mouth); incremental response on repetitive nerve stimulation.
  • Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy: clubbing with painful periostitis of long bones, mostly with NSCLC.
  • Trousseau syndrome: migratory thrombophlebitis from a hypercoagulable state, especially with mucin-producing adenocarcinoma.
Hypercalcemia in a smoker with a lung mass is usually PTHrP from squamous cell carcinoma, not bone metastases, and the PTH is suppressed. Hyponatremia points the other way, to small cell carcinoma.

Local spread syndromes

Superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumours arise at the lung apex and invade the lower brachial plexus (C8–T1: shoulder and medial arm pain, weakness and wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles) and the cervical sympathetic chain (ipsilateral Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). Superior vena cava syndrome follows compression or invasion of the SVC by a central tumour (most often small cell carcinoma) or mediastinal lymphoma: facial and arm swelling, plethora and distended neck and chest-wall veins, worse when lying down. Other routes: recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarseness, more often on the left, where the nerve loops under the aortic arch), phrenic nerve (raised hemidiaphragm), pericardium (effusion) and pleura (malignant effusion). Common distant sites are brain, bone, liver and adrenal glands.

Horner syndrome localises along a three-neuron path; a Pancoast tumour interrupts the second (preganglionic) neuron as it crosses the lung apex toward the superior cervical ganglion.
