s23b-s-090202-s1-02.bodyHtml:
More than 90% of cancers of the oral cavity, pharynx and larynx are squamous cell carcinomas arising from the mucosal lining. Two separate pathways lead there.

Tobacco and alcohol pathway

Smoking and heavy alcohol use act synergistically. These tumours occur in older patients, carry TP53 mutations, arise through visible precursor lesions (leukoplakia, erythroplakia, dysplasia) and are surrounded by a field of mutated mucosa, so second primary tumours of the upper aerodigestive tract and lung are common.

HPV pathway

High-risk human papillomavirus, mostly type 16, causes a growing share of oropharyngeal cancers (tonsil and base of tongue). The viral oncoprotein E6 promotes degradation of p53 and E7 binds and inactivates Rb; the loss of Rb function raises p16 expression, so strong p16 staining is used as a surrogate marker. Patients tend to be younger, often have little tobacco exposure, frequently present with a painless, sometimes cystic neck node from a small primary, and have a better prognosis than with tobacco-related disease. HPV vaccination is expected to prevent many of these cancers.

Larynx

Laryngeal cancer is strongly tobacco-related. Glottic (vocal cord) tumours cause hoarseness early and, because the true cords have few lymphatics, rarely spread to nodes at first; this is the most common site and has the best prognosis. Supraglottic tumours present later (sore throat, odynophagia, referred ear pain) and spread to neck nodes early. Subglottic tumours are rare.

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

Strongly linked to Epstein-Barr virus, with high incidence in southern China, Southeast Asia, North Africa and Arctic populations; diet (salt-preserved fish) and genetic factors contribute. The common histology is nonkeratinizing (undifferentiated) carcinoma with a dense lymphoid infiltrate. The tumour sits in the fossa of Rosenmüller next to the eustachian tube opening, so a classic early sign in an adult is a persistent one-sided middle-ear effusion, along with a neck mass, nasal obstruction, epistaxis and cranial nerve palsies from skull-base spread. It is very radiosensitive.

FeatureTobacco/alcohol HNSCCHPV oropharyngealNasopharyngeal
AgentCarcinogens, TP53 mutationHPV-16 E6/E7EBV
Typical patientOlder, heavy smoker and drinkerYounger, light or no tobaccoHigher risk in East and Southeast Asian and North African ancestry
MarkerKeratinizing SCCp16 positiveEBV-encoded RNA in tumour cells
PrognosisWorse; second primaries commonBetterRadiosensitive
A new unilateral serous otitis media in an adult is not just a cold: look at the nasopharynx.
Persistent hoarseness in a smoker localises to the true vocal cord; early nodal spread localises to the supraglottis.

The lung is the organ most often involved by metastases, because it receives the whole cardiac output through the first capillary bed downstream of the systemic veins, and it drains a dense lymphatic network. Metastases are more common than primary lung cancers in surgical and autopsy series. The pleura is reached by direct invasion, lymphatic spread or seeding.

Patterns of spread

PatternWhat it looks likeTypical primaries
Hematogenous nodulesMultiple, well-circumscribed, round nodules of different sizes, peripheral and basal (where blood flow is greatest); large ones are called cannonball lesionsColorectal, breast, kidney, sarcomas, melanoma, germ cell tumors, head and neck, thyroid

EndobronchialTumor inside a bronchus: cough, hemoptysis, wheeze, collapse of the segment beyondKidney, breast, colon, melanoma
PleuralEffusion, pleural nodules or thickeningLung, breast, lymphoma, ovary, stomach
Hemorrhagic nodulesNodules surrounded by ground-glass halo of bleeding; hemoptysisChoriocarcinoma, angiosarcoma, renal cell carcinoma, melanoma

Pearl. Multiple round nodules in a patient with a known cancer are metastases until proved otherwise. A single new nodule is different: it may be a new primary lung cancer, especially in a smoker, so it is sampled.

Telling the primary from the biopsy

Morphology narrows the field and immunohistochemistry usually settles it:

MarkerPoints to
TTF-1, napsin ALung adenocarcinoma (TTF-1 also thyroid)
CDX2 with CK20 positive / CK7 negativeColorectal adenocarcinoma
GATA3, estrogen receptorBreast (GATA3 also urothelial)
PAX8Renal cell, ovarian and thyroid carcinoma
SOX10, S-100, melan-AMelanoma
PSA / NKX3.1Prostate
Calretinin, WT1, D2-40, CK5/6Mesothelioma (negative for TTF-1, CEA, claudin-4)

Two metastases worth special mention: choriocarcinoma (after a molar pregnancy, or from a testicular germ cell tumor) spreads early through the blood and produces hemorrhagic lung nodules with a very high hCG; histology shows sheets of cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast with no chorionic villi. Osteosarcoma of the metaphysis in adolescents most often metastasises to the lung, and its metastases can calcify because they make osteoid.

Malignant pleural effusion

Tumor on the pleura makes capillaries leaky and blocks lymphatic outflow through the parietal pleura, so fluid accumulates and is an exudate. Light criteria classify fluid as an exudate if any one of these holds: pleural/serum protein ratio above 0.5; pleural/serum LDH ratio above 0.6; pleural LDH above two-thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum. Malignant effusions are often bloody and lymphocyte predominant; a low pleural glucose and pH indicate a heavy tumor burden and a worse prognosis. Cytology is positive in roughly half to two-thirds of malignant effusions on the first sample.

Malignant mesothelioma

  • Cause: asbestos, especially the needle-like amphibole fibers (crocidolite, amosite), which penetrate to the pleura and persist. The latency is long, typically 30 to 40 years. Smoking does not add to mesothelioma risk (it does multiply asbestos-related lung carcinoma risk). Germline BAP1 variants predispose to mesothelioma, uveal and cutaneous melanoma and renal cell carcinoma.
  • Pathology: the tumor spreads along the pleura and encases the lung like a rind, with a recurrent hemorrhagic effusion. Histologic types are epithelioid (best prognosis), sarcomatoid and biphasic. Electron microscopy shows long, slender, branching microvilli (adenocarcinoma has short, stubby microvilli).
  • Pleural plaques (often calcified, on the parietal and diaphragmatic pleura) are the most common sign of past asbestos exposure. They are benign and do not turn into mesothelioma; they simply mark exposure.

Bridge. Asbestosis is interstitial fibrosis of the lower lobes with ferruginous (asbestos) bodies; the pleura gets plaques; the cancer risk is highest for bronchogenic carcinoma, then mesothelioma.

Superior vena cava syndrome

The SVC is thin-walled and low-pressure, so a mass in the right paratracheal or anterior mediastinum compresses it easily. Venous return from the head, neck and arms backs up: facial and arm swelling, plethora, distended neck and chest-wall veins (collaterals through the azygos, internal thoracic and epigastric systems), headache and dyspnea that are worse lying down or bending forward. Most cases are caused by cancer, above all small cell lung carcinoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma; indwelling catheters and pacemaker leads are the main benign causes.

Exam trap. Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumors cause Horner syndrome and C8–T1 pain; SVC syndrome is from a central mediastinal mass. Do not mix the two.

s23b-s-090301-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Diagnosis

Suspect asthma with episodic wheeze, cough (often nocturnal), chest tightness and dyspnea that vary over time and are triggered by allergens, exercise, cold air, viral infections, smoke or NSAIDs. The best initial test in anyone old enough to perform it (usually 5–6 years and older) is spirometry before and after a bronchodilator: an obstructive pattern with significant reversibility confirms it. If spirometry is normal and suspicion remains, perform a bronchoprovocation (methacholine) challenge, or document variability with serial peak flows. Chest x-ray is not needed for typical asthma; get one for red flags (fever, focal signs, hemoptysis, weight loss, atypical age).

Consider mimics: vocal cord dysfunction (inspiratory stridor, flattened inspiratory limb of the flow–volume loop during symptoms, normal oxygenation), COPD, heart failure, foreign body (children, unilateral wheeze), eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (asthma plus eosinophilia, neuropathy, sinus disease), and ABPA (asthma that worsens with central bronchiectasis and very high IgE).

Long-term management

Current strategy (GINA-style) places an inhaled corticosteroid in every step, because SABA-only treatment is associated with more severe exacerbations and asthma deaths.

SeverityPreferred approach in adults and adolescents
Mild, infrequent symptomsAs-needed low-dose ICS–formoterol (one inhaler as the reliever). Alternative: a low-dose ICS taken whenever SABA is used, or a daily low-dose ICS with SABA as needed.
ModerateDaily low-dose ICS–formoterol as maintenance and reliever (MART)
Moderate to severeMedium-dose ICS–formoterol MART; add a long-acting muscarinic antagonist
Severe, uncontrolledSpecialist referral; phenotype (blood eosinophils, FeNO, IgE, allergen sensitization); add a biologic (anti-IgE, anti-IL-5/5R, anti-IL-4Rα, anti-TSLP). Avoid maintenance oral corticosteroids where possible.

Before stepping up, always check inhaler technique, adherence, exposures (smoking, allergens, occupational agents), comorbidities (rhinosinusitis, GERD, obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, anxiety) and whether the diagnosis is right. Step down after about 3 months of good control. Every patient needs a written action plan and influenza vaccination; review exercise-induced symptoms (a reliever before exercise, plus a controller if control is poor).

Acute exacerbation

  1. Assess severity: ability to speak, respiratory rate, accessory muscle use, pulse oximetry, peak flow or FEV1 as % predicted. A silent chest, drowsiness, confusion, exhaustion, bradycardia or cyanosis signal life-threatening disease.
  2. Controlled oxygen to an SpO2 of about 93–95% in adults.
  3. Repeated short-acting β2 agonist (inhaler with spacer or nebulizer), plus ipratropium in moderate–severe attacks.
  4. Systemic corticosteroids early (oral is as effective as IV if the patient can swallow), usually 5–7 days in adults.
  5. Severe or poorly responding attacks: IV magnesium sulfate. Intramuscular epinephrine is reserved for asthma with anaphylaxis.
  6. Blood gas when severe. In an attack the patient hyperventilates, so PaCO2 should be low. A normal or rising PaCO2 means fatigue and impending respiratory failure.
  7. Endotracheal intubation for drowsiness, exhaustion, rising PaCO2 with acidosis or arrest. Ventilate with a low rate and long expiratory time to avoid dynamic hyperinflation (auto-PEEP), barotrauma and hypotension.

Discharge on an ICS-containing regimen (never SABA alone), with an action plan and follow-up within days.

Exam trap: antibiotics are not routine in asthma exacerbations, which are mostly viral. Chest x-ray is not routine either unless pneumothorax, pneumonia or another diagnosis is suspected.

Pearl: in pregnancy, continue controller therapy; uncontrolled asthma is more dangerous to the fetus than inhaled corticosteroids.

s23b-s-090301-ck-02.bodyHtml:
Diagnosis and assessment of COPD

Suspect COPD in an adult with chronic dyspnea, cough or sputum and exposure to smoke or dust. Post-bronchodilator spirometry with FEV1/FVC below 0.70 confirms persistent airflow limitation. Severity of airflow limitation is graded by FEV1 % predicted, but treatment choices depend more on symptoms (a dyspnea or symptom score) and on exacerbation history in the past year. Test every patient with COPD once for α1-antitrypsin deficiency (serum level, then phenotype or genotype if low), especially when young, a light smoker, or with basal emphysema or liver disease. Chest imaging excludes other disease and identifies candidates for lung-volume reduction; CBC shows polycythemia or anemia; blood eosinophils guide inhaled corticosteroid use.

Interventions that change outcomes

  • Smoking cessation is the single intervention that slows the decline of FEV1 and lowers mortality. Use counseling plus pharmacotherapy (varenicline, nicotine replacement, bupropion).
  • Long-term oxygen therapy (at least 15 hours a day) prolongs survival in stable patients with severe resting hypoxemia: PaO2 ≤ 55 mm Hg or SaO2 ≤ 88%, or PaO2 56–59 mm Hg with cor pulmonale, edema or hematocrit above 55%. It does not improve survival in moderate desaturation.
  • Noninvasive ventilation at home can help selected patients with persistent severe hypercapnia after a hospitalization.
  • Lung-volume reduction (surgical or endobronchial valves) for upper-lobe-predominant emphysema with poor exercise capacity; lung transplantation in selected end-stage disease.

Pharmacotherapy (GOLD-style concepts)

SituationApproach
All patientsA short-acting bronchodilator for relief
Few symptoms, no or one moderate exacerbationA single long-acting bronchodilator (LAMA or LABA)
More symptoms, or exacerbationsLAMA + LABA combination
Exacerbations despite LAMA + LABA and blood eosinophils ≥ 300/µL (or ≥ 100/µL with ongoing exacerbations)Add an inhaled corticosteroid (triple therapy)
Exacerbations with eosinophils below 100/µLICS unlikely to help; consider roflumilast (chronic bronchitis, FEV1 below 50%) or azithromycin (especially in former smokers), and newer type 2 biologics for eosinophilic disease in selected patients

ICS in COPD raises the risk of pneumonia, so it is not added without a reason. Theophylline is rarely used. Other essentials: pulmonary rehabilitation (improves dyspnea, exercise capacity and quality of life), vaccines (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, RSV for older adults, Tdap), inhaler technique, nutrition and weight (low BMI predicts mortality), and screening for anxiety, depression and osteoporosis.

Exacerbation

An acute worsening of dyspnea, sputum volume or purulence, usually from viral or bacterial infection or pollution; exclude pneumonia, heart failure, pneumothorax and pulmonary embolism.

  1. Controlled oxygen to SpO2 88–92%. Uncontrolled high-flow oxygen worsens hypercapnia, mainly by releasing hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (worse V/Q matching) and through the Haldane effect.
  2. Inhaled short-acting β2 agonist ± short-acting muscarinic antagonist.
  3. Systemic corticosteroids for about 5 days.
  4. Antibiotics when sputum purulence increases together with more dyspnea or sputum volume, or when ventilation is needed.
  5. Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation for acute hypercapnic respiratory acidosis (pH ≤ 7.35 with PaCO2 above 45 mm Hg) in a patient who can protect the airway. It lowers intubation and mortality. Intubate if NIV fails or is contraindicated (coma, vomiting, inability to clear secretions, hemodynamic instability).

Bronchiectasis and cystic fibrosis

Confirm bronchiectasis with high-resolution CT; then look for a cause: CBC, immunoglobulins, sputum cultures including mycobacteria, testing for ABPA (total IgE, Aspergillus-specific IgE) and, where suggested, sweat chloride or CFTR genetics, ciliary testing (nasal NO, ciliary biopsy). Treatment: airway clearance (physiotherapy, devices, hypertonic saline), culture-directed antibiotics for exacerbations, long-term macrolides for frequent exacerbations, and eradication when Pseudomonas is first isolated. ABPA is treated with systemic corticosteroids, with itraconazole as an adjunct or steroid-sparing agent.

Cystic fibrosis is usually found by newborn screening (immunoreactive trypsinogen, then CFTR variants) and confirmed by sweat chloride testing; adults may present with bronchiectasis, recurrent pancreatitis, chronic sinusitis or infertility from absent vas deferens. CFTR modulators (correctors plus potentiators) improve the function of misfolded or poorly gating channels in eligible genotypes and have transformed lung function and survival. Other care: airway clearance, inhaled dornase alfa and hypertonic saline, pancreatic enzymes, fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), a high-calorie diet, and screening for CF-related diabetes and liver disease.

Exam trap: in a COPD exacerbation with acute hypercapnic acidosis, the next step in an alert patient is noninvasive ventilation, not intubation and not more oxygen.

Pearl: an FEV1/FVC above 0.70 with a low FVC is not obstruction; think restriction, and confirm with lung volumes (TLC).

s23b-s-090301-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Asthma is chronic airway inflammation with variable, reversible airflow obstruction and bronchial hyperresponsiveness. The variability is the defining feature: symptoms and spirometry change over hours to weeks, and airflow improves with a bronchodilator or with time.

Immunopathology

In the common allergic (type 2-high) form, inhaled allergens are presented by dendritic cells to naive CD4 T cells, which become Th2 cells. Their cytokines drive the disease:

  • IL-4 (and IL-13): B-cell class switching to IgE. IgE coats mast cells through high-affinity FcεRI.
  • IL-5: eosinophil maturation, recruitment and survival.
  • IL-13: goblet-cell metaplasia, mucus hypersecretion and airway hyperresponsiveness.
  • Epithelial alarmins (TSLP, IL-33, IL-25) released by injured epithelium start and amplify the type 2 cascade.

Re-exposure cross-links IgE on mast cells. The early phase (minutes) is mediated by preformed histamine and newly made leukotrienes C4/D4/E4 and prostaglandin D2: bronchoconstriction, edema and mucus. The late phase (4–8 hours) is an eosinophil-rich infiltrate that sustains obstruction and hyperresponsiveness. Some patients have type 2-low (neutrophilic or paucigranulocytic) disease, often linked to obesity, smoking or later onset, and respond less to inhaled corticosteroids.

Pathology

  • Thickened subepithelial basement membrane (collagen deposition), smooth-muscle hypertrophy and hyperplasia, submucosal gland and goblet-cell hyperplasia, eosinophils in the wall.
  • Mucus plugs containing spiral casts of shed epithelium and mucus (Curschmann spirals) and needle-shaped crystals formed from an eosinophil protein, galectin-10 (Charcot-Leyden crystals).
  • Over years, remodeling can make part of the obstruction fixed.

Physiology and tests

Narrowed airways raise resistance (resistance varies with the fourth power of the radius), so expiratory flow falls: FEV1 and the FEV1/FVC ratio fall, air trapping raises residual volume, and in an attack the patient breathes at high lung volume. Spirometry with a bronchodilator shows reversibility (a rise in FEV1 of at least 12% and 200 mL is the usual threshold). When spirometry is normal between episodes, a methacholine (or mannitol) challenge shows hyperresponsiveness; a negative challenge makes current asthma unlikely. DLCO is normal or slightly high, which helps separate asthma from emphysema. Fractional exhaled nitric oxide and blood eosinophils are markers of type 2 inflammation.

Pharmacology by mechanism

ClassMechanismKey adverse effects / notes
β2 agonists: short-acting (albuterol) and long-acting (salmeterol, formoterol, vilanterol)Gs → adenylyl cyclase → ↑ cAMP → protein kinase A → smooth-muscle relaxationTremor, tachycardia, hypokalemia (K+ shifts into cells). Formoterol has a fast onset, so it can serve as a reliever. A LABA is never given without an ICS in asthma.
Inhaled corticosteroids (budesonide, fluticasone, beclomethasone)Bind cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor → suppress inflammatory gene transcription (e.g. via NF-κB inhibition), ↓ cytokines and eosinophilsOral candidiasis and dysphonia (rinse the mouth); at high doses, adrenal suppression and lower bone density. The main controller.
Muscarinic antagonists (tiotropium long-acting; ipratropium short-acting)Block M3 receptors on airway smooth muscle and glandsDry mouth, urinary retention, rarely acute angle-closure glaucoma
Leukotriene modifiers: montelukast, zafirlukast (CysLT1 receptor antagonists); zileuton (5-lipoxygenase inhibitor)Block leukotriene signaling or synthesisMontelukast: neuropsychiatric effects (agitation, sleep disturbance, suicidality). Zileuton: hepatotoxicity. Useful in aspirin-exacerbated disease.
Methylxanthine (theophylline)Nonselective phosphodiesterase inhibition (↑ cAMP) and adenosine antagonismNarrow therapeutic index; arrhythmias and seizures; cytochrome P450 interactions
OmalizumabAnti-IgE: binds free IgE so it cannot attach to FcεRIAllergic asthma with raised IgE; rare anaphylaxis
Mepolizumab, reslizumab (anti-IL-5); benralizumab (anti-IL-5 receptor α)Reduce eosinophils; benralizumab depletes them through antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicityEosinophilic asthma
Dupilumab (anti-IL-4 receptor α); tezepelumab (anti-TSLP)Dupilumab blocks IL-4 and IL-13 signaling; tezepelumab blocks an upstream alarminDupilumab can raise blood eosinophils transiently; tezepelumab works in type 2-high and type 2-low disease

Exam trap: a nonselective β-blocker (even timolol eye drops) can precipitate bronchospasm. Aspirin and other COX-1 inhibitors can provoke attacks in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (asthma, nasal polyps and NSAID sensitivity): shunting arachidonic acid toward leukotrienes is the mechanism.

Pearl: hypokalemia, hyperglycemia and tachycardia after repeated nebulized albuterol are expected β2 effects, not a new disease.

Bridge to the clinic: because inflammation drives the disease, an inhaled corticosteroid belongs in every step of modern asthma treatment; a reliever alone treats the symptom, not the cause.

s23b-s-090301-s1-02.bodyHtml:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is persistent, not fully reversible airflow limitation caused by chronic inflammation of airways and lung parenchyma in response to noxious particles, most often tobacco smoke (also biomass fuel smoke and occupational dusts). Two overlapping lesions produce it: emphysema and small-airway disease/chronic bronchitis.

Emphysema

Emphysema is permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole with destruction of alveolar walls and no obvious fibrosis. The central mechanism is a protease–antiprotease imbalance: smoke recruits neutrophils and macrophages that release elastase and matrix metalloproteinases, while oxidants in smoke inactivate α1-antitrypsin.

Centriacinar (centrilobular)Panacinar
CauseTobacco smokeα1-antitrypsin deficiency
Part of the acinusRespiratory bronchioles; distal alveoli sparedWhole acinus evenly
DistributionUpper lobesLower lobes

Loss of elastic tissue has two consequences. Lung recoil falls, so compliance rises and the lung sits at a higher volume (raised TLC, RV and FRC; hyperinflated, flattened diaphragms). Loss of the radial traction that holds small airways open lets them collapse during forced expiration: the point along the airway at which surrounding pressure equals intraluminal pressure moves toward the alveoli, and flow becomes limited no matter how hard the patient blows. Pursed-lip breathing raises airway pressure and delays this collapse. Destroyed alveolar–capillary surface lowers the DLCO.

α1-antitrypsin deficiency

α1-antitrypsin is a serine protease inhibitor made in the liver. In the common severe genotype (PiZZ, a single amino-acid substitution), the protein misfolds and polymerizes inside the endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes. Too little reaches the lung (unopposed neutrophil elastase → early panacinar emphysema, worse with smoking), and the retained protein injures the liver (PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules; neonatal cholestasis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma). Inheritance is codominant. A null variant causes lung disease without liver disease because no protein is made to be retained.

Chronic bronchitis

Clinically, a productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years. Pathology: hypertrophy and hyperplasia of submucosal mucous glands (a larger gland layer relative to wall thickness, the Reid index, normally below about 0.4), goblet-cell hyperplasia, squamous metaplasia and small-airway inflammation and fibrosis. Mucus plugging and V/Q mismatch cause hypoxemia and, with time, hypercapnia, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

PFT pattern

Obstruction: FEV1 ↓↓, FVC ↓ (less), FEV1/FVC ↓ (below 0.70 after a bronchodilator defines COPD), TLC normal or ↑, RV ↑. DLCO is low in emphysema and near normal in pure chronic bronchitis or asthma.

Bronchiectasis

Bronchiectasis is permanent dilation of bronchi from a cycle of infection, inflammation and impaired clearance that destroys muscle and elastic tissue in the wall. Patients have daily cough with large volumes of purulent sputum, recurrent infections (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Haemophilus influenzae, nontuberculous mycobacteria) and hemoptysis. CT shows airways wider than the accompanying artery (signet-ring sign), lack of tapering and "tram tracks".

  • Cystic fibrosis: autosomal recessive variants of CFTR, an ATP-gated chloride channel. The most common variant (F508del) misfolds, is degraded in the endoplasmic reticulum and never reaches the apical membrane. In airways, poor chloride secretion and increased sodium absorption dehydrate the surface liquid, so mucus is thick and clearance fails. In the sweat duct, CFTR normally reabsorbs chloride; loss of function leaves sweat salty (high sweat chloride). Other features: pancreatic insufficiency with fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, meconium ileus, distal intestinal obstruction, biliary cirrhosis, and congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens.
  • Primary ciliary dyskinesia: autosomal recessive defects in axonemal dynein arms (or other ciliary proteins). Chronic sinusitis, otitis, bronchiectasis, male infertility (immotile sperm), reduced female fertility and ectopic pregnancy; about half have situs inversus (Kartagener syndrome). Nasal nitric oxide is low.
  • Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis: type I (IgE) and type III (immune-complex) hypersensitivity to Aspergillus colonizing the airways of a person with asthma or cystic fibrosis; central bronchiectasis, very high total IgE, eosinophilia and fleeting infiltrates.
  • Others: post-infectious (measles, pertussis, tuberculosis), localized obstruction by tumor or foreign body, immunodeficiency (hypogammaglobulinemia).

Exam trap: a patient with cystic fibrosis whose sweat chloride is high has a reabsorption defect in the duct, not excess secretion; the secretory coil works normally.

s23b-s-090401-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Approach to suspected interstitial lung disease

Think of ILD in any adult with months of exertional dyspnea and dry cough, fine inspiratory crackles at the bases, clubbing, or exertional desaturation, especially when the chest radiograph shows reticular opacities or reduced lung volumes. The work-up answers three questions: is there interstitial disease, is there a cause, and how severe is it?

  1. History: occupation and hobbies (birds, feather bedding, moldy environments, hot tubs, dusts), medications (amiodarone, nitrofurantoin, methotrexate, bleomycin, checkpoint inhibitors), radiation, smoking, connective tissue disease symptoms (Raynaud phenomenon, arthritis, rash, dysphagia, proximal weakness), family history.
  2. Pulmonary function tests: restriction (low TLC) with a low DLCO; a 6-minute walk test for exertional desaturation.
  3. High-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest: the key test. A definite UIP pattern (subpleural, basal reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis) in the right clinical setting with no alternative cause is enough to diagnose IPF without a biopsy.
  4. Serology for connective tissue disease: ANA, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP, and myositis antibodies when suggested.
  5. Bronchoalveolar lavage or biopsy when HRCT is indeterminate; decisions are made in a multidisciplinary discussion.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: management

  • Antifibrotic therapy: nintedanib (a tyrosine kinase inhibitor; diarrhea and raised aminotransferases) or pirfenidone (photosensitivity rash, nausea, raised aminotransferases). Both slow the decline in FVC; neither reverses fibrosis. Nintedanib is also used for other progressive fibrosing ILDs.
  • Avoid glucocorticoids and the old combination of prednisone, azathioprine and N-acetylcysteine for stable IPF; it increased deaths and hospitalizations.
  • Supportive: supplemental oxygen for resting or exertional hypoxemia, pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, RSV for eligible older adults), treatment of reflux when symptomatic, smoking cessation.
  • Lung transplant referral early for suitable candidates; it is the only treatment that improves survival substantially. Median survival without transplant is about 3–5 years from diagnosis.
  • Acute exacerbation: sudden worsening over less than a month with new bilateral ground-glass opacities after infection, heart failure and pulmonary embolism are excluded; prognosis is poor; high-dose glucocorticoids are often used despite limited evidence.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis and smoking-related ILD

The most important intervention in hypersensitivity pneumonitis is identifying and removing the antigen (rehoming birds, replacing feather bedding, remediating mold, changing work duties). Systemic glucocorticoids are added for severe or progressive disease. Chronic fibrotic disease has a worse outlook, especially when the antigen is never found. RB-ILD and DIP improve chiefly with smoking cessation.

Connective tissue disease–associated ILD

Systemic sclerosis (anti-topoisomerase I/Scl-70), dermatomyositis and the antisynthetase syndrome (anti-Jo-1: ILD, myositis, arthritis, mechanic's hands, Raynaud) and rheumatoid arthritis are the commonest. The pattern is often NSIP. Treatment is immunosuppression (mycophenolate is commonly used), with nintedanib added for progressive fibrosis. Screen patients with new systemic sclerosis with PFTs including DLCO and HRCT.

Reading the HRCT: common patterns

HRCT patternKey featuresThink of
UIPBasal, subpleural reticulation, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis; little ground glassIPF; also rheumatoid arthritis, chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, asbestosis
NSIPSymmetric basal ground glass and fine reticulation, often with subpleural sparingSystemic sclerosis, myositis, drugs
Fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitisUpper- or mid-zone fibrosis, centrilobular nodules, mosaic attenuation with air trapping on expirationBird, mold or other organic antigen
Perilymphatic nodules with hilar nodesNodules along fissures and bronchovascular bundles, symmetric hilar adenopathySarcoidosis, berylliosis
Organizing pneumoniaPatchy, migratory peripheral or peribronchial consolidation, "reversed halo"Cryptogenic, drugs, connective tissue disease

Monitoring and prognosis

Disease activity is followed with symptoms, forced vital capacity, DLCO and the 6-minute walk test every 3–6 months. A fall in FVC of 10% or more (or 5–10% with worse symptoms or imaging) marks progression and predicts mortality. Complications include pulmonary hypertension (suspect when DLCO falls out of proportion to FVC or exertional desaturation worsens; screen with echocardiography), lung cancer (higher incidence in IPF), and acute exacerbations. Discuss goals of care and palliation of breathlessness and cough as disease advances; low-dose opioids can ease refractory dyspnea.

Clubbing is common in IPF and asbestosis but is not a feature of sarcoidosis, uncomplicated COPD or hypersensitivity pneumonitis; in a smoker with new clubbing, look for lung cancer.

Occupational lung disease: what the clinician does

  • Take the exposure history for every patient with ILD or unexplained pleural disease. Latency is long: asbestosis appears 15–30 years after exposure and mesothelioma often 30–40 years.
  • Asbestos-related disease: pleural plaques alone need no treatment and do not progress to cancer, but they confirm exposure. The most effective way to lower lung cancer risk is smoking cessation, because asbestos and tobacco multiply each other's risk. Offer lung cancer screening with annual low-dose CT to those who meet age and smoking criteria. New unilateral effusion, chest pain or weight loss raises concern for mesothelioma (pleural biopsy, usually by thoracoscopy).
  • Silicosis: remove from exposure; screen for latent tuberculosis (interferon-γ release assay or tuberculin skin test) and treat latent infection if positive, because silicosis raises the risk of active TB substantially. Watch for accelerated disease in engineered-stone workers. There is no drug that reverses silicosis; transplant for end-stage disease.
  • Chronic beryllium disease: confirm with the beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test plus granulomas on biopsy; remove from exposure; glucocorticoids for impaired function.
  • Prevention and reporting: dust control and respiratory protection, workplace surveillance with spirometry and imaging, and workers' compensation documentation are part of care. Notify public-health or occupational authorities where required.

Sarcoidosis: diagnosis and treatment

Diagnosis requires a compatible picture, noncaseating granulomas in tissue, and exclusion of infection (mycobacteria, fungi) and other granulomatous causes. The least invasive accessible tissue is sampled first: a skin lesion, peripheral node, or mediastinal nodes by endobronchial ultrasound–guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA). Löfgren syndrome (fever, erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar adenopathy and ankle arthritis) is distinctive enough to be diagnosed clinically and usually resolves on its own; NSAIDs relieve the joint pain.

All patients should have an ECG (heart block), eye examination (uveitis), serum calcium and creatinine, liver tests, and PFTs. Many patients with asymptomatic hilar adenopathy and normal lung function never need treatment.

Treat with systemic glucocorticoids (first line)Observe
Symptomatic pulmonary disease with impaired or declining function; cardiac or neurologic sarcoidosis; posterior uveitis or uveitis not controlled by topical drops; symptomatic hypercalcemia or renal involvement; disfiguring skin diseaseAsymptomatic hilar adenopathy; stable mild parenchymal disease with normal or near-normal function; Löfgren syndrome

Steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate first, then others such as azathioprine or TNF inhibitors like infliximab) are used for chronic disease or steroid toxicity. Cardiac sarcoidosis may need a pacemaker or an implantable defibrillator.

Eosinophilic lung disease: management pointers

  • Peripheral eosinophilia with infiltrates: check travel and stool studies; test for Strongyloides (serology) before giving glucocorticoids to anyone from an endemic area, because steroids can trigger fatal hyperinfection.
  • Acute and chronic eosinophilic pneumonia: BAL eosinophils above about 25% supports the diagnosis; treat with systemic glucocorticoids after excluding infection.
  • Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis: glucocorticoids; add cyclophosphamide or rituximab for organ- or life-threatening disease; mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) for relapsing or refractory disease without severe organ threat.
  • Hypereosinophilic syndrome: assess the heart (echocardiography, troponin); glucocorticoids for most; imatinib for the FIP1L1-PDGFRA variant.

Comparing the granulomatous and fibrotic diseases

SarcoidosisHypersensitivity pneumonitisIPFChronic beryllium disease
Typical patientYoung or middle-aged adultAny age with an antigen exposureOlder adult, often ex-smokerBeryllium worker
BALLymphocytosis, high CD4:CD8Marked lymphocytosis (often low CD4:CD8)Neutrophils, few lymphocytesLymphocytosis; positive BeLPT
GranulomasTight, noncaseatingLoose, poorly formed, bronchiolocentricNoneTight, noncaseating
First treatment stepObserve or glucocorticoids by organ threatRemove antigenAntifibroticRemove from exposure

Smoking is associated with a lower risk of sarcoidosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis, but with a higher risk of IPF, RB-ILD, DIP and pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis, so a smoking history helps sort the differential.

Upper-zone fibrosis has a short list: silicosis, coal, sarcoidosis, chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis, tuberculosis, ankylosing spondylitis, and radiation (depending on the field). Lower-zone fibrosis: IPF, asbestosis, connective tissue disease, and many drug reactions.

Restrictive lung disease means the lungs hold less air than predicted: total lung capacity (TLC) is reduced. Spirometry alone can only suggest restriction (a reduced FVC with a normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio); lung volumes by body plethysmography or gas dilution confirm it. The diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) then splits the causes into two groups.

Two kinds of restriction

Parenchymal (interstitial) restrictionExtraparenchymal restriction
ProblemStiff, scarred or inflamed alveolar wallsNormal lung trapped by a weak pump or a stiff/small chest
ExamplesIdiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, pneumoconioses, sarcoidosis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, drug-induced fibrosisObesity, kyphoscoliosis, neuromuscular disease (myasthenia gravis, ALS, Guillain–Barré), large pleural effusion, diaphragm paralysis
TLCReducedReduced
FEV1/FVCNormal or increased (radial traction holds airways open; FEV1 falls less than FVC)Normal
DLCOReduced (thickened membrane, lost capillary bed)Normal (corrected for alveolar volume)
A–a gradientWidened, worse with exerciseUsually normal; hypoventilation raises PaCO2
ComplianceLow (stiff lung); high elastic recoilLung compliance normal; chest wall compliance low in obesity and kyphoscoliosis

In neuromuscular weakness, maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures fall, and the vital capacity drops further when the patient lies flat if the diaphragm is weak. Serial forced vital capacity is the bedside measure used to watch for impending ventilatory failure.

Pneumoconioses: inorganic dust

Inhaled mineral particles 1–5 μm across reach the respiratory bronchioles and alveoli, where macrophages engulf them. Fibrogenic dusts damage or activate those macrophages, which release oxidants and cytokines (IL-1, TNF-α, TGF-β, PDGF) that recruit fibroblasts. The result is nodular or diffuse fibrosis that keeps progressing years after exposure ends. A useful anatomic rule: dusts that are cleared poorly by the lymphatics of the upper zones (silica, coal) favour the upper lobes; asbestos fibres, which are long and thin and settle by interception, favour the lower lobes and the pleura.

DustTypical exposureZoneSignature findingsAssociated risks
AsbestosShipbuilding, pipefitting, insulation, brake linings, demolition, roofingLower lobes, pleuraCalcified parietal pleural plaques (marker of exposure, not disease), diffuse interstitial fibrosis; ferruginous bodies (iron- and protein-coated fibres that look golden-brown and beaded and stain with Prussian blue)Bronchogenic carcinoma (the most common cancer after exposure; risk multiplied by smoking), malignant mesothelioma (no smoking link), benign pleural effusion, rounded atelectasis
SilicaSandblasting, quarrying, stone cutting, foundries, engineered-stone countertops, miningUpper lobesWhorled hyalinized silicotic nodules with birefringent particles; "eggshell" calcification of hilar nodes; progressive massive fibrosisTuberculosis and nontuberculous mycobacteria (silica damages macrophage phagolysosomes), lung cancer, autoimmune disease
Coal dustUnderground coal miningUpper lobesCoal macules around respiratory bronchioles, small nodules, progressive massive fibrosis in advanced diseaseRheumatoid pneumoconiosis (multiple peripheral nodules in a dust-exposed person with rheumatoid arthritis)
BerylliumAerospace, electronics, nuclear and dental-alloy workDiffuse, often hilar nodesNoncaseating granulomas identical to sarcoidosis; diagnosis needs a positive beryllium lymphocyte proliferation testBehaves as a cell-mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity; lung cancer

Anthracotic pigment in hilar nodes of city dwellers is harmless carbon carried by macrophages; it is not coal workers' pneumoconiosis. The disease needs heavy, sustained occupational dust.

Organic dusts and gases

  • Byssinosis: cotton, flax or hemp dust. Chest tightness and wheeze are worst on the first day back at work after a break and ease as the week goes on. It behaves like occupational airway disease rather than a fibrotic pneumoconiosis.
  • Silo-filler's disease: nitrogen dioxide accumulates above fresh silage in the first days to weeks after filling. NO2 forms nitric acid on moist airway surfaces, causing pulmonary edema hours after exposure and, weeks later, bronchiolitis obliterans.
  • Bagassosis (moldy sugar cane) and farmer's lung (moldy hay with thermophilic actinomycetes) are forms of hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis

Repeated inhalation of an organic antigen (bird proteins, mold, thermophilic bacteria in hay or humidifiers, isocyanates) in a sensitized person causes an immune-complex (type III) reaction early and a T-cell–mediated (type IV) granulomatous reaction with continued exposure. Pathology shows bronchiolocentric lymphocytic inflammation with poorly formed, loose granulomas. The acute form produces fever, cough and dyspnea 4–8 hours after exposure; the chronic form can become fibrotic and resemble idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, often with upper- and mid-zone predominance and air trapping. Bronchoalveolar lavage typically shows a lymphocytosis.

Type I (IgE) hypersensitivity is not the mechanism of hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Its symptoms are delayed by hours, there is no wheeze-predominant immediate reaction, and eosinophils are not the main cell.

Granulomas in the lung come from T-helper-1 cells releasing interferon-γ that activates macrophages into epithelioid cells; TNF-α maintains the granuloma. The same biology explains why TNF inhibitors reactivate tuberculosis and why beryllium disease and sarcoidosis look alike under the microscope.

This section covers the interstitial lung diseases that are not caused by mineral dust: the idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, sarcoidosis and the eosinophilic lung diseases.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)

IPF is the most common idiopathic interstitial pneumonia. It affects older adults (usually over 60), more often men and former smokers. The current model is repeated microinjury to alveolar epithelial cells with failed repair: type II pneumocytes cannot regenerate the epithelium (short telomeres and surfactant-protein gene variants are risk factors), and TGF-β–driven activation of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts lays down collagen. Inflammation is minor, which is why glucocorticoids do not help.

The histologic pattern is usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP): patchy, subpleural and basal fibrosis with temporal heterogeneity (old dense collagen next to active fibroblastic foci and normal lung) and honeycomb cysts lined by bronchiolar epithelium. Clinically: insidious dry cough and exertional dyspnea, fine bibasilar "velcro" crackles, digital clubbing, and eventually hypoxemia and pulmonary hypertension with cor pulmonale.

Other interstitial pneumonias

PatternWhoHistologyCourse
UIP (IPF)Older adults, often ex-smokersPatchy, temporally heterogeneous fibrosis, fibroblastic foci, honeycombingProgressive; antifibrotics slow decline
Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP)Middle-aged, often women; connective tissue disease (systemic sclerosis, myositis), drugsUniform (temporally homogeneous) inflammation and/or fibrosisBetter prognosis; often responds to immunosuppression
Respiratory bronchiolitis–ILD and desquamative interstitial pneumonia (DIP)Current smokersPigmented ("smoker's") macrophages filling bronchioles (RB-ILD) or alveoli diffusely (DIP)Improve with smoking cessation
Cryptogenic organizing pneumoniaAdults, may follow infection or drugsPlugs of granulation tissue (Masson bodies) in alveolar ducts and alveoliSteroid-responsive; relapses common
Acute interstitial pneumoniaPreviously well adultsDiffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranesFulminant, ARDS-like

Sarcoidosis

A multisystem disease of noncaseating granulomas from an exaggerated Th1 (and Th17) response to an unknown antigen. It is more common and often more severe in Black Americans, and in the US is more common in women. The lung and intrathoracic nodes are involved in about 90% of patients.

  • Chest imaging: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, often with right paratracheal nodes; perilymphatic upper-zone nodules; fibrosis in advanced disease.
  • Other organs: anterior uveitis, erythema nodosum and lupus pernio, parotid enlargement, facial nerve palsy, cardiac involvement (heart block, ventricular arrhythmias, sudden death), hepatic granulomas.
  • Calcium: activated macrophages in granulomas express 1α-hydroxylase and make calcitriol independently of PTH, causing hypercalciuria (stones) and sometimes hypercalcemia; PTH is suppressed.
  • Labs: serum ACE often raised (made by epithelioid cells) but neither sensitive nor specific; lymphopenia; BAL with a high CD4:CD8 ratio.
  • Histology: tight epithelioid granulomas with multinucleated giant cells, which may contain Schaumann (laminated calcium) or asteroid bodies. Caseation should prompt a search for tuberculosis or fungi.

Eosinophilic lung diseases

  • Simple pulmonary eosinophilia (Loeffler syndrome): transient, migrating infiltrates with blood eosinophilia, usually from helminth larvae passing through the lungs (Ascaris, hookworm, Strongyloides) or a drug. Often mild and self-limited.
  • Acute eosinophilic pneumonia: abrupt hypoxemic respiratory failure, typically in a young person who has just started smoking or vaping; BAL eosinophils are high even when blood counts are initially normal; dramatic response to glucocorticoids.
  • Chronic eosinophilic pneumonia: weeks to months of cough, fever, weight loss; peripheral, pleural-based infiltrates (described as the photographic negative of pulmonary edema); often a history of asthma; responds to glucocorticoids but relapses.
  • Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis: adult-onset asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis, eosinophilia, then necrotizing small-vessel vasculitis (mononeuritis multiplex, purpura, cardiomyopathy); p-ANCA (anti-MPO) in under half.
  • Hypereosinophilic syndrome: sustained marked eosinophilia with organ damage (heart, lungs, skin, nerves) and no secondary cause; a myeloid neoplasm with the FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion responds to imatinib.
  • Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (asthma or cystic fibrosis, central bronchiectasis, high IgE) is covered with obstructive airway disease.

Granulomas that are noncaseating do not prove sarcoidosis: beryllium disease, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, drug reactions and some fungal infections produce them too. Sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of compatible clinical picture plus granulomas plus exclusion of alternatives.

s23b-s-090501-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Recognizing and supporting acute respiratory failure

Assess the work of breathing (rate, accessory muscles, paradox, ability to speak), mental state and airway protection, then obtain an arterial blood gas. Pulse oximetry is a poor guide to ventilation: a patient on oxygen can have a normal saturation with a dangerously high PaCO2.

SupportBest suited forAvoid or stop when
Conventional oxygen (nasal cannula, mask)Mild hypoxemia; target SpO2 about 92–96% in most patients, about 88–92% when chronic CO2 retention is a riskRising PaCO2 or fatigue
High-flow nasal oxygenAcute hypoxemic failure (e.g. pneumonia) in a patient who protects the airway; delivers heated humidified gas at high flow with a little PEEP and dead-space washoutWorsening despite therapy; hypercapnic failure is usually better served by NIV
Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP or CPAP)Hypercapnic COPD exacerbation with pH < 7.35 (strongest evidence); cardiogenic pulmonary edema; selected immunocompromised patientsAltered mental status or coma, inability to clear secretions or protect the airway, vomiting or upper GI bleeding, hemodynamic instability, facial trauma, failure to improve within 1–2 h
Intubation and mechanical ventilationApnea, coma, airway compromise, shock, refractory hypoxemia, failure of NIV, exhaustion—
A hypercapnic, drowsy COPD patient is not a candidate for "more oxygen through a nonrebreather". Uncontrolled oxygen worsens V/Q matching and the Haldane effect and raises PaCO2. Titrate oxygen and add NIV.

ARDS: management

There is no specific drug for ARDS. Treat the trigger (antibiotics and source control for sepsis or pneumonia) and protect the lung from the ventilator.

  1. Low tidal volume ventilation: about 6 mL/kg of predicted body weight (from height and sex, not actual weight), within a range of 4–8 mL/kg. Predicted body weight is 50 kg (men) or 45.5 kg (women) + 0.91 × (height in cm − 152.4).
  2. Plateau pressure ≤ 30 cm H2O; lower tidal volume further if it is higher. Accept a modest rise in PaCO2 and fall in pH (permissive hypercapnia) unless contraindicated, for example by raised intracranial pressure.
  3. PEEP keeps alveoli open and reduces the FIO2 needed; higher PEEP is used for moderate to severe ARDS. Target PaO2 about 55–80 mm Hg or SpO2 about 88–95%.
  4. Prone positioning for severe ARDS (PaO2/FIO2 < 150) for long sessions (at least 12–16 h a day) improves survival by recruiting dorsal lung and evening out ventilation.
  5. Conservative fluid strategy once shock has resolved; short-term neuromuscular blockade for severe ventilator dyssynchrony.
  6. Rescue: venovenous ECMO at experienced centers for refractory hypoxemia despite the above.

Not recommended routinely: high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (harmful in trials), inhaled nitric oxide (improves oxygenation but not survival), and surfactant in adults. Corticosteroids are an area of active change; they are used for ARDS from some causes (for example severe community-acquired pneumonia), so check current guidance before choosing them as a general rule.

Prognosis. Mortality rises with severity and with the cause (sepsis carries the worst outlook). Survivors often have muscle weakness, cognitive impairment, anxiety and depression for months; lung function usually recovers substantially.

Enteral feeding and respiratory failure

Nasogastric or nasoenteric tubes placed blindly can enter the airway, especially in sedated, intubated or neurologically impaired patients with a weak cough. Feeding into the lung causes pneumonitis, pneumothorax and respiratory failure. Auscultating an air bolus ("whoosh test") cannot tell a bronchial from a gastric position; confirm the tip position with a radiograph before the first feed (and after any suspected displacement). To lower aspiration risk during feeding: raise the head of the bed 30–45°, prefer post-pyloric feeding in patients with high aspiration risk, and stop feeds before procedures as required. Nutrition support is itself important in respiratory failure: underfeeding worsens respiratory muscle strength, and early enteral nutrition is preferred to parenteral nutrition when the gut works.

In ARDS the numbers to know are 6 (mL/kg predicted body weight) and 30 (cm H2O plateau pressure). Calculate predicted body weight from height; using actual weight in an obese patient delivers dangerous volumes.

Pulmonary embolism: diagnosis

Start with clinical probability, using a validated score (Wells or the revised Geneva score) or gestalt.

  1. Low probability: apply the PE rule-out criteria (PERC; age under 50, pulse under 100, SpO2 95% or more, no hemoptysis, no estrogen use, no prior VTE, no unilateral leg swelling, no recent surgery or trauma). If all are met, no testing is needed.
  2. Low or intermediate probability (PE "unlikely"): measure D-dimer. A normal result excludes PE. Age-adjusted cut-offs (age × 10 µg/L after 50) reduce false positives in older adults. A raised D-dimer leads to imaging.
  3. High probability (PE "likely"): skip D-dimer and go straight to CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA). Start anticoagulation while waiting for imaging if bleeding risk is acceptable.
  4. Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scanning replaces CTPA when iodinated contrast is a problem (severe contrast allergy, significant kidney impairment) and is a reasonable choice in pregnancy when the chest x-ray is normal.
  5. Unstable patient (hypotension) too sick for CT: bedside echocardiography showing RV dilation supports treating as PE; compression ultrasound may find the source DVT.

Pregnancy. D-dimer rises normally through pregnancy, so it is less useful (pregnancy-adapted algorithms exist). With leg symptoms, begin with compression ultrasonography of the legs: finding a DVT justifies treatment and avoids chest radiation. Otherwise use a chest x-ray, then V/Q scanning or CTPA; both expose the fetus to very little radiation, far less than the risk of a missed PE. Treat with low-molecular-weight heparin; warfarin is teratogenic and DOACs are avoided in pregnancy.

Risk stratification and treatment

CategoryFeaturesTreatment
High risk ("massive")Sustained hypotension (systolic < 90 mm Hg for 15 min or needing vasopressors), obstructive shock or arrestAnticoagulation with unfractionated heparin plus systemic thrombolysis (alteplase) if no contraindication; surgical or catheter-directed embolectomy if thrombolysis is contraindicated or fails
Intermediate risk ("submassive")Normotensive but RV dysfunction on echo or CT and/or raised troponinAnticoagulation and close monitoring; rescue thrombolysis if the patient decompensates. Routine thrombolysis is not advised (bleeding, including intracranial, outweighs benefit)
Low riskNormotensive, no RV strain, normal biomarkers, low PESI or sPESIAnticoagulation; suitable patients can be treated as outpatients

Anticoagulant choice. A direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban or dabigatran; the last two after a short course of parenteral heparin) is first line for most patients. Use low-molecular-weight heparin in pregnancy; warfarin (overlapped with heparin for at least 5 days and until the INR is 2–3 for 24 h) for antiphospholipid syndrome, mechanical valves or severe kidney failure. For cancer-associated thrombosis, DOACs (apixaban, edoxaban, rivaroxaban) or LMWH are options; GI and genitourinary cancers carry more bleeding risk with some DOACs. Unfractionated heparin is preferred when thrombolysis or a procedure may be needed or kidney function is very poor, because it is short-acting and reversible with protamine.

Duration. At least 3 months for every PE. Stop after 3 months when a major transient risk factor (surgery, major trauma) provoked it. Consider extended, indefinite therapy for unprovoked PE or a persistent risk factor (active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome) when bleeding risk is acceptable, with periodic review.

IVC filter only for acute proximal DVT or PE when anticoagulation is contraindicated (for example active bleeding) or must be interrupted; remove retrievable filters when anticoagulation becomes possible. A filter is not a substitute for anticoagulation and does not treat the clot.

Hypotension changes everything: normotensive RV strain alone is not an indication for systemic thrombolysis, but shock from PE is.

Pulmonary hypertension: evaluation and management

  1. Suspect from symptoms and examination; transthoracic echocardiography is the screening test (estimated RV systolic pressure, RV size and function, left heart disease).
  2. Look for the common causes first: left heart disease (echo) and lung disease or hypoxia (pulmonary function tests, high-resolution CT, overnight oximetry or sleep study).
  3. Always obtain a V/Q scan to screen for CTEPH; it is more sensitive than CT angiography for chronic thromboembolic disease. A normal V/Q scan essentially excludes CTEPH.
  4. Other tests: HIV, liver tests and abdominal ultrasound (portopulmonary disease), autoantibodies (systemic sclerosis), thyroid function.
  5. Right heart catheterization confirms the diagnosis (mPAP > 20 mm Hg) and classifies it (PCWP, pulmonary vascular resistance); vasoreactivity testing is done in idiopathic, heritable and drug-associated PAH.

Treatment depends on the group. Groups 2 and 3: treat the heart or lung disease and correct hypoxemia (long-term oxygen if resting PaO2 ≤ 55 mm Hg or SpO2 ≤ 88%). PAH-specific drugs are generally not used in group 2 and can worsen pulmonary edema. Group 1: referral to a specialist center; initial combination of an endothelin receptor antagonist and a PDE-5 inhibitor for most, adding parenteral prostacyclin for high-risk disease; diuretics for right heart failure; exercise rehabilitation; avoid pregnancy; lung transplantation for refractory disease. Group 4 (CTEPH): lifelong anticoagulation and evaluation for pulmonary endarterectomy, which can be curative; balloon pulmonary angioplasty or riociguat when surgery is not possible.

Unexplained exertional dyspnea months after an acute PE: think CTEPH and order a V/Q scan.

s23b-s-090501-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Respiratory failure means the lungs cannot keep arterial blood gases in a safe range. Two patterns matter, and most exam questions turn on telling them apart from the arterial blood gas and the alveolar–arterial (A–a) oxygen gradient.

FeatureHypoxemic (type 1)Hypercapnic (type 2)
Defining gasPaO2 < 60 mm Hg with normal or low PaCO2PaCO2 > 45–50 mm Hg with acidemia (pH < 7.35)
Core problemOxygen transfer: V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion limitationVentilation: the pump (brain stem, nerves, muscles, chest wall) or a very high dead-space load
A–a gradientRaisedNormal if pure hypoventilation; raised if lung disease coexists
Typical causesPneumonia, ARDS, pulmonary edema, pulmonary embolism, atelectasisOpioid or sedative overdose, neuromuscular weakness (myasthenic crisis, Guillain-Barré), severe COPD or asthma exacerbation, obesity hypoventilation, kyphoscoliosis

The five mechanisms of hypoxemia

The alveolar gas equation estimates alveolar oxygen: PAO2 = FIO2(Patm − PH2O) − PaCO2/R. Breathing room air at sea level this is about 150 − PaCO2/0.8. A normal A–a gradient is roughly (age/4) + 4 mm Hg, about 5–15 mm Hg in a young adult.

  • Low inspired oxygen (altitude): normal A–a gradient; corrects with supplemental oxygen.
  • Alveolar hypoventilation: PaCO2 rises and PAO2 falls by about 1.25 mm Hg for every 1 mm Hg rise in PaCO2; the A–a gradient stays normal.
  • Diffusion limitation (interstitial fibrosis, exercise at altitude): raised gradient, corrects with oxygen.
  • V/Q mismatch: the commonest cause in practice; low-V/Q units lower PaO2; raised gradient; improves with oxygen.
  • Right-to-left shunt (V/Q = 0: alveoli filled with fluid, pus or collapsed; intracardiac shunts; pulmonary arteriovenous malformations): raised gradient and poor response to 100% oxygen, because shunted blood never meets the added oxygen.
Give 100% oxygen as a bedside test: a large rise in PaO2 points to V/Q mismatch or diffusion limitation; little rise points to shunt.

Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)

ARDS is acute, diffuse, inflammatory lung injury that makes the alveolar–capillary barrier leaky. The current consensus definition (the Berlin concept) needs four things: onset within 1 week of a known insult or new symptoms; bilateral opacities on chest imaging not fully explained by effusions, collapse or nodules; respiratory failure not fully explained by heart failure or fluid overload; and impaired oxygenation graded by the PaO2/FIO2 ratio on at least 5 cm H2O of PEEP: mild 201–300, moderate 101–200, severe ≤ 100 mm Hg.

Triggers. Direct lung injury: pneumonia (the commonest cause overall), aspiration of gastric contents, inhalation injury, near-drowning, lung contusion. Indirect injury: sepsis (the commonest extrapulmonary cause), severe trauma with shock, multiple transfusions (transfusion-related acute lung injury), acute pancreatitis, burns, drug overdose.

Pathogenesis. Activated neutrophils and macrophages release proteases, reactive oxygen species and cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α). Endothelial and type I pneumocyte damage lets protein-rich fluid flood the alveoli; surfactant is diluted and inactivated, so alveoli collapse. Shunt through flooded and collapsed units causes refractory hypoxemia, and compliance falls (stiff lungs).

PhaseTimingHistology
ExudativeDays 1–7Diffuse alveolar damage: interstitial and alveolar edema, necrosis of type I pneumocytes, eosinophilic hyaline membranes (fibrin plus cell debris) lining alveolar ducts
ProliferativeAbout days 7–21Type II pneumocyte hyperplasia (they are the progenitors that regenerate the epithelium), organization of exudate
FibroticAfter about 3 weeks (some patients)Interstitial fibrosis, persisting restriction and gas-exchange abnormality

Cardiogenic versus noncardiogenic pulmonary edema

Starling forces explain the difference. In cardiogenic (hydrostatic) edema a raised left atrial pressure pushes low-protein fluid out of intact capillaries; pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) is high, the heart is often enlarged, and there may be Kerley B lines and effusions. In ARDS the barrier itself is damaged, so protein-rich fluid leaks at normal pressure: PCWP is normal (≤ 18 mm Hg is the classic cut-off), the heart is normal-sized and the opacities are patchy and peripheral. A pulmonary artery catheter is no longer needed to make the diagnosis; echocardiography usually answers the question. Other noncardiogenic causes: high-altitude pulmonary edema, neurogenic edema after a severe brain injury, re-expansion edema, and opioid or salicylate toxicity.

Surfactant (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, made by type II pneumocytes) lowers surface tension; by the law of Laplace (P = 2T/r) small alveoli would otherwise empty into large ones. Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is surfactant deficiency; adult ARDS is surfactant inactivation on top of barrier injury, which is why giving surfactant helps neonates but not adults.
A normal A–a gradient with hypoxemia means hypoventilation (or altitude). Do not label an opioid overdose as "V/Q mismatch" unless aspiration has been added.

Pulmonary embolism: pathophysiology

Most pulmonary emboli are thrombi from the deep veins of the legs (proximal veins above the knee carry most of the risk) or pelvis. Virchow's triad of stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability explains the risk factors: recent surgery or trauma, immobilization and long travel, active cancer, pregnancy and the postpartum period, estrogen-containing contraceptives or hormone therapy, inherited thrombophilia (factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene variant, protein C, protein S or antithrombin deficiency), antiphospholipid syndrome, obesity and prior venous thromboembolism.

  • Gas exchange. The occluded segment becomes dead space (ventilated, unperfused). Hypoxemia arises mainly because blood is diverted to the remaining vessels, creating low-V/Q units, plus some shunt through atelectatic lung. Hypoxemia drives hyperventilation, so the typical gas is respiratory alkalosis with a raised A–a gradient; PaO2 can be normal in a young patient.
  • Hemodynamics. Obstruction plus vasoconstrictors (thromboxane A2, serotonin) raise pulmonary vascular resistance. The thin-walled right ventricle dilates, its wall stress and oxygen demand rise, and the septum bows into the left ventricle, reducing LV filling. Falling cardiac output then lowers coronary perfusion of the RV, a spiral that ends in obstructive shock.
  • Infarction is uncommon because the lung has a dual blood supply (pulmonary and bronchial arteries). When it occurs (usually with pre-existing heart failure or a small peripheral embolus), it is hemorrhagic, wedge-shaped and pleural-based, giving pleuritic pain, hemoptysis and sometimes a peripheral wedge opacity on imaging.

Clinical picture. Sudden dyspnea and tachypnea are the most common findings; pleuritic chest pain, cough, hemoptysis, syncope (large embolus) and signs of DVT (unilateral calf swelling) may occur. The commonest ECG finding is sinus tachycardia; signs of RV strain (right axis deviation, new right bundle branch block, T-wave inversion in V1–V4, the S1Q3T3 pattern) are less frequent and insensitive.

S1Q3T3 is famous but uncommon. A normal ECG or plain sinus tachycardia does not exclude PE.

Other emboli

EmbolusSettingClues
FatLong-bone (especially femur) or pelvic fractures, orthopedic surgery; 24–72 h after injuryTriad of hypoxemia, neurologic change (confusion), and petechiae over the upper trunk, axillae and conjunctivae; marrow fat both obstructs vessels and is broken into toxic free fatty acids that injure the endothelium
Air (venous)Central venous line insertion or removal with the patient upright, neurosurgery in the sitting position, traumaSudden dyspnea, hypotension, a churning "mill-wheel" murmur; large volumes form an air lock in the RV outflow. Air can cross a patent foramen ovale and cause stroke (paradoxical embolism)
Amniotic fluidLabor, delivery or just afterAbrupt hypoxemia, hypotension or cardiac arrest, and disseminated intravascular coagulation; fetal squamous cells may be found in the maternal pulmonary circulation
SepticRight-sided endocarditis (injection drug use), infected central lines, septic thrombophlebitisMultiple peripheral nodules that cavitate
Air enters a vein when venous pressure is below atmospheric pressure: upright posture and deep inspiration make central venous pressure negative. That is why lines are inserted and removed with the patient flat or head-down and asked to exhale or hum.

Pulmonary hypertension

Pulmonary hypertension is now defined at right heart catheterization by a mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) above 20 mm Hg at rest (the older threshold was 25). Precapillary disease adds a PCWP ≤ 15 mm Hg and raised pulmonary vascular resistance; postcapillary disease has PCWP > 15 mm Hg (left heart disease).

GroupCauseExamples
1Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH)Idiopathic, heritable (BMPR2), drugs and toxins (amphetamines, historical anorexigens), connective tissue disease (systemic sclerosis), HIV, portal hypertension, congenital shunts
2Left heart diseaseHeart failure with reduced or preserved ejection fraction, mitral and aortic valve disease. The most common cause overall
3Lung disease or hypoxiaCOPD, interstitial lung disease, obstructive sleep apnea, obesity hypoventilation, high altitude
4Pulmonary artery obstructionChronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH)
5Unclear or multifactorialSarcoidosis, myeloproliferative disorders, chronic hemolysis (sickle cell disease), chronic kidney disease on dialysis

Mechanism in PAH. Loss-of-function variants in BMPR2 (a receptor of the TGF-β superfamily, autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance) remove a brake on smooth muscle proliferation. The arterioles show medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis and, in severe disease, plexiform lesions. There is too little vasodilator signaling (nitric oxide, prostacyclin) and too much vasoconstrictor signaling (endothelin-1). Chronic hypoxia (group 3) constricts pulmonary arterioles directly, the opposite of the systemic response.

Findings. Exertional dyspnea and fatigue, then exertional syncope and chest pain; a loud pulmonic component of S2, right ventricular heave, tricuspid regurgitation, raised jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly and edema (cor pulmonale). The chest x-ray shows enlarged central pulmonary arteries with pruned peripheral vessels.

Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations

Direct artery-to-vein connections bypass the capillary bed, creating an anatomic right-to-left shunt. Most occur in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (autosomal dominant; ENG or ACVRL1, also TGF-β pathway genes): recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasias on lips, tongue and fingertips, GI bleeding and iron deficiency. The shunt causes hypoxemia that responds poorly to oxygen, clubbing, and paradoxical emboli: stroke and brain abscess, because the lung's filter is bypassed. Lower-lobe lesions cause platypnea-orthodeoxia (dyspnea and desaturation when upright).

Approach to the hypoxemic patient

  1. Confirm with an arterial blood gas when the oximeter may mislead (poor perfusion, dark skin pigmentation can cause overestimation, dyshemoglobins, very low saturations).
  2. Look at PaCO2. High PaCO2 means hypoventilation is at least part of the problem.
  3. Calculate the A–a gradient. Normal → hypoventilation or low inspired oxygen. Increased → V/Q mismatch, shunt or diffusion limitation.
  4. Check the response to supplemental oxygen. Little improvement on high FiO2 suggests shunt (consolidation, atelectasis, ARDS, edema, intracardiac or pulmonary AV shunt).

Give oxygen to target SpO2 about 92–96% in most acutely ill adults and 88–92% in those at risk of hypercapnia (COPD, obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular or chest wall disease). Hyperoxia offers no benefit and may harm.

Drug-induced hypoventilation

Opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol and other sedatives depress central chemoreceptor responsiveness to CO2. Watch for drowsiness, a slow or shallow respiratory rate and pinpoint pupils with opioids. Supplemental oxygen can keep SpO2 normal while PaCO2 climbs, so oximetry on oxygen does not exclude hypoventilation; use clinical assessment, capnography or a blood gas. Treat opioid toxicity with naloxone, titrated to adequate breathing rather than full arousal in opioid-dependent patients; support ventilation with a bag-valve mask meanwhile. Flumazenil is generally avoided because it can precipitate seizures in benzodiazepine-dependent patients or mixed overdoses.

Obstructive sleep apnea

Repeated upper-airway collapse during sleep causes apneas and hypopneas, oxygen desaturation, arousals and sympathetic surges. Risk factors: obesity, male sex, older age, large neck circumference, retrognathia, tonsillar hypertrophy (the main cause in children), hypothyroidism and acromegaly. Symptoms: loud snoring, witnessed apneas, gasping, unrefreshing sleep, daytime sleepiness and morning headache. Consequences: resistant hypertension, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, stroke, insulin resistance, pulmonary hypertension and motor vehicle crashes.

  • Diagnosis: in-laboratory polysomnography is the reference standard; home sleep apnea testing is acceptable for adults with a high pretest probability and no major cardiopulmonary, neuromuscular or sleep comorbidity. Severity uses the apnea–hypopnea index (events per hour: 5–14 mild, 15–29 moderate, 30 or more severe).
  • Treatment: CPAP is first-line for moderate–severe or symptomatic disease and improves sleepiness and blood pressure. Add weight loss (lifestyle, anti-obesity medicines such as tirzepatide, bariatric surgery), positional therapy, avoidance of alcohol and sedatives, and treatment of nasal obstruction. Mandibular advancement devices suit mild–moderate disease or CPAP intolerance; hypoglossal nerve stimulation is an option for selected CPAP-intolerant patients. Adenotonsillectomy is first-line in children with tonsillar hypertrophy.
  • Counsel on drowsy driving; avoid sedatives and use caution with opioids after surgery.

Obesity hypoventilation syndrome

Defined by obesity (BMI ≥ 30), awake daytime hypercapnia (PaCO2 ≥ 45 mm Hg) and no other cause of hypoventilation. Most patients also have OSA. A raised serum bicarbonate (≥ 27 mEq/L) is a useful screening clue, and the blood gas typically shows compensated respiratory acidosis. Complications: pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, secondary polycythemia, and acute hypercapnic failure after sedatives or with uncontrolled oxygen. Treatment: positive airway pressure during sleep (CPAP when severe OSA coexists; bilevel noninvasive ventilation otherwise or when CPAP fails), substantial weight loss, and avoidance of respiratory depressants.

Central sleep apnea

Absent effort, not airway collapse, causes the apneas. Causes: heart failure with Cheyne–Stokes breathing (crescendo–decrescendo ventilation from delayed circulation and a sensitive CO2 response), opioids, stroke and brainstem disease, and high altitude. In heart failure, first optimize heart failure therapy; CPAP or oxygen may help. Adaptive servo-ventilation should not be used when ejection fraction is 45% or less, because it increased cardiovascular mortality in that group.

Exam trap: a post-operative patient on an opioid with SpO2 92% on nasal oxygen and a respiratory rate of 7 is hypoventilating; give naloxone and support ventilation, not more oxygen.

s23b-s-090601-ck-02.bodyHtml:
Carbon monoxide poisoning

Suspect it with headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion, syncope, seizures, chest pain or several ill members of one household, especially in winter, after fires, or with generators or vehicles in enclosed spaces. Check for co-exposure to cyanide after smoke inhalation (lactic acidosis, hypotension).

  • Diagnosis: carboxyhemoglobin by co-oximetry on an arterial or venous sample. Standard pulse oximetry and PaO2 are normal and misleading. Levels correlate imperfectly with symptoms (smokers can have several percent at baseline). Obtain an ECG and troponin (myocardial injury is common), and a pregnancy test in women of reproductive age.
  • Treatment: remove from the source and give 100% oxygen by non-rebreather mask (or intubation if needed) immediately. This shortens the carboxyhemoglobin half-life from about 4–5 hours on room air to roughly 1–1.5 hours.
  • Hyperbaric oxygen shortens it further and may reduce delayed neurologic sequelae. Commonly used criteria include loss of consciousness or syncope, neurologic deficits or altered mental status, seizures, carboxyhemoglobin above about 25% (lower thresholds in pregnancy, because fetal hemoglobin binds CO avidly), signs of myocardial ischemia and severe acidosis. Decisions are made with a hyperbaric or toxicology specialist.
  • Arrange follow-up for delayed neurologic sequelae, and inspect the home (detectors, appliance repair) before return.

Methemoglobinemia

Suspect it in cyanosis with a normal PaO2, SpO2 around 85% that does not improve with oxygen, and chocolate-colored blood, often minutes to hours after a topical anesthetic spray (endoscopy, transesophageal echocardiography), dapsone or a nitrite. Confirm with co-oximetry. Stop the offending agent and give oxygen. Give intravenous methylene blue to symptomatic patients or those with high levels (often above about 20–30%). If methylene blue fails or the patient has G6PD deficiency (it can be ineffective and cause hemolysis), options include exchange transfusion and hyperbaric oxygen, with ascorbic acid as a slow adjunct. Dapsone has a long half-life, so methemoglobin can recur and repeated doses may be needed. Methylene blue is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor and can precipitate serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs.

Altitude illness

SyndromeFeaturesTreatmentPrevention
Acute mountain sicknessHeadache plus nausea, fatigue, dizziness or poor sleep within 6–12 hours of ascent, usually above 2,500 mStop ascending, rest, analgesics and antiemetics; descend if worsening; acetazolamide or dexamethasoneGradual ascent; acetazolamide for those at moderate–high risk (dexamethasone as an alternative)
High-altitude cerebral edemaAtaxia, confusion or drowsiness on a background of AMSDescent, oxygen, dexamethasone; portable hyperbaric bag if descent is impossibleAs for AMS
High-altitude pulmonary edemaExertional dyspnea progressing to dyspnea at rest, dry then frothy cough, crackles, low SpO2, often on day 2–4Descent and supplemental oxygen; nifedipine when descent or oxygen is unavailableSlow ascent; nifedipine (or a PDE5 inhibitor) for people with previous HAPE

Pre-existing conditions that worsen at altitude include COPD, pulmonary hypertension, sickle cell disease and heart failure. Diuretics are not used for HAPE, because these patients are not volume overloaded.

Pearl: for every altitude syndrome, descent is the definitive treatment; drugs buy time.

Exam trap: a normal pulse oximetry reading in a confused patient from a house with a faulty heater does not exclude CO poisoning; order co-oximetry and start 100% oxygen.
