s23b-s-090601-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Gas exchange depends on three things: getting air to the alveoli (ventilation), getting blood to the same alveoli (perfusion), and moving gas across the alveolar–capillary membrane (diffusion). Hypoxemia means a low arterial PO2; hypoxia means inadequate oxygen at the tissue level, which can also come from anemia, low cardiac output or poisoned oxygen use.

The alveolar gas equation and the A–a gradient

Alveolar PO2 is estimated as PAO2 = FiO2 × (Patm − PH2O) − PaCO2 / R. At sea level (760 mm Hg, water vapor 47 mm Hg) breathing room air (FiO2 0.21) with R = 0.8, this simplifies to PAO2 ≈ 150 − PaCO2/0.8. With a normal PaCO2 of 40, PAO2 is about 100 mm Hg.

The A–a gradient (PAO2 − PaO2) reflects how well the lung transfers oxygen. In young adults it is about 5–15 mm Hg; it widens with age (a rough upper limit is age/4 + 4) and with higher FiO2. A normal gradient with hypoxemia means the lungs are working and the problem is in the air delivered to them.

Five mechanisms of hypoxemia

MechanismA–a gradientResponse to 100% O2Examples
Low inspired PO2NormalCorrectsHigh altitude, enclosed spaces
HypoventilationNormal (PaCO2 high)CorrectsOpioids, sedatives, neuromuscular disease, chest wall disease, obesity hypoventilation
V/Q mismatchIncreasedCorrects wellCOPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia (partly), interstitial disease
Right-to-left shunt (V/Q = 0)IncreasedPoor correctionAtelectasis, lobar consolidation, ARDS, pulmonary edema, intracardiac or pulmonary arteriovenous shunts
Diffusion limitationIncreasedCorrectsInterstitial fibrosis, emphysema; worse during exercise

Why shunt is different: shunted blood never meets alveolar gas, so raising FiO2 cannot oxygenate it, and because hemoglobin in ventilated units is already almost saturated, those units cannot compensate. By contrast, extra oxygen eventually raises PO2 even in poorly ventilated (low V/Q) units, so V/Q mismatch improves with oxygen.

Ventilation–perfusion relationships

A unit with V/Q of zero behaves like mixed venous blood (PO2 about 40, PCO2 about 46 mm Hg). A unit with infinite V/Q (dead space) has the composition of inspired air (PO2 about 150, PCO2 about 0). In the upright lung, both ventilation and perfusion increase toward the base, but perfusion increases more, so V/Q is highest at the apex (about 3) and lowest at the base (below 1). The apex therefore has the highest PAO2 and lowest PACO2, one reason reactivation tuberculosis favors the apices. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood away from poorly ventilated units to preserve V/Q matching; it is unique to the pulmonary circulation (systemic arterioles dilate in hypoxia).

Diffusion

By Fick's law, gas transfer is proportional to area and the partial-pressure difference, and inversely proportional to membrane thickness. Normally, capillary blood equilibrates with alveolar oxygen within the first third of the roughly 0.75-second transit time (perfusion-limited). When the membrane is thickened (fibrosis) or surface area is lost (emphysema), equilibration is slower; during exercise, faster flow shortens transit time and exercise desaturation appears. Carbon monoxide is diffusion-limited, which is why it is used to measure DLCO.

Control of breathing

  • Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to the pH of cerebrospinal fluid, which follows arterial PCO2 (CO2 crosses the blood–brain barrier; H+ does not). They provide most of the minute-to-minute drive.
  • Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies via the glossopharyngeal nerve, aortic bodies via the vagus) respond mainly to a low PaO2 (strongly below about 60 mm Hg), and also to high PaCO2 and low pH. They are the only receptors that sense hypoxemia.
  • Lung stretch receptors (Hering–Breuer reflex) and J receptors (juxtacapillary, stimulated by interstitial edema, causing rapid shallow breathing) modify the pattern.

Hypoventilation and compensation

PaCO2 is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation (alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × rate). Rapid, shallow breathing raises dead-space fraction and can raise PaCO2 even when the rate is high. Acute respiratory acidosis raises bicarbonate by only about 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in PaCO2 (buffering); chronic respiratory acidosis raises it by about 3.5–4 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg through renal compensation over days.

Exam trap: a hypoxemic patient with high PaCO2 and a normal A–a gradient has pure hypoventilation (e.g. an opioid overdose). Calculate before you call it lung disease.

Pearl: PaO2 does not fall in anemia or carbon monoxide poisoning; oxygen content does. PaO2 reflects dissolved oxygen only.

s23b-s-090601-s1-02.bodyHtml:
Oxygen content and delivery

Arterial oxygen content = (1.34 × hemoglobin × SaO2) + (0.003 × PaO2). Almost all oxygen is carried by hemoglobin; dissolved oxygen matters only at very high PaO2 (as in hyperbaric therapy). Oxygen delivery = cardiac output × arterial content. Anemia, low cardiac output and abnormal hemoglobins reduce delivery even when PaO2 is normal.

The oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve

The sigmoid shape reflects cooperative binding: hemoglobin shifts from the tense (T, low affinity) to the relaxed (R, high affinity) state as heme groups bind oxygen. The flat upper part protects saturation when alveolar PO2 falls modestly; the steep middle part lets tissues unload large amounts of oxygen for small drops in PO2. P50 (the PO2 at 50% saturation) is about 26–27 mm Hg.

  • Right shift (higher P50, more unloading): ↑ H+ and ↑ CO2 (the Bohr effect), ↑ temperature, ↑ 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, exercise, high altitude (through 2,3-BPG).
  • Left shift (lower P50, tighter binding): alkalosis, hypothermia, ↓ 2,3-BPG (e.g. stored blood), fetal hemoglobin (γ chains bind 2,3-BPG poorly), carbon monoxide and methemoglobin.

The Haldane effect is the reverse: deoxygenated hemoglobin carries more CO2 (as carbamino compounds and by buffering H+), so oxygenation in the lung releases CO2.

Carbon monoxide

CO binds hemoglobin with an affinity more than 200 times that of oxygen. It reduces oxygen content (fewer sites) and shifts the curve left (remaining hemes hold oxygen tightly), so tissue delivery falls sharply. It also binds cytochrome c oxidase and myoglobin and triggers inflammatory brain injury. Sources: house fires, faulty furnaces and heaters, generators or vehicles in enclosed spaces. Several people in one household with headache, nausea and confusion, worse at home, is the classic clue. PaO2 is normal and standard pulse oximetry reads falsely normal, because carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light like oxyhemoglobin; a co-oximeter measures it. Cherry-red skin is an unreliable, late sign. Delayed neurologic sequelae (memory, personality and movement disorders) can follow days to weeks later; injury to the globus pallidus is typical.

Methemoglobinemia

Methemoglobin contains ferric (Fe3+) iron, which cannot bind oxygen and makes the remaining ferrous hemes hold oxygen more tightly (left shift). Causes: oxidizing drugs such as topical anesthetics (benzocaine, lidocaine sprays), dapsone, nitrates and nitrites (including well water in infants), primaquine and rasburicase; rarely, congenital cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency or hemoglobin M. Signs: cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen, chocolate-brown blood, pulse oximetry stuck near 85%, and a normal PaO2 (a "saturation gap"). Normally, NADH-dependent cytochrome b5 reductase keeps methemoglobin below about 1–2%. Methylene blue provides a second route: it is reduced to leucomethylene blue by NADPH–methemoglobin reductase, then reduces Fe3+ back to Fe2+. NADPH comes from the pentose phosphate pathway (G6PD), so methylene blue may fail and can provoke hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

High altitude

Barometric pressure falls with altitude, so inspired PO2 falls although FiO2 stays 0.21. Acclimatization:

  1. Immediate: low PaO2 stimulates the carotid bodies → hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis (which itself limits the ventilatory rise at first).
  2. Days: the kidneys excrete bicarbonate, correcting pH and allowing ventilation to rise further; 2,3-BPG increases.
  3. Weeks: erythropoietin increases red cell mass; hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction raises pulmonary arterial pressure, which can cause right ventricular hypertrophy with chronic exposure.

Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, causing bicarbonate diuresis and a metabolic acidosis that stimulates ventilation and speeds acclimatization. Exaggerated, uneven hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction causes high-altitude pulmonary edema (a noncardiogenic, high-pressure leak); vasogenic brain edema causes high-altitude cerebral edema.

Exam trap: CO poisoning and methemoglobinemia both lower oxygen content with a normal PaO2, but pulse oximetry reads near-normal in CO poisoning and about 85% in methemoglobinemia.

Bridge: fetal hemoglobin's left shift lets the fetus take oxygen from maternal blood across the placenta, and it is why hydroxyurea (which raises HbF) helps sickle cell disease.

s23b-s-090701-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Evaluating a pleural effusion

  1. Imaging. Upright chest x-ray shows blunting of the costophrenic angle at about 200 mL (the lateral film shows less); ultrasound detects small effusions, reveals septations and guides needle placement. CT shows pleural thickening, masses and the underlying lung.
  2. Diagnostic thoracentesis for any new effusion without an obvious cause, any effusion with fever (rule out infection), or a "heart failure" effusion that is unilateral, unequal, painful or fails to resolve with diuresis. Bilateral, symmetric effusions in decompensated heart failure can be treated with diuresis first. Ultrasound guidance lowers the risk of pneumothorax.
  3. Send: protein, LDH (with serum values), glucose, pH (in a blood gas syringe, for suspected infection), cell count and differential, Gram stain and culture, cytology; add triglycerides (milky fluid), amylase, adenosine deaminase (tuberculosis), or hematocrit as the setting suggests.

Parapneumonic effusion and empyema

CategoryFluidManagement
Uncomplicated parapneumonicFree-flowing, pH ≥ 7.2, glucose ≥ 60 mg/dL, Gram stain and culture negativeAntibiotics alone; reassess if no improvement
Complicated parapneumonicpH < 7.2, glucose < 60 mg/dL, or loculated, or large (more than half the hemithorax)Antibiotics plus chest tube drainage
EmpyemaFrank pus, or organisms on Gram stain or cultureAntibiotics plus chest tube drainage

If loculations prevent drainage, instill intrapleural tissue plasminogen activator with DNase; failure leads to video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) for debridement, and decortication for an organized peel. Antibiotics for empyema need anaerobic coverage and usually continue for several weeks.

Other effusions

  • Malignant effusion: confirmed by cytology (repeat once if negative) or pleuroscopic biopsy. Recurrent symptomatic effusions are palliated with an indwelling pleural catheter or talc pleurodesis (needs a lung that re-expands); repeated thoracenteses are a poor long-term plan.
  • Chylothorax: drain, then a low-fat diet with medium-chain triglycerides (absorbed directly into portal blood, bypassing lymphatics) or bowel rest with parenteral nutrition; octreotide is sometimes used; thoracic duct ligation or embolization for persistent high-output leaks; treat lymphoma if present. Prolonged leaks cause malnutrition, lymphopenia and immunodeficiency.
  • Tuberculous effusion: lymphocytic exudate with high adenosine deaminase; pleural biopsy has the highest yield (fluid culture is often negative).
  • Effusion in a patient on diuretics that meets Light's criteria narrowly: a serum-minus-pleural albumin gradient > 1.2 g/dL (or protein gradient > 3.1 g/dL) supports a transudate from heart failure.

Hemothorax after trauma

Place a large-bore chest tube. Proceed to urgent thoracotomy if the initial drainage is about 1,500 mL or more, if bleeding continues at about 200 mL per hour for 2–4 hours, or if the patient remains unstable despite resuscitation. A retained clot that the tube does not clear is removed by early VATS (within about a week) to prevent empyema and fibrothorax.

Pneumothorax

  • Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis: hypotension, distended neck veins, absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation in a trauma or ventilated patient. Decompress immediately (needle decompression at the 4th–5th intercostal space in the midaxillary line or the 2nd intercostal space in the midclavicular line, or finger thoracostomy), then place a chest tube. Do not wait for an x-ray.
  • Primary spontaneous, clinically stable: small and minimally symptomatic → observation (supplemental oxygen speeds reabsorption) with a repeat chest radiograph; larger or symptomatic → needle aspiration or a small-bore chest drain. Conservative management is increasingly accepted even for larger collections when the patient is stable and comfortable.
  • Secondary spontaneous: almost always admit and drain (small-bore tube), because reserve is poor.
  • Recurrence: after a second ipsilateral episode, a first contralateral one, bilateral or persistent air leak (more than 3–5 days), or in high-risk occupations (pilots, divers), offer VATS with bleb resection and pleurodesis. Smoking cessation lowers recurrence. Avoid air travel until resolved and avoid scuba diving permanently unless definitive surgery has been done.
  • Open ("sucking") chest wound: cover with an occlusive dressing taped on three sides, then a chest tube away from the wound.

Pneumomediastinum and mediastinitis

Spontaneous pneumomediastinum in a young person with asthma or after a Valsalva effort is benign: analgesia and observation. If it follows forceful vomiting, with severe chest pain, fever or a left effusion, suspect esophageal rupture (Boerhaave syndrome): confirm with water-soluble contrast esophagography or CT with oral contrast (barium is avoided first because it inflames the mediastinum if it leaks), keep the patient nil by mouth, give broad-spectrum antibiotics with antifungal cover, and arrange early surgical repair. Post-sternotomy mediastinitis (fever, sternal instability or "click", wound drainage, usually 1–3 weeks after surgery; S aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci) needs surgical debridement and IV antibiotics. Descending necrotizing mediastinitis from a dental abscess needs drainage of both the neck and the mediastinum.

Mediastinal masses

CT with contrast localizes the mass. Anterior masses in a young man: measure β-hCG and AFP (germ cell tumors) and LDH; check for symptoms of myasthenia before anesthesia. Thymomas are resected. Large anterior masses can cause airway collapse on induction of general anesthesia; biopsy under local anesthesia when possible.

Two numbers for pleural fluid: pH < 7.2 means drain the infected effusion; triglycerides > 110 mg/dL means chylothorax.

s23b-s-090701-s1-01.bodyHtml:
The pleural space

The visceral pleura covers the lung; the parietal pleura lines the chest wall, diaphragm and mediastinum. Only the parietal pleura has somatic pain fibers (intercostal nerves; the central diaphragm via the phrenic nerve, so its irritation refers pain to the shoulder). A few milliliters of fluid are filtered from parietal systemic capillaries and removed by parietal lymphatic stomata, which can increase their clearance many-fold. An effusion forms when filtration exceeds lymphatic removal.

MechanismFluid typeExamples
Raised capillary hydrostatic pressureTransudateHeart failure (the commonest cause of all effusions; often bilateral, right larger than left)
Low plasma oncotic pressureTransudateNephrotic syndrome, severe hypoalbuminemia
Fluid crossing the diaphragm or from another spaceTransudateCirrhosis (hepatic hydrothorax, usually right-sided), peritoneal dialysis, urinothorax
Increased capillary permeability (pleural inflammation)ExudatePneumonia (parapneumonic), tuberculosis, PE, autoimmune disease (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis), pancreatitis
Impaired lymphatic drainageExudateMalignancy (lung, breast, lymphoma, mesothelioma), chylothorax

Light's criteria: an effusion is an exudate if any one is met: pleural/serum protein > 0.5; pleural/serum LDH > 0.6; pleural LDH > two-thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum. The criteria are very sensitive for exudates but misclassify about a quarter of transudates in patients already on diuretics; a serum-minus-pleural albumin gradient > 1.2 g/dL then favors a transudate.

Physical examination of the chest

ConditionPercussionTactile fremitusBreath soundsTrachea
Pleural effusionDull ("stony")DecreasedDecreasedAway if large

Special effusions

  • Complicated parapneumonic effusion and empyema. Bacteria and neutrophils in the pleural space consume glucose and produce lactic acid and CO2, so pleural pH falls below 7.2 and glucose below 60 mg/dL; LDH climbs. Empyema is frank pus or organisms on Gram stain or culture. Fibrin deposition then loculates the fluid and, untreated, a fibrous peel can trap the lung. Common organisms: Streptococcus species (including the S anginosus group), S aureus, anaerobes after aspiration, and gram-negative rods.
  • Chylothorax. Milky fluid with triglycerides > 110 mg/dL (chylomicrons). The thoracic duct ascends through the aortic hiatus, runs in the posterior mediastinum between the aorta and azygos vein, crosses to the left at about T4–T5 and empties at the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins. Injury during esophageal, aortic or spinal surgery, or obstruction by lymphoma, causes chylothorax; injury below the crossing gives a right-sided collection, above it a left-sided one.
  • Hemothorax: pleural hematocrit more than half the blood hematocrit; trauma, iatrogenic injury, rarely malignancy or anticoagulation.
  • Low glucose effusions: empyema, rheumatoid arthritis (very low glucose), tuberculosis, malignancy, lupus. Lymphocyte-predominant exudates: tuberculosis, malignancy, lymphoma. A high pleural amylase suggests pancreatitis or esophageal rupture.

Pneumothorax

Air in the pleural space removes the negative pressure that holds the lung expanded, so the lung recoils inward and the chest wall springs outward.

  • Primary spontaneous: no known lung disease; tall, thin young men, smoking (the strongest modifiable risk). Rupture of apical subpleural blebs. Sudden pleuritic pain and dyspnea at rest.
  • Secondary spontaneous: underlying disease, most often COPD with bullae; also cystic fibrosis, Pneumocystis pneumonia, Marfan syndrome, lymphangioleiomyomatosis, catamenial (endometriosis). Less reserve, so symptoms are worse.
  • Traumatic and iatrogenic: rib fractures, penetrating injury, central line placement, lung biopsy, barotrauma on a ventilator.
  • Tension pneumothorax: a one-way valve lets air in but not out. Pleural pressure becomes positive throughout the cycle, the mediastinum shifts to the opposite side, and venous return falls (vena caval compression and kinking, high intrathoracic pressure): obstructive shock with distended neck veins, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, absent breath sounds and hypoxemia.

The mediastinum

CompartmentContentsTypical masses
Anterior (prevascular)Thymus, fat, lymph nodesThymoma, teratoma and other germ cell tumors, lymphoma, retrosternal thyroid goiter
Middle (visceral)Heart, great vessels, trachea, esophagus, lymph nodesLymphadenopathy (lymphoma, sarcoidosis, metastasis), bronchogenic and pericardial cysts, aortic aneurysm, esophageal lesions
Posterior (paravertebral)Sympathetic chain, nerve rootsNeurogenic tumors: schwannoma and neurofibroma in adults; neuroblastoma and ganglioneuroma (neural crest) in children

Thymoma is associated with myasthenia gravis (antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor), pure red cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinemia. Germ cell tumors in young men raise serum hCG or AFP. Anterior masses can compress the airway or superior vena cava, which matters for sedation and anesthesia.

  • Pneumomediastinum: air tracks from ruptured alveoli along the bronchovascular sheaths into the mediastinum (Macklin effect) in asthma, forceful Valsalva or inhaled drug use; it can also come from the esophagus (Boerhaave syndrome after forceful vomiting) or the airway. A crunching sound synchronous with the heartbeat (Hamman sign) and subcutaneous emphysema in the neck are clues.
  • Mediastinitis: acute after esophageal perforation, sternotomy (deep sternal wound infection) or spread from a dental or pharyngeal infection along the deep neck spaces (descending necrotizing mediastinitis). Chronic fibrosing mediastinitis follows histoplasmosis or tuberculosis.

The chest wall

Costochondritis is inflammation of the costochondral or costosternal junctions, usually of ribs 2–5, giving sharp anterior chest pain reproduced by pressing on the joints, without swelling. Tietze syndrome is rarer and causes visible, tender swelling, usually of one upper costal cartilage. Both are diagnoses of exclusion: reproducible tenderness does not rule out acute coronary syndrome, so obtain an ECG in adults with risk factors. Treatment is reassurance, NSAIDs and stretching.

Pleuritis (pleurisy) causes sharp pain on inspiration and a pleural friction rub. Causes: viral infection (coxsackievirus B can also cause epidemic pleurodynia), pneumonia, PE, SLE and other autoimmune diseases, drug-induced lupus, and uremia.

Trachea pulled toward an opaque hemithorax means collapse (obstructed bronchus); pushed away means a large effusion or tension pneumothorax.
Rheumatoid effusions have strikingly low glucose and pH and high LDH; they can look like empyema, so read the clinical setting along with the numbers.

Upper airway emergencies are judged by time to obstruction. The first question is always whether the patient can keep the airway open and how fast that is changing. Signs of a threatened airway include stridor, a muffled or hoarse voice, drooling or inability to swallow secretions, tripod posture, rising work of breathing, and falling consciousness. Oxygen saturation is a late sign.

Choking and foreign-body airway obstruction

  • Effective cough (can speak or cough forcefully): encourage coughing and watch closely; do not perform blind finger sweeps or blows that could push the object deeper.
  • Severe obstruction in a conscious adult or child older than 1 year (cannot speak, silent cough, hands at the throat): abdominal thrusts, repeated until the object comes out or the patient becomes unresponsive. Use chest thrusts instead in late pregnancy or marked obesity.
  • Severe obstruction in a conscious infant (younger than 1 year): cycles of 5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts, with the head held lower than the chest. Abdominal thrusts are avoided in infants because of the risk to the liver.
  • Unresponsive: start CPR; look in the mouth before rescue breaths and remove a visible object.

A toddler with a sudden choking episode, then cough and a unilateral wheeze or reduced breath sounds, has an aspirated foreign body until proven otherwise, even when the episode was not witnessed. Most objects (nuts, seeds, small toy parts) are not radiopaque, so a normal plain film does not exclude one; expiratory or bilateral decubitus views may show air trapping on the affected side. Rigid bronchoscopy under general anesthesia is both diagnostic and therapeutic and is the treatment of choice when the history or examination is suggestive.

Smoke inhalation and airway burns

Clues: an enclosed-space fire, facial burns, singed nasal hairs, soot in the mouth or carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness, stridor, and drooling. Supraglottic swelling progresses over the first day, especially once fluid resuscitation starts. Intubate early when there are signs of airway involvement (hoarseness, stridor, deep facial or neck burns, rising work of breathing); waiting can turn an easy intubation into an impossible one. Give 100% oxygen by a tight-fitting non-rebreather mask or through the endotracheal tube until carboxyhemoglobin is measured on a co-oximetry blood gas; pulse oximetry is unreliable. 100% oxygen shortens the half-life of carboxyhemoglobin from several hours on room air to roughly an hour. Hyperbaric oxygen is considered for severe carbon monoxide poisoning (for example loss of consciousness, neurologic deficits, cardiac ischemia, pregnancy with a high level). Suspect cyanide with severe lactic acidosis, and treat empirically with hydroxocobalamin.

Angioedema

  • Anaphylaxis (urticaria, wheeze, hypotension, often a trigger such as food, sting or drug): intramuscular epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh first, repeated every 5–15 minutes as needed; then fluids, oxygen, and adjuncts (antihistamines, glucocorticoids, inhaled β2-agonist). Adjuncts never replace epinephrine.
  • ACE inhibitor angioedema (lips, tongue, floor of mouth; no hives; can appear years after starting the drug): stop the ACE inhibitor permanently and never restart any drug of the class; protect the airway (early fiberoptic intubation if the tongue or larynx is involved). Epinephrine, antihistamines and steroids are often given but usually have little effect. An ARB has a small risk of recurrence and is usually avoided soon after an episode, so an unrelated class (thiazide, calcium channel blocker) is the simplest replacement for blood pressure.
  • Hereditary angioedema (recurrent swelling of the face, limbs, bowel wall with colicky abdominal pain; often a family history; onset in childhood or adolescence; attacks triggered by trauma, dental work, estrogen): screen with C4, then confirm with C1 inhibitor level and function. Treat a laryngeal attack with C1 inhibitor concentrate, icatibant or ecallantide, and prepare for a surgical airway. Fresh frozen plasma (which contains C1 inhibitor) is a fallback when targeted drugs are not available. Give short-term prophylaxis before dental or surgical procedures; avoid estrogen-containing contraceptives and ACE inhibitors.

Postoperative neck hematoma

After thyroid, parathyroid or carotid surgery, an expanding hematoma can compress the airway and cause venous congestion of the larynx. Stridor, respiratory distress or a tense swelling under the wound needs immediate opening of the incision at the bedside (skin and deep sutures) to evacuate the clot, then return to the operating room. Do not wait for imaging; intubation through a swollen, deviated larynx can fail.

Laryngeal trauma

A blow to the front of the neck (steering wheel, clothesline injury, strangulation) can fracture the larynx. The classic triad is hoarseness, subcutaneous emphysema and palpable fracture (loss of the thyroid prominence, crepitus), with pain on swallowing, hemoptysis and stridor. If the airway is stable, CT of the larynx and flexible laryngoscopy define the injury. If the airway is threatened, a tracheostomy under local anesthesia is preferred; blind orotracheal intubation can create a false passage or complete a partial tear, and a cricothyrotomy places the opening at or next to the injured segment.

Surgical airway

A cricothyrotomy is the emergency surgical airway in adults when the airway cannot be secured by intubation and the patient cannot be oxygenated (for example massive midface trauma, severe swelling, or failed intubation with failing bag-mask ventilation). In children younger than about 10–12 years, needle cricothyrotomy with jet ventilation is generally preferred to a surgical cricothyrotomy because the membrane is small and the cricoid is the main support of the airway.

Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury after neck surgery

  • Unilateral: hoarse, weak, breathy voice and sometimes aspiration of thin liquids. Confirm with laryngoscopy; many recover over months; voice therapy or medialization procedures if not.
  • Bilateral: inspiratory stridor and respiratory distress soon after extubation, with a near-normal voice. This is an airway emergency: reintubate, then a tracheostomy is often needed.

Epistaxis

Steps for anterior bleeding: sit the patient upright leaning forward and apply firm continuous pressure to the soft part of the nose for 10–15 minutes; if bleeding continues, apply a topical vasoconstrictor (oxymetazoline) and anesthetic, find the bleeding point and cauterize it (silver nitrate, one side of the septum at a time); then anterior packing if needed. Posterior bleeding (bleeding from both nostrils or down the throat despite anterior packing) needs a posterior pack or balloon, admission, and often ENT for endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation or embolization. Check the blood count and clotting tests in heavy or recurrent bleeding, and ask about anticoagulants. Recurrent unilateral bleeding in an adolescent boy with nasal obstruction suggests juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, which must not be biopsied in clinic.

Nasal fracture and septal hematoma

Always look inside the nose after nasal trauma. A septal hematoma is a soft, bluish or red bulge of the septum that does not shrink with a vasoconstrictor. It needs prompt incision and drainage and packing, with antibiotics in many protocols, to prevent cartilage necrosis, abscess and saddle-nose deformity. An isolated nasal bone fracture with no hematoma is reassessed after the swelling settles (several days), with closed reduction if the nose is deformed.

Tracheostomy bleeding

Small streaks of blood are common soon after the procedure, but bright red bleeding from 3 days to several weeks after a tracheostomy suggests a tracheoinnominate fistula. A sentinel bleed in a stable patient calls for urgent bronchoscopy in the operating room with a surgeon present. A massive bleed calls for overinflating the tracheostomy cuff to tamponade the bleeding and, if that fails, inserting a finger through the stoma to compress the artery against the back of the sternum, while the patient goes straight to the operating room.

Exam trap. In laryngeal fracture, the instinct to perform a cricothyrotomy is wrong: the surgical airway should be placed below the injury (tracheostomy).

High yield. Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes stridor with a nearly normal voice, because both folds rest close together.

Thoracic injuries are found and treated during the primary survey (airway with cervical spine protection, breathing, circulation with hemorrhage control, disability, exposure). Several can kill within minutes and are treated on clinical grounds alone, before any imaging.

Immediately life-threatening injuries

InjuryKey findingsImmediate treatment
Tension pneumothoraxRespiratory distress, hypotension, absent breath sounds and hyperresonance on one side, distended neck veins; tracheal deviation is lateNeedle decompression (4th or 5th intercostal space just in front of the midaxillary line in adults, or 2nd intercostal space in the midclavicular line) or finger thoracostomy, then a chest tube. Do not wait for an x-ray.
Open pneumothoraxChest wall wound that bubbles or sucks air with breathingSterile occlusive dressing taped on three sides (a flutter valve) or a vented chest seal, then a chest tube away from the wound and later surgical closure
Massive hemothoraxShock, dullness and absent breath sounds on one side, flat neck veinsLarge-bore IV access and blood products, chest tube; thoracotomy if the initial drainage is about 1,500 mL or more, or if drainage continues at roughly 200 mL/h for 2–4 hours, or if the patient remains unstable
Flail chest with pulmonary contusionParadoxical chest wall motion, crepitus, hypoxemiaOxygen, strong analgesia, careful fluids; ventilation if respiratory failure develops
Cardiac tamponadeHypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds; pericardial fluid on FASTSee the pericardium and cardiac trauma sections

Tension pneumothorax

This is a clinical diagnosis. In a patient with hypotension and absent breath sounds on one side after trauma, or a ventilated patient whose peak and plateau pressures rise suddenly with hypotension and one silent hemithorax, decompress immediately. Bedside ultrasound (absent lung sliding) helps when available but should not delay treatment. Needle decompression converts the tension to a simple pneumothorax; a chest tube must follow.

Hemothorax

A hemothorax large enough to see on a chest x-ray is drained with a chest tube, which both evacuates the blood (preventing a trapped lung, fibrothorax and empyema) and measures the rate of bleeding. Small hemothoraces in stable patients may be observed. Blood that remains after the tube (retained hemothorax) is evacuated early, usually by video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery within the first several days. An autotransfusion setup can return the drained blood.

Rib fractures and flail chest

The main danger of rib fractures is pneumonia from poor cough and splinting. Risk rises with the number of fractured ribs and with age; older adults with multiple fractures are often admitted for observation, sometimes to intensive care. Management is multimodal analgesia (scheduled acetaminophen, NSAIDs if safe, opioids sparingly) plus regional anesthesia such as a thoracic epidural or paravertebral or serratus anterior plane block when oral analgesia is not enough, incentive spirometry and early mobilization. Surgical rib fixation is an option for selected patients with flail chest or severe displacement. In flail chest, avoid unnecessary fluid loading, because contused lung is prone to edema; intubate when gas exchange or work of breathing fails rather than for the flail itself.

Tracheobronchial injury

Suspect it when a chest tube shows a large continuous air leak and the lung does not re-expand, or when pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema keep increasing. Bronchoscopy confirms the diagnosis; operative repair is usually needed. A second chest tube may be required while awaiting surgery, and intubation may need to be guided into the uninjured bronchus.

Diaphragmatic injury

Blunt rupture is most often on the left. The chest x-ray may show an elevated or obscured hemidiaphragm, bowel gas in the chest, or a nasogastric tube that curls up into the left chest; CT helps but can miss small tears. Penetrating wounds below the nipple line or the tip of the scapula can injure the diaphragm even when imaging looks normal, and laparoscopy finds occult tears. Acute injuries are repaired surgically, usually through a laparotomy, which also allows the frequently associated abdominal injuries to be treated. Unrepaired tears enlarge and can present years later with bowel obstruction or strangulation.

Mechanically ventilated patients

FindingPeak pressurePlateau pressureTypical causes
Increased airway resistanceHighNormalMucus plug, biting or kinked tube, bronchospasm
Decreased respiratory system complianceHighHighTension pneumothorax, mainstem intubation, pulmonary edema, ARDS, auto-PEEP, abdominal distension

In a sudden crisis, disconnect the ventilator and bag by hand with 100% oxygen while checking the tube, listening to both sides and looking for pneumothorax.

Drowning (submersion injury)

  • Rescue breaths and oxygenation come first, because the arrest is hypoxic; the cervical spine is immobilized only when there is a history suggesting injury (diving, high-energy mechanism).
  • Abdominal thrusts to remove water are not recommended; they delay ventilation and cause vomiting.
  • Patients who are alert with normal oxygen saturation and a normal lung examination after a period of observation in the emergency department (commonly 4–8 hours) can usually be discharged; anyone with persistent hypoxemia, abnormal lung findings or altered mental status is admitted.
  • Prophylactic antibiotics and glucocorticoids are not routinely given.

Diving injuries

Neurologic symptoms within minutes of surfacing (stroke-like deficits, confusion, loss of consciousness) suggest arterial gas embolism. Joint pain, skin changes, or spinal cord symptoms appearing over hours suggest decompression sickness. Both are treated with 100% oxygen, the patient lying flat, and urgent hyperbaric oxygen therapy; an associated pneumothorax is drained first.

Exam trap. If the scenario describes hypotension with absent breath sounds on one side, the answer is decompression, never "obtain a chest x-ray".

High yield. A large persistent air leak with a lung that will not re-expand after a chest tube means a tracheobronchial injury: arrange bronchoscopy.

Large-bore IV access and blood products, chest tube; thoracotomy if the initial drainage is about 1,500 mL or more, or if drainage continues at roughly 200 mL/h for 2–4 hours, or if the patient remains unstable
Paradoxical chest wall motion, crepitus, hypoxemia
Oxygen, strong analgesia, careful fluids; ventilation if respiratory failure develops
Hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds; pericardial fluid on FAST
See the pericardium and cardiac trauma sections

This is a clinical diagnosis. In a patient with hypotension and absent breath sounds on one side after trauma, or a ventilated patient whose peak and plateau pressures rise suddenly with hypotension and one silent hemithorax, decompress immediately. Bedside ultrasound (absent lung sliding) helps when available but should not delay treatment. Needle decompression converts the tension to a simple pneumothorax; a chest tube must follow.

A hemothorax large enough to see on a chest x-ray is drained with a chest tube, which both evacuates the blood (preventing a trapped lung, fibrothorax and empyema) and measures the rate of bleeding. Small hemothoraces in stable patients may be observed. Blood that remains after the tube (retained hemothorax) is evacuated early, usually by video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery within the first several days. An autotransfusion setup can return the drained blood.

The main danger of rib fractures is pneumonia from poor cough and splinting. Risk rises with the number of fractured ribs and with age; older adults with multiple fractures are often admitted for observation, sometimes to intensive care. Management is multimodal analgesia (scheduled acetaminophen, NSAIDs if safe, opioids sparingly) plus

such as a thoracic epidural or paravertebral or serratus anterior plane block when oral analgesia is not enough, incentive spirometry and early mobilization. Surgical rib fixation is an option for selected patients with flail chest or severe displacement. In flail chest, avoid unnecessary fluid loading, because contused lung is prone to edema; intubate when gas exchange or work of breathing fails rather than for the flail itself.
Suspect it when a chest tube shows a large continuous air leak and the lung does not re-expand, or when pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema keep increasing.
confirms the diagnosis; operative repair is usually needed. A second chest tube may be required while awaiting surgery, and intubation may need to be guided into the uninjured bronchus.

Blunt rupture is most often on the left. The chest x-ray may show an elevated or obscured hemidiaphragm, bowel gas in the chest, or a nasogastric tube that curls up into the left chest; CT helps but can miss small tears. Penetrating wounds below the nipple line or the tip of the scapula can injure the diaphragm even when imaging looks normal, and laparoscopy finds occult tears. Acute injuries are repaired surgically, usually through a laparotomy, which also allows the frequently associated abdominal injuries to be treated. Unrepaired tears enlarge and can present years later with bowel obstruction or strangulation.
Mucus plug, biting or kinked tube, bronchospasm
Tension pneumothorax, mainstem intubation, pulmonary edema, ARDS, auto-PEEP, abdominal distension
In a sudden crisis, disconnect the ventilator and bag by hand with 100% oxygen while checking the tube, listening to both sides and looking for pneumothorax.
Rescue breaths and oxygenation come first, because the arrest is hypoxic; the cervical spine is immobilized only when there is a history suggesting injury (diving, high-energy mechanism).
Abdominal thrusts to remove water are not recommended; they delay ventilation and cause vomiting.

Patients who are alert with normal oxygen saturation and a normal lung examination after a period of observation in the emergency department (commonly 4–8 hours) can usually be discharged; anyone with persistent hypoxemia, abnormal lung findings or altered mental status is admitted.
Prophylactic antibiotics and glucocorticoids are not routinely given.

Neurologic symptoms within minutes of surfacing (stroke-like deficits, confusion, loss of consciousness) suggest arterial gas embolism. Joint pain, skin changes, or spinal cord symptoms appearing over hours suggest decompression sickness. Both are treated with 100% oxygen, the patient lying flat, and urgent
therapy; an associated pneumothorax is drained first.
If the scenario describes hypotension with absent breath sounds on one side, the answer is decompression, never "obtain a chest x-ray".
A large persistent air leak with a lung that will not re-expand after a chest tube means a tracheobronchial injury: arrange bronchoscopy.

s23b-s-090801-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Upper airway injury is mostly an anatomy problem: where the narrowest point is, which nerve moves which fold, which vessel lies next to a tube. Step 1 tests the structures and mechanisms; Step 2 CK tests what to do first.

Surface anatomy of the front of the neck

From above down in the midline: the hyoid bone, the thyrohyoid membrane, the thyroid cartilage (laryngeal prominence), the cricothyroid membrane, the cricoid cartilage (the only complete ring of the airway), then the tracheal rings with the thyroid isthmus usually over rings 2–4. The cricothyroid membrane is the target for an emergency surgical airway because it lies just under skin and fascia, with no major vessels or muscles in the midline at that level.

The vocal folds sit at the level of the thyroid cartilage, a little above the cricothyroid membrane, so a cricothyrotomy enters the airway below the glottis. In infants and young children the narrowest part of the airway has traditionally been taught as the subglottis at the cricoid ring; a small amount of mucosal swelling there sharply raises airflow resistance, because resistance rises steeply as the radius falls (to the fourth power in laminar flow).

Nerves of the larynx

NerveMotorSensoryInjury pattern
Recurrent laryngeal (vagus)All intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroidBelow the vocal foldsUnilateral: hoarse, breathy voice. Bilateral: both folds lie near the midline, so the airway narrows with inspiratory stridor
Superior laryngeal, external branchCricothyroid (tenses the folds)—Loss of high pitch and projection; voice tires easily
Superior laryngeal, internal branch—Above the vocal folds (supraglottis)Loss of the cough reflex in the supraglottis, so aspiration

The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that abducts (opens) the vocal folds. It is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, so bilateral recurrent nerve injury leaves both folds adducted. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch near the ligamentum arteriosum and the right loops under the right subclavian artery; both run in the tracheoesophageal groove, close to the inferior thyroid artery, which is why thyroid and parathyroid surgery puts them at risk. The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid vessels.

Bridge. A long left recurrent nerve explains hoarseness from causes in the chest: an aortic arch aneurysm, a large left atrium, or a tumor at the aortopulmonary window.

Foreign bodies

An aspirated object in an older child or adult usually enters the right main bronchus, which is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left. In a person lying on the back, aspirated material reaches the posterior segments of the upper lobes and the superior segments of the lower lobes; when upright, the basal segments of the right lower lobe. A partial obstruction can act as a one-way valve: air enters on inspiration and is trapped on expiration, so the affected side looks hyperlucent and hyperinflated, especially on an expiratory or decubitus film. A complete obstruction instead causes collapse (atelectasis) distal to the object.

Angioedema: histamine versus bradykinin

Mast-cell (histamine) angioedemaBradykinin angioedema
ExamplesAnaphylaxis, allergic angioedemaHereditary angioedema (C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency or dysfunction), ACE inhibitor angioedema
Urticaria, itchUsually presentAbsent
OnsetMinutesHours; attacks can last days
Response to epinephrine, antihistamines, glucocorticoidsGoodPoor
Targeted therapyEpinephrineC1 inhibitor concentrate, bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist (icatibant), kallikrein inhibitor

C1 esterase inhibitor normally restrains the complement C1 complex and kallikrein. Without it, kallikrein cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen into bradykinin, which increases vascular permeability. Unchecked C1 also consumes C4, so a low C4 level, including between attacks, is the usual screening clue. In type I hereditary angioedema the C1 inhibitor level is low; in type II the level is normal or high but the protein does not work, so the functional assay is low. ACE (kininase II) normally breaks down bradykinin, so ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin levels; the same mechanism causes the dry cough.

Epinephrine works in anaphylaxis because α1 stimulation constricts mucosal vessels and reduces edema, β1 supports the heart, and β2 relaxes bronchial smooth muscle and stabilizes mast cells.

Burns and inhalation injury

Hot gas rarely injures the airway below the vocal folds, because the upper airway absorbs heat efficiently; thermal injury mostly causes swelling of the supraglottis, which can close the airway over hours. Below the cords, injury is chemical (toxic smoke). Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with roughly 200–250 times the affinity of oxygen, lowers oxygen content while the dissolved oxygen (PaO2) stays normal, and shifts the oxygen–hemoglobin curve to the left, so the remaining oxygen is released poorly. Standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin and reads falsely normal. Cyanide from burning plastics blocks cytochrome oxidase and causes a lactic acidosis.

Nose

About 90% of nosebleeds are anterior, from the Kiesselbach plexus on the anterior septum, where branches of the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial arteries meet. Posterior bleeds come mostly from the sphenopalatine artery (a branch of the maxillary artery) and are heavier and harder to control. The septal cartilage has no blood supply of its own; it is nourished by the overlying perichondrium. A septal hematoma lifts the perichondrium off the cartilage, so the cartilage can die within days and become infected, giving a septal abscess or perforation and a saddle-nose deformity.

Tracheostomy and the innominate artery

The brachiocephalic (innominate) artery crosses in front of the trachea low in the neck. A low-placed tracheostomy, or pressure from the tube's tip or cuff, can erode through the anterior tracheal wall into it. The result, a tracheoinnominate fistula, typically appears in the first weeks after the procedure; a small "sentinel" bleed often comes before a massive one.

High yield. Opening the vocal folds depends on one muscle (posterior cricoarytenoid) and one nerve (recurrent laryngeal). Pitch depends on the cricothyroid and the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

Exam trap. Angioedema without hives in a patient on an ACE inhibitor or with a family history is bradykinin mediated; antihistamines and steroids will not stop it, and the airway may still need to be secured.

s23b-s-090802-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Chest trauma kills by two routes: failure of gas exchange (the lung or chest wall cannot ventilate, or blood shunts past collapsed or bruised lung) and failure of circulation (blood loss, or obstruction of venous return). Step 1 asks why each injury produces its signs.

Pleural pressure and the pneumothorax

At rest the lung's elastic recoil pulls inward and the chest wall pulls outward, so pressure in the pleural space is below atmospheric (about −5 cm H2O at the end of a normal breath). Any opening between the pleural space and the air (a chest wall wound) or the airways (a torn lung or bronchus) lets air in until the pressure equalizes; the lung collapses from its own recoil and the chest wall springs slightly outward.

In a tension pneumothorax the leak behaves as a one-way valve. Air enters with each breath but cannot leave, so pressure in that hemithorax rises above atmospheric. The mediastinum is pushed to the other side, the vena cavae are compressed and kinked, venous return falls, and cardiac output falls: this is obstructive shock, with distended neck veins (unless the patient is also bleeding), tachycardia and hypotension. On the affected side breath sounds are absent and the percussion note is hyperresonant; the trachea deviates away late, if at all.

Intercostal vessels and the intercostal nerve run in the costal groove along the lower border of each rib (vein, artery, nerve from top to bottom). Needles and chest tubes are therefore passed just over the upper border of the rib below the chosen space.

Open pneumothorax

A chest wall defect larger than roughly two-thirds of the tracheal diameter offers less resistance than the airway, so with each inspiration air moves preferentially through the wound ("sucking chest wound") and ventilation of the lungs fails.

Flail chest and pulmonary contusion

When several adjacent ribs are each broken in two or more places, a segment of chest wall loses its bony continuity with the rest of the cage. During inspiration the falling pleural pressure pulls the segment inward, and during expiration it moves outward: paradoxical movement.

The hypoxemia that follows is mostly due to the underlying pulmonary contusion, not the flail segment itself. A contusion is bleeding and edema into the alveoli and interstitium; perfused alveoli that are not ventilated act as a right-to-left shunt and areas of low ventilation lower V/Q, so the alveolar–arterial (A–a) oxygen gradient widens and supplemental oxygen corrects the hypoxemia only partly. Contusions typically worsen over the first 24–72 hours and may not be visible on the first chest film. Pain from the fractures causes splinting and shallow breaths, leading to atelectasis, retained secretions and pneumonia, which is why older adults with rib fractures do badly.

Hemothorax

Each hemithorax can hold a large share of the blood volume, so bleeding into it can cause hemorrhagic shock without any external sign. The usual sources are intercostal and internal thoracic (mammary) arteries, lung parenchyma, and great vessels. Signs: dullness to percussion and reduced breath sounds on the affected side, with flat neck veins if hypovolemic. Retained clot can organize into a fibrothorax or become infected (empyema).

Airway disruption

Most tracheobronchial ruptures from blunt trauma occur close to the carina, where the relatively fixed carina meets the mobile lungs during sudden deceleration or compression against a closed glottis. Clues are a pneumothorax with a large continuous air leak that does not re-expand despite a working chest tube, pneumomediastinum, subcutaneous emphysema and hemoptysis. A completely torn main bronchus can let the lung drop to the dependent part of the hemithorax away from the hilum ("fallen lung" sign).

Diaphragm

The diaphragm develops from the septum transversum, the pleuroperitoneal membranes, the dorsal esophageal mesentery and the body wall, and is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5), which explains pain referred to the shoulder after diaphragmatic irritation. Traumatic rupture is diagnosed far more often on the left, because the liver buffers the right hemidiaphragm. Abdominal contents (stomach, colon, spleen) herniate upward under the positive intra-abdominal pressure gradient.

Pressure and gas laws

  • Boyle's law (P × V constant at a fixed temperature): gas in the lungs of a diver who ascends while holding the breath expands as the surrounding pressure falls. Overdistended alveoli rupture, giving pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum or arterial gas embolism (air enters pulmonary veins and reaches the brain within minutes of surfacing). Decompression sickness is different: dissolved nitrogen comes out of solution in tissues when pressure falls too quickly (Henry's law).
  • Ventilator barotrauma: high pressures or volumes overdistend alveoli, causing air leak; lung-protective ventilation limits tidal volume and plateau pressure.
  • Primary blast injury: the pressure wave damages air-containing organs at air–tissue interfaces: the tympanic membrane (most often), the lungs (blast lung: alveolar hemorrhage and edema, the commonest fatal primary injury) and the bowel. Secondary injury is from flying fragments, tertiary from the body being thrown, and quaternary includes burns and toxic exposures.

Traumatic asphyxia

A sudden crush of the chest against a closed glottis forces blood backward from the right heart into the valveless veins of the head and neck. The result is striking craniofacial congestion and petechiae, subconjunctival hemorrhage and sometimes neurologic symptoms, with a sharp line at the level of the compression. Outcome depends on the associated injuries.

Drowning

The main harm in drowning is hypoxemia. Aspirated water, fresh or salt, washes out and inactivates surfactant and causes alveolar edema, so alveoli collapse and shunt rises, sometimes progressing to ARDS within hours. The old distinction between fresh-water and salt-water drowning has little practical importance because the volumes usually aspirated are small.

High yield. Tension pneumothorax and cardiac tamponade both cause hypotension with distended neck veins (obstructive shock). Breath sounds separate them: absent on one side in tension pneumothorax, normal in tamponade.

Exam trap. Hypoxemia after a flail chest is driven by the lung contusion beneath it, not by the paradoxical motion itself.

s23b-s-090901-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Signs of neonatal respiratory distress are tachypnea (above 60/min), grunting, nasal flaring, retractions and cyanosis. Start with gestational age, delivery history and a chest radiograph; check glucose and temperature, and consider sepsis (blood culture and antibiotics) in any infant whose cause is unclear, because group B streptococcal pneumonia can look like any of the conditions below.

ConditionTypical infantChest radiographManagement
Respiratory distress syndromePreterm (risk falls with each week), infant of a diabetic mother, maleLow volumes, diffuse fine granular (ground-glass) opacity with air bronchogramsCPAP from birth; intratracheal surfactant when oxygen needs rise on CPAP; mechanical ventilation if failing
Transient tachypnea of the newbornTerm or late preterm, cesarean without labor, maternal diabetesPerihilar streaking, fluid in the fissures, mild hyperinflationSupportive (oxygen, sometimes CPAP); resolves in 1–3 days
Meconium aspiration syndromeTerm or post-term, meconium-stained fluid, often fetal distressPatchy infiltrates, hyperinflation, air leakSupportive ventilation; watch for pneumothorax and persistent pulmonary hypertension
Congenital pneumonia or sepsisMaternal fever, prolonged rupture of membranes, GBS colonisationVariable; may mimic RDSCultures and empiric ampicillin plus gentamicin
Congenital diaphragmatic herniaOften diagnosed prenatallyBowel loops in the (usually left) chest, mediastinal shiftImmediate intubation, gastric decompression, gentle ventilation; delayed surgical repair
PneumothoraxAfter resuscitation or ventilation, meconiumAir without lung markingsNeedle aspiration or chest tube if significant

Preventing respiratory distress syndrome

A single course of antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone or dexamethasone) given to a pregnant person at risk of preterm delivery within 7 days, generally between 24 and 34 weeks, lowers neonatal death, RDS and intraventricular hemorrhage; it is also considered at the limit of viability and in selected late-preterm cases. Avoid scheduled cesarean delivery before 39 weeks without a medical indication.

Delivery room priorities

  • Meconium-stained fluid: a vigorous infant gets routine care. A non-vigorous infant is resuscitated in the usual sequence (warm, dry, position, clear the airway, then positive-pressure ventilation within the first minute if apneic or the heart rate is below 100/min). Routine intubation for tracheal suctioning is no longer recommended; it is reserved for an airway obstructed by meconium.
  • Known or suspected diaphragmatic hernia: avoid bag-mask ventilation, which inflates the bowel in the chest and further compresses the lungs. Intubate immediately, place an orogastric tube on suction, and ventilate gently. Repair is delayed until the infant is physiologically stable; survival depends mainly on the degree of pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension.
  • Suspected esophageal atresia (excess drooling, a tube that will not pass): nothing by mouth, keep the head raised, continuous suction of the upper pouch to prevent aspiration, look for VACTERL anomalies (echocardiography, renal ultrasound, spine films), then surgical repair.
A scaphoid abdomen and a shifted heart in a cyanotic newborn mean no bag and mask: intubate.

Cystic fibrosis on the newborn screen

Every US state screens newborns for cystic fibrosis, starting with blood immunoreactive trypsinogen (raised because pancreatic ducts are obstructed), often followed by a CFTR variant panel. A positive screen is not a diagnosis: the next step is a sweat chloride test at a CF centre (60 mmol/L or more confirms CF; intermediate values need further testing). Meconium ileus in a newborn is CF until proved otherwise. Infants with CF need pancreatic enzymes with feeds, fat-soluble vitamins and salt supplementation, and CFTR modulator therapy where the genotype qualifies.

Persistent unexplained respiratory distress, lobar collapse or a daily wet cough from birth in a term infant, especially with situs inversus, should prompt testing for primary ciliary dyskinesia.

(betamethasone or dexamethasone) given to a pregnant person at risk of preterm delivery within 7 days, generally between 24 and 34 weeks, lowers neonatal death, RDS and intraventricular hemorrhage; it is also considered at the limit of viability and in selected late-preterm cases. Avoid scheduled cesarean delivery before 39 weeks without a medical indication.

: a vigorous infant gets routine care. A non-vigorous infant is resuscitated in the usual sequence (warm, dry, position, clear the airway, then positive-pressure ventilation within the first minute if apneic or the heart rate is below 100/min). Routine intubation for tracheal suctioning is no longer recommended; it is reserved for an airway obstructed by meconium.

: avoid bag-mask ventilation, which inflates the bowel in the chest and further compresses the lungs. Intubate immediately, place an orogastric tube on suction, and ventilate gently. Repair is delayed until the infant is physiologically stable; survival depends mainly on the degree of pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension.

(excess drooling, a tube that will not pass): nothing by mouth, keep the head raised, continuous suction of the upper pouch to prevent aspiration, look for VACTERL anomalies (echocardiography, renal ultrasound, spine films), then surgical repair.
A scaphoid abdomen and a shifted heart in a cyanotic newborn mean no bag and mask: intubate.
Cystic fibrosis on the newborn screen
Every US state screens newborns for cystic fibrosis, starting with blood
(raised because pancreatic ducts are obstructed), often followed by a CFTR variant panel. A positive screen is not a diagnosis: the next step is a

at a CF centre (60 mmol/L or more confirms CF; intermediate values need further testing). Meconium ileus in a newborn is CF until proved otherwise. Infants with CF need pancreatic enzymes with feeds, fat-soluble vitamins and salt supplementation, and CFTR modulator therapy where the genotype qualifies.
Persistent unexplained respiratory distress, lobar collapse or a daily wet cough from birth in a term infant, especially with situs inversus, should prompt testing for primary ciliary dyskinesia.

Describe the sound first. Stertor (snoring) comes from the nose or pharynx; inspiratory stridor from the supraglottis or glottis; biphasic stridor from the subglottis or upper trachea or a fixed lesion; expiratory wheeze from the intrathoracic airway. Red flags for urgent evaluation are apneas, cyanosis, failure to thrive, severe retractions, feeding difficulty with aspiration and progressive worsening.

ConditionCluesDiagnosisManagement
LaryngomalaciaMost common cause of infant stridor; inspiratory, starts in the first weeks, louder supine, with feeding, crying and colds; better prone; growing wellClinical; flexible laryngoscopy shows supraglottic collapse on inspirationReassurance; usually resolves by 12–24 months; treat reflux if present; supraglottoplasty for failure to thrive, apneas or cyanosis
Bilateral choanal atresiaNeonate cyanotic at rest and during feeding, pinker when crying (mouth open); a catheter will not pass through either nostril; may be part of CHARGECT of the nasal cavityOral airway (or intubation) immediately, then surgical repair

Subglottic hemangiomaBiphasic stridor that worsens over the first months, often with a facial hemangioma in a beard distributionAirway endoscopyPropranolol
Vascular ringBiphasic stridor or wheeze, recurrent infections, feeding difficulty or dysphagiaCT or MR angiography (esophagram shows posterior indentation)Surgical division
TracheomalaciaExpiratory, low-pitched wheeze unresponsive to bronchodilators; often after esophageal atresia repairBronchoscopyUsually improves with growth
A newborn who turns blue while calm or feeding and pinks up when crying is breathing through the mouth only when crying: think of blocked choanae and put in an oral airway.

Lung masses found before or after birth

Most congenital pulmonary airway malformations and sequestrations are found on prenatal ultrasound. After birth, obtain chest CT with contrast (CT angiography) to define the lesion and any systemic arterial supply. Symptomatic lesions (distress, recurrent infection) are resected; asymptomatic lesions are often removed electively because of infection and, for some airway malformations, a small risk of malignant change, though observation is an option. Bronchogenic cysts are removed because they can enlarge, compress the airway and become infected.

Recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe

Repeated pneumonia in one location suggests a local cause: a retained foreign body, a congenital malformation (sequestration, airway malformation, bronchogenic cyst), extrinsic compression or an endobronchial lesion. Pneumonias in different lobes suggest a systemic cause: aspiration (including an H-type fistula), cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia or immunodeficiency.

Same lobe again and again: look for a structural lesion. Different lobes: look for aspiration, CF, cilia or immunity.

s23b-s-090901-s1-01.bodyHtml:
The respiratory tract starts in the fourth week as the respiratory diverticulum (lung bud), an outgrowth of the ventral wall of the foregut. Endoderm forms the epithelium of the larynx, trachea, bronchi and alveoli; the surrounding splanchnic mesoderm forms cartilage, smooth muscle, connective tissue and the visceral pleura. Longitudinal tracheoesophageal folds fuse to form the tracheoesophageal septum, dividing the foregut into the trachea in front and the esophagus behind. Incomplete or misplaced septation produces esophageal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula.

Stages of lung development

StageApproximate weeksMain eventsClinical link
Embryonic4–7Lung bud, main and lobar bronchiTracheoesophageal fistula, bronchogenic cyst, sequestration
Pseudoglandular5–17Branching of the conducting airways down to terminal bronchioles; no gas exchange possibleDiaphragmatic hernia and other causes of lung compression act here, limiting branching (pulmonary hypoplasia)
Canalicular16–26Respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts form, capillaries come close to the airway epithelium, type I and type II cells differentiateGas exchange first becomes possible: the limit of viability (about 22–24 weeks)
Saccular26–36Terminal sacs, thinning of the interstitium, rising surfactantPreterm infants born now are at risk of RDS
Alveolar36 weeks to about 8 yearsSeptation into true alveoli; most alveoli form after birthLung growth continues through early childhood

Lung growth needs space, normal fetal breathing movements and enough amniotic fluid held in the airways. Pulmonary hypoplasia follows anything that removes these: a diaphragmatic hernia, a large effusion or mass, or severe oligohydramnios (bilateral renal agenesis, obstructive uropathy, prolonged rupture of membranes), which also causes the flattened face and limb deformities of the oligohydramnios (Potter) sequence.

Surfactant

Surfactant is made by type II pneumocytes, stored in lamellar bodies and secreted onto the alveolar surface. It is mainly phospholipid, chiefly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (lecithin), plus surfactant proteins. Production begins around 20 weeks and usually becomes adequate around 34–35 weeks.

The pressure needed to keep an alveolus open follows the law of Laplace: P = 2T / r. Without surfactant, small alveoli (small r) need the highest pressure and empty into larger ones, so the lung collapses at end-expiration. Surfactant lowers surface tension, and lowers it most as the alveolus shrinks and the film is compressed, so alveoli of different sizes stay stable. It also raises compliance (less work of breathing) and keeps fluid out of the alveoli.

  • Speeds maturation: glucocorticoids (the basis of antenatal corticosteroids), thyroid hormone, labor and the catecholamine surge of birth.
  • Delays maturation: fetal hyperinsulinemia in maternal diabetes (insulin opposes the glucocorticoid effect), male sex, prematurity, cesarean birth without labor.

Fetal lung maturity was once estimated from amniotic fluid: a lecithin-to-sphingomyelin ratio above 2 or the presence of phosphatidylglycerol suggested mature lungs. These tests are rarely used now, but the ratio remains a classic concept.

Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is a surfactant deficiency disease: diffuse atelectasis, right-to-left shunting through collapsed lung, and hyaline membranes made of fibrin and cell debris lining the alveolar ducts.
The infant of a diabetic mother is large but has immature lungs: macrosomia does not mean maturity.

Complications of treating immature lungs

Supplemental oxygen and ventilation of the preterm lung can cause bronchopulmonary dysplasia (oxygen need beyond 36 weeks' postmenstrual age, with arrested alveolar development), and high oxygen also drives retinopathy of prematurity. Other problems of the very preterm infant include intraventricular hemorrhage, persistent patent ductus arteriosus and necrotizing enterocolitis.

s23b-s-090901-s1-02.bodyHtml:
Esophageal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula

Faulty division of the foregut by the tracheoesophageal septum. The most common arrangement, by far, is a blind upper esophageal pouch with a fistula from the trachea to the lower esophagus. Clues: maternal polyhydramnios (the fetus cannot swallow fluid), drooling and frothy secretions at birth, coughing, choking and cyanosis with the first feed, and a feeding tube that will not pass and coils in the upper pouch on radiograph. Air entering the stomach through the distal fistula gives a gas-filled abdomen; a gasless abdomen suggests atresia without a distal fistula. An H-type fistula without atresia presents later with coughing during feeds and recurrent aspiration pneumonia. About half have other anomalies (the VACTERL association: vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, limb).

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia

Failure of the pleuroperitoneal membranes to close lets abdominal organs enter the chest. Most defects are posterolateral (Bochdalek) and left-sided; the less common anterior retrosternal (Morgagni) hernia is often small and found later. The herniated organs compress the developing lung during the pseudoglandular stage, so the ipsilateral (and often the contralateral) lung is hypoplastic, with fewer airway branches, fewer arteries and thick-walled arterioles: persistent pulmonary hypertension follows. At birth: respiratory distress, a scaphoid abdomen, bowel sounds in the chest and heart sounds displaced to the right.

Cystic and solid malformations

LesionOriginAirway connectionBlood supplyTypical presentation
Bronchogenic cystAbnormal budding of the foregutUsually nonePulmonary/bronchialRound fluid-filled cyst in the middle mediastinum (often near the carina); wall has respiratory epithelium, cartilage, smooth muscle and glands; compression or infection
Congenital pulmonary airway malformationAbnormal branching of the distal airwayYesPulmonary arteryMulticystic lung mass on prenatal ultrasound; neonatal distress if large; later infection
Pulmonary sequestrationAccessory lung budNoSystemic artery, usually from the aortaNonfunctioning lung tissue, usually in the lower lobes; intralobar type (inside normal pleura) causes recurrent pneumonia in older children; extralobar type (own pleura, systemic venous drainage) is often found in infancy with other anomalies
Before resecting a lower-lobe lung mass in a child, image the vessels: an unexpected systemic artery from the aorta (sequestration) can bleed catastrophically if cut blind.

Disorders of cilia

Primary ciliary dyskinesia is usually autosomal recessive, caused by defects in axonemal structures, most often the dynein arms that power ciliary bending. Poor mucociliary clearance causes neonatal respiratory distress in term infants, daily wet cough from infancy, chronic rhinosinusitis, recurrent otitis media and bronchiectasis. Embryonic nodal cilia set left-right asymmetry, so about half of patients have situs inversus (Kartagener syndrome: situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis). Sperm flagella share the axoneme, so men are usually infertile with immotile sperm; women may have reduced fertility and ectopic pregnancy. Nasal nitric oxide is low.

Vascular rings

Abnormal persistence or regression of the paired aortic arches can encircle the trachea and esophagus. A double aortic arch (both fourth arches persist because the distal right dorsal aorta fails to regress) is the most common symptomatic ring; a right arch with an aberrant left subclavian artery and left ligamentum is next. Infants have noisy breathing that can be biphasic, recurrent respiratory infections, and feeding difficulty; the esophagram shows a posterior esophageal indentation.

Inspiratory stridor = extrathoracic obstruction (laryngomalacia, croup): during inspiration the pressure inside the extrathoracic airway falls below atmospheric and the floppy segment collapses inward. Expiratory noise = intrathoracic obstruction (tracheomalacia, asthma). Fixed lesions give biphasic stridor.

s23b-s-091001-ck-01.bodyHtml:
Recognizing drug-induced lung disease

Drug-induced pulmonary disease is a diagnosis of exposure, timing and exclusion. Every patient with new infiltrates, effusion or bronchospasm needs a complete medication history, including recent chemotherapy, antiarrhythmics, antibiotics taken as prophylaxis, biologics and immunotherapy, inhaled or vaped products and illicit drugs. Infection (including opportunistic organisms in immunosuppressed patients), heart failure and progression of the underlying disease must be excluded, often with CT, echocardiography and bronchoscopy with lavage.

Management principles

  1. Stop the suspected drug. This is the single most important step and is often enough for mild disease.
  2. Systemic glucocorticoids for moderate or severe pneumonitis (amiodarone, methotrexate, checkpoint inhibitors, bleomycin, acute nitrofurantoin reactions), after infection has been reasonably excluded.
  3. Do not rechallenge after significant pneumonitis from bleomycin, amiodarone or methotrexate. Document the reaction as an allergy or intolerance. Checkpoint inhibitor rechallenge after mild pneumonitis is a specialist decision.
  4. Prevention and monitoring: baseline chest radiograph and PFTs with DLCO before long-term amiodarone, and evaluation of new respiratory symptoms; serial DLCO during bleomycin therapy, with the drug stopped if DLCO falls significantly or symptoms appear; minimize FiO2 in patients who have received bleomycin; avoid nitrofurantoin as long-term prophylaxis in older adults with reduced kidney function (it is on the Beers list).

Airway emergencies and medication changes

  • ACE inhibitor angioedema: assess the airway first; stridor, voice change or tongue swelling that obstructs the view needs early, controlled intubation (often awake fiberoptic) in a setting prepared for a surgical airway. Antihistamines, glucocorticoids and epinephrine work poorly because the mediator is bradykinin, although epinephrine is often given when allergic angioedema cannot be excluded. Stop the ACE inhibitor permanently and do not substitute another ACE inhibitor. Use a drug from another class (for example a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker or thiazide); ARBs carry a small risk of recurrence and are used with caution, if at all, after angioedema.
  • ACE inhibitor cough: stop the drug; cough resolves within days to a few weeks. An ARB is an appropriate substitute because it rarely causes cough.
  • Beta-blockers in asthma or COPD: avoid nonselective agents (including ophthalmic timolol) in asthma. When a beta-blocker is strongly indicated (after myocardial infarction, for HFrEF), a cardioselective agent is generally tolerated in COPD and in stable, mild asthma with monitoring.
  • Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease: avoid aspirin and nonselective NSAIDs; acetaminophen in modest doses and COX-2 inhibitors are usually tolerated; leukotriene modifiers help; aspirin desensitization followed by daily aspirin is an option for refractory polyps.

Overdose and oxygen

  • Opioid overdose: support ventilation with a bag-valve mask first if apneic, then give naloxone (intravenous, intramuscular or intranasal), titrated to adequate breathing rather than full arousal to avoid precipitating severe withdrawal. Observe after reversal of long-acting opioids; a naloxone infusion may be needed. Offer take-home naloxone and treatment for opioid use disorder.
  • Benzodiazepine overdose: usually supportive care with airway protection; isolated benzodiazepine overdose rarely causes deep respiratory depression. Avoid flumazenil in chronic users, patients with seizure disorders or unknown co-ingestions.
  • COPD with CO2 retention: titrate oxygen to SpO2 88–92% (controlled-delivery devices such as a Venturi mask help); check a blood gas after starting oxygen. If acidosis persists, start noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation. Never withhold oxygen from a severely hypoxemic patient for fear of CO2 retention.
  • Methemoglobinemia: stop the oxidant; give methylene blue for symptoms or high levels; in G6PD deficiency, use exchange transfusion or high-dose ascorbic acid instead.

Vaping and inhalants

Suspect EVALI in a young person who vapes (especially THC products) with respiratory, gastrointestinal and constitutional symptoms and bilateral ground-glass opacities. Test for infection, including influenza and COVID-19; treat empirically for pneumonia when it cannot be excluded; give systemic glucocorticoids for significant disease; and counsel to stop vaping. Arrange follow-up imaging and spirometry.

A patient with "pneumonia that does not respond to antibiotics" who takes amiodarone, nitrofurantoin or methotrexate, or who has recently started immunotherapy, has drug-induced pneumonitis until proven otherwise.
