s23b-s-091001-s1-01.bodyHtml:
Drugs injure the respiratory system in a few recurring ways: direct cytotoxic damage to the alveolar epithelium and endothelium, immune-mediated pneumonitis, changes in airway smooth-muscle tone, suppression of the drive to breathe, and changes in hemoglobin that impair oxygen carriage. Knowing the mechanism predicts the timing, the imaging and the treatment.

Cytotoxic and immune pneumonitis

DrugMechanism and patternHigh-yield details
Bleomycin (Hodgkin lymphoma, germ cell tumors)Forms iron–oxygen complexes that generate free radicals and break DNA strands. Lung and skin have little bleomycin hydrolase, the enzyme that inactivates the drug, so they bear the brunt. Pneumonitis progresses to fibrosis.Risk rises with cumulative dose, age, renal impairment (renally cleared), thoracic radiation and high inspired oxygen. A falling DLCO is an early sign. Little myelosuppression.
AmiodaroneAn iodinated, highly lipophilic amphiphilic drug that accumulates in tissue and inhibits lysosomal phospholipases, causing phospholipidosis: foamy, lipid-laden alveolar macrophages. Patterns include chronic interstitial pneumonitis, organizing pneumonia and, rarely, acute ARDS-like injury.Risk rises with dose and duration; the very long half-life (weeks to months) means injury can progress after stopping. Also thyroid, liver, corneal, skin (blue-gray) and neuropathy effects.
MethotrexateHypersensitivity pneumonitis (lymphocytic interstitial inflammation, sometimes granulomas), independent of dose; usually in the first year.Cough, fever, dyspnea, bilateral infiltrates; peripheral eosinophilia in some. Exclude infection (including Pneumocystis) because patients are immunosuppressed.
NitrofurantoinAcute: hypersensitivity reaction within days to weeks (fever, eosinophilia, infiltrates, effusion). Chronic: interstitial fibrosis after months to years of prophylaxis.Classic patient: older woman on long-term prophylaxis for recurrent urinary infections.
Busulfan and other alkylatorsDirect alveolar epithelial injury with atypical type II pneumocytes, then fibrosis.Busulfan also causes skin hyperpigmentation and adrenal insufficiency–like features.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1, anti-CTLA-4)Loss of T-cell tolerance causes immune-related pneumonitis, often an organizing-pneumonia pattern.Can occur weeks to months into therapy; treated by holding the drug and giving glucocorticoids.

Bleomycin acts in the G2 phase of the cell cycle. The free-radical chemistry that kills tumor cells is amplified by oxygen, which is why a patient previously given bleomycin is at risk of acute lung injury when given high inspired oxygen during anesthesia years later.

Airway reactions

  • ACE inhibitors: ACE (kininase II) normally degrades bradykinin and substance P. Accumulation of these peptides in the airway sensitizes cough receptors and causes a dry cough in a substantial minority of patients; it is a class effect. Bradykinin-mediated angioedema (lips, tongue, larynx, bowel) is less common, more frequent in Black patients, can occur after years on the drug, and lacks urticaria and itch. Angiotensin receptor blockers do not block bradykinin breakdown, so cough is rare.
  • Beta-blockers: blocking β2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle removes adrenergic bronchodilation and can trigger severe bronchospasm in asthma. Nonselective agents (propranolol, nadolol, timolol eye drops) are the most dangerous; cardioselective β1 agents are safer but not perfectly selective.
  • Aspirin and nonselective NSAIDs: in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity), COX-1 inhibition lowers protective prostaglandin E2 and shunts arachidonic acid toward the 5-lipoxygenase pathway, raising cysteinyl leukotrienes that constrict airways. Selective COX-2 inhibitors are usually tolerated.
  • Cholinergic drugs (pyridostigmine, bethanechol) and organophosphate poisoning increase bronchial secretions and bronchoconstriction through muscarinic receptors.

Depressed ventilatory drive

Opioids act on μ receptors in the brainstem respiratory centres (pre-Bötzinger complex), lowering the respiratory rate and flattening the ventilatory response to CO2. Benzodiazepines, barbiturates, alcohol and gabapentinoids enhance or add to this effect. The result is hypoventilation: a high PaCO2, acute respiratory acidosis, and hypoxemia with a normal A–a gradient. Pinpoint pupils point to opioids.

Naloxone reverses opioid respiratory depression but has a shorter duration than many opioids (methadone, extended-release formulations); patients can slip back into respiratory depression after it wears off. Flumazenil can precipitate seizures in chronic benzodiazepine users or after tricyclic co-ingestion.

Oxygen as a drug

  • Pulmonary oxygen toxicity: prolonged high inspired oxygen (roughly above 60% for more than a day or two) generates reactive oxygen species that injure the alveolar epithelium and endothelium, causing tracheobronchitis, absorption atelectasis and diffuse alveolar damage. Use the lowest FiO2 that achieves the target saturation.
  • Absorption atelectasis: nitrogen normally splints alveoli open; breathing pure oxygen behind a partly obstructed airway lets the oxygen be absorbed completely, and the alveoli collapse.
  • Hyperoxia-induced hypercapnia in COPD: excessive oxygen in a patient with chronic CO2 retention raises PaCO2. The main mechanisms are worsened V/Q matching (oxygen releases hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, sending blood to poorly ventilated units and increasing dead space) and the Haldane effect (oxygenated hemoglobin binds less CO2). Loss of "hypoxic drive" contributes less than traditionally taught. Target SpO2 of about 88–92%.
  • Retinopathy of prematurity: high oxygen in preterm infants suppresses VEGF and halts retinal vessel growth; when the infant returns to room air, the avascular retina becomes hypoxic, VEGF surges and abnormal neovascularization follows. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is the pulmonary counterpart of oxygen and ventilator injury in preterm lungs.

Hemoglobin poisons

MethemoglobinemiaCarbon monoxide
CausesOxidant drugs and chemicals convert heme iron from Fe2+ to Fe3+: nitrites (amyl or butyl nitrite inhalants, "poppers"), benzocaine and other topical anesthetics, dapsone, primaquine, nitratesSmoke, faulty heaters, engine exhaust; methylene chloride (paint stripper) is metabolized to CO
PhysiologyFe3+ cannot carry O2; remaining hemes hold O2 more tightly (left shift)CO binds hemoglobin with about 200–250 times the affinity of O2; left shift; also inhibits cytochrome oxidase
PaO2NormalNormal
Pulse oximetryReads about 85% regardless of severity ("saturation gap")Falsely normal
ClueChocolate-brown blood, cyanosis unresponsive to oxygenHeadache, confusion, cherry-red color (unreliable)
TreatmentMethylene blue (reduced by NADPH–methemoglobin reductase to leukomethylene blue, which reduces Fe3+ back to Fe2+); avoid in G6PD deficiency100% oxygen; hyperbaric oxygen for severe cases

Tobacco, nicotine, vaping and inhaled drugs

  • Nicotine stimulates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (ligand-gated cation channels) in autonomic ganglia, the adrenal medulla and the brain (α4β2 subtype, dopamine release in the mesolimbic reward pathway). Acute effects: tachycardia, higher blood pressure, vasoconstriction, increased alertness. Cigarette smoke adds carbon monoxide, oxidants that inactivate α1-antitrypsin, and ciliary paralysis with goblet cell hyperplasia.
  • E-cigarette or vaping product use–associated lung injury (EVALI): acute or subacute respiratory illness with bilateral ground-glass opacities, often with gastrointestinal symptoms and fever, strongly linked to THC-containing products adulterated with vitamin E acetate. BAL may show lipid-laden macrophages. It is a diagnosis of exclusion; vaping can also trigger acute eosinophilic pneumonia.
  • Volatile inhalants (solvents, aerosol propellants, butane): sensitize the myocardium to catecholamines and can cause fatal ventricular arrhythmia ("sudden sniffing death"); toluene causes renal tubular acidosis and neurotoxicity; nitrite inhalants cause methemoglobinemia.
  • Cocaine: smoked crack causes "crack lung" (diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and infiltrates with fever and hemoptysis), barotrauma (pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum from deep inhalation and Valsalva), thermal airway injury and bronchospasm. Methamphetamine and old anorexigens (fenfluramine, aminorex) cause pulmonary arterial hypertension.
  • Drug-induced lupus (procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid) commonly produces pleuritis and pleural effusion, with anti-histone antibodies and usually without renal or CNS disease.

Irritant gases: solubility predicts the site of injury

Water solubilityExamplesSite and timing of injury
HighAmmonia, chlorine (intermediate-high), sulfur dioxideDissolve in the moist upper airway: immediate eye and throat burning, laryngeal edema; warning symptoms make people escape quickly
LowPhosgene, nitrogen dioxide, ozoneReach the alveoli with few early symptoms: pulmonary edema hours later; NO2 can cause bronchiolitis obliterans weeks later

Cyanide (smoke from burning plastics, nitroprusside in excess) blocks cytochrome oxidase: lactic acidosis with a normal PaO2 and high venous oxygen; hydroxocobalamin is the antidote in smoke inhalation.

"Normal PaO2, low measured oxygen content, and a patient who stays cyanotic on oxygen" means an abnormal hemoglobin (methemoglobin or carboxyhemoglobin). Order co-oximetry, not just a pulse oximeter or a blood gas.
